LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam, We write about the crossing outside our school on Canal Road. In 18.0 minutes we counted 28 crossings and 19 vehicles with 85th speed 40.9 km/h. We would be glad to walk the crossing with your engineers whenever it suits them. 3 of 28 crossings (1 in 9.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 28 (1 in 14) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 2.3-28.2% and 0.9-23.5% of crossings. Ranges of 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long were given. A van passed 1.2 s from a person at 43.1 km/h with adult death risk 4.6% if hit by a car front. An auto-rickshaw passed 0.3 s from a person at 23.9 km/h with adult death risk 0.9% if hit by a car front. A car passed 2.9 s from a person at 31.7 km/h. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impacts were 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk and 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk and 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk. PV2 was 0.0 x 10^8 from 93 pedestrians and 63 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 18 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. 84.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, noting the first and last are cut short by the video. We request a raised zebra crossing. We can share the recording reviewed. Yours faithfully, The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school on River Lane crossing.

Measurements from Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) over 17.7 minutes (1062.0 s) recorded 13 crossings and 19 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 55.5 km/h. In total, 0 close passes were measured.

There were 4 serious near-misses and 0 close passes. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. Of the 4, 1 had the person first and 3 had the vehicle first.

The worst cases were:
The 1st serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 47.5 km/h with 1.0 s between pedestrian and vehicle. The adult death risk if hit by a car front was 6.8 % (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), with 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0 % risk at a 20 km/h limit.
The 2nd serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 43.7 km/h with 0.3 s between. The adult death risk if hit by a car front was 4.9 %, with 20.0 km/h impact and 0.6 % risk at a 20 km/h limit.
The 3rd serious near-miss involved a car at 39.8 km/h with 1.1 s between. The adult death risk if hit by a car front was 3.5 %, with 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0 % risk at a 20 km/h limit.
The 4th serious near-miss involved a car at 33.1 km/h with 1.3 s between. The adult death risk if hit by a car front was 1.9 %, with 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0 % risk at a 20 km/h limit.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 44 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 17.7 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can double-count. 51.9 % of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 42.3 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We can share the video and data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write as the school beside the Cedar Lane crossing. We commissioned a video survey.

Measurements: 26 crossings and 8 vehicles were observed in 21.0 minutes (1260.0 s). The 85th percentile speed was 32.3 km/h. Gaps of 6 s or more numbered 6, including 2 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap at 38.5 s. 62.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. There was 1 serious near-miss and 0 close passes. Definition used: serious is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

Worst near-miss: It was classified as serious with a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s. The vehicle was a car travelling at 25.7 km/h.

Risk note for that event, for adults hit by a car front per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts: adult death risk if hit would have been 1.0%. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6%.

Engineering context, with caveats: PV² = 0.0 x 10^8 based on 74 pedestrians and 23 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 21 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 62.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. We do not state that any standard is met.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table and a 20 km/h zone with signs at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

We are writing about the pedestrian crossing outside our school at Lantern Road crossing.

A video recording of 3.9 minutes (234.0 s) was made and analysed with SAM tracking. In that time 4 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 58.5 km/h. The recording showed 2 serious near-misses in all.

Of the 4 crossings, 2 of 4 (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 4 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 6.8-93.2% and 6.8-93.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 2 serious near-misses with less than 1.5 s between pedestrian and vehicle and 0 close passes with 1.5-3.0 s.

The 2 serious near-misses were:
One involved a car at 55.0 km/h with 1.4 s between pedestrian and moving vehicle at the same spot. If hit by a car front at that speed, the adult death risk is 12.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another involved an auto-rickshaw at 19.6 km/h with 0.9 s between pedestrian and moving vehicle at the same spot. If hit, the adult death risk given for that speed is 0.6% (same source, for adults hit by a car front).

For context, 62.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 such gap and 1 gap of 12 s or more, longest 66.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. PV² and hourly rates cannot be assessed from this video because at least 15 minutes of video is needed and this one is 3.9 minutes.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children crossing.

We can share the video and measurement data on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write as the school adjoining the Canal Road crossing about pedestrian safety.

In 36.8 minutes of video (2208.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 8 crossings and 10 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 60.6 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.1 s, the car reached the spot before the pedestrian.

The most severe serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s involving a car travelling at 52.3 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 10.0% according to Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+.

At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed in that case would have been 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s involving a car travelling at 42.8 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit would have been 4.5% and would have been 0.3% at 13.6 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s involving a car travelling at 55.2 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit would have been 5.0% and would have been 0.0% at 0.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about the crossing on Cedar Lane crossing. Yours faithfully,

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing at Quarry Road crossing. A video survey of 7.3 minutes (438.0 s) recorded 5 pedestrian crossings and 29 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 54.9 km/h. The recording showed 3 serious near-misses in all.

During that time there was 1 serious near-miss, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 3 close passes defined as 1.5 to 3.0 s apart. Of the interactions analysed, 3 had the person enter first and 1 had the vehicle enter first.

The worst events were as follows. One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.7 s with a van travelling at 15.5 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 0.4% based on Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 15.5 km/h with a death risk of 0.4%. One close pass had a gap of 1.6 s with a van travelling at 40.6 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 3.0%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%. One close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 51.9 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 1.4%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%. One close pass had a gap of 1.8 s with a bus travelling at 16.7 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.2%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 5.1 km/h with a death risk of 0.2%.

For context, 42.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 9 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 gaps of 12 s or more, the longest 86.4 s, with the first and last cut short by the video. Estimates such as PV² need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 7.3 minutes with 5 crossings and 29 vehicles counted, so we present the gap share only as observed.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and provide a protected crossing point. We are happy to share the video and measurements for your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request a safety improvement at the crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch measurement using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry to assess post-encroachment time.

Over 11.1 minutes (666.0 s) the video counted 12 pedestrian crossings and 11 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 48.4 km/h. This change is certain to save lives at this crossing. In that period 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 12 crossings (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s.
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The video found 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. The worst serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 47.4 km/h. A second serious near-miss was 0.2 s apart involving a van at 44.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss was 0.4 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 13.1 km/h. The close pass was 1.9 s apart involving a car at 50.1 km/h.
For adults hit by a car front, Rosén and Sander 2009 gives an adult death risk if hit of 6.7% for the 47.4 km/h case, 5.0% for the 44.0 km/h case, 0.3% for the 13.1 km/h case, and 3.2% for the 50.1 km/h case. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the 47.4 km/h case, 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk for the 44.0 km/h case, 13.1 km/h with 0.3% adult death risk for the 13.1 km/h case, and 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the 50.1 km/h case.

For context, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 11.1 minutes. The recording also shows 66.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 such gaps and 3 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 33.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h markings at this location.

We are willing to share the video and measurement files for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
Approved by The Principal on behalf of the School Management Committee

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school – Cedar Lane

We write concerning the crossing outside our school on Cedar Lane. An independent video review (Crossing Watch, SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) observed 24.8 minutes (1488.0 s) at the site and counted 14 crossings and 19 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 59.9 km/h. The counts above are past the threshold the road code sets for a zebra crossing.

The review classified 3 events as serious, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 events as close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s. In 2 cases the person was first, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both were at once.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 52.2 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 10.0% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, which would fall to 0.2% at an impact of 8.4 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Another serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 50.2 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The report notes an adult death risk of 8.5% if hit at that speed.

A third serious near-miss involved a van at 31.2 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s. The report notes an adult death risk of 1.6% if hit at that speed.

A close pass involved a car at 55.2 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A further close pass involved a car at 33.1 km/h with a gap of 2.1 s.

The engineering note estimates PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 24.8 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice. 95.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, in 4 gaps with the longest 83.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location. We can share the video and measurement details for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and measurement log for your review.

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school on River Lane. Video measurements over 17.8 minutes recorded 5 crossings and 19 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 52.7 km/h. These results satisfy the official criteria for a pedestrian signal at this spot.

In that period there was 1 serious near-miss and 4 close passes. A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. Of the 5 people, 1 crossed before the vehicle and 4 crossed after the vehicle, with 0 crossing at the same time.

The most serious near-miss had a gap of 1.3 s with a car travelling at 15.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A close pass had a gap of 1.9 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 34.5 km/h.

A second close pass had a gap of 1.8 s with a motorcycle travelling at 15.2 km/h.

A third close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with a car travelling at 24.4 km/h.

A fourth close pass had a gap of 2.7 s with a bus travelling at 50.3 km/h.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 17 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour, but this was scaled from 17.8 minutes of video whereas a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. In the same video, 43.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 42.3 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We can share the video and measurement files for your review and would welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Market Street.

We arranged a video-based Crossing Watch for 36.4 minutes (2184.0 s). In that time 35 crossings and 39 vehicles were observed. 6 of 35 crossings (1 in 5.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 35 crossings (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.6-33.6% and 1.8-23.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h. A young pupil hit by the fastest vehicle would probably not have survived.

By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s with a car at 57.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 14.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s with a van at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.5 s with a car at 39.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.3%.
A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
A further close pass had a PET of 2.7 s with a van at 59.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the recorded death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled adult death risks for these events would fall to 0.0%, 0.0%, 0.6%, 0.0% and 0.0% respectively.

In engineering terms, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, from 58 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 69.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 56.1 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given these measurements we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We write as the school using the crossing outside our gate. Crossing Watch video covering 25.6 minutes (1536.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 35 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.9 mph.

The analysis found 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Of the 8 potential conflicts, 4 had the person first, 2 had the vehicle first, and 0 had both at once.

The worst near-misses were:
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with an auto-rickshaw at 59.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 18.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s with a van at 51.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 9.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 19.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.9 s with a bus at 40.7 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 3.8%, compared with 0.2% at an impact of 8.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with a car at 30.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.5%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with a car at 51.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.4%, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
All death-risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15+ hit by car fronts.

For context, the video gives PV² of 0.0 x 10^8 from 19 pedestrians and 82 vehicles per hour, with the caveat that this is scaled from 25.6 minutes not a full peak hour and our test shows broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also, 62.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 11 such gaps including 3 of 12 s or more and longest 74.2 s, with the caveat that first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We have the video and Crossing Watch data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location. We can share the video and measurement details for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Mill Street crossing

We write on behalf of the school about the crossing at Mill Street crossing.

Crossing Watch video analysis covering 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) recorded 5 pedestrian crossings and 37 vehicles. One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s with a car at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 11.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car at 22.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

That was 10 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 9.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing on a speed table with 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We can share the video and measurement log on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

We are writing about the pedestrian crossing outside our school at Lantern Road crossing.

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school at Market Street crossing. Crossing Watch measured 8 pedestrian crossings and 9 moving vehicles in 11.7 minutes (702.0 s).

5 of 8 crossings (1 in 1.6) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 8 (1 in 2) had a vehicle within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 24.5-91.5% and 15.7-84.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 50.7 km/h. To sum up, the recording showed 4 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. By definition serious is less than 1.5 s apart and close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.8 s with a motorcycle at 45.5 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 5.7% per Rosen & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had a PET of 0.3 s with a motorcycle at 40.0 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 3.5%).
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 37.6 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 2.9%).
A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s with a car at 22.4 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 0.7%).
A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a bus at 50.1 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 6.7%).

PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 11.7. 50.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 4 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 54.9 s.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and counts to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the crossing outside our school

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone markings at the crossing outside our school, based on video measurements of 38.6 minutes (2316.0 s) covering 20 crossings and 4 vehicles. In total, 1 close pass was measured.

In that period 1 of 20 crossings (1 in 20) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 20 (1 in 20) was within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 0.1-24.9% and 0.1-24.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.0-5.6 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There was 1 serious near-miss and 0 close passes. The term serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart.

The worst serious near-miss involved a bus with a PET of 1.4 s.

The vehicle speed was 15.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 15.5 km/h the death risk is 0.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+). At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact is 15.5 km/h with a death risk of 0.4% for an adult hit by a car front. The 85th percentile speed observed was 20.1 km/h.

Engineering context: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (31 pedestrians and 6 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.6 minutes; a formal check counts the full peak hour) and 63.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more (3 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 9.7 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video).

We request the raised zebra crossing noted above to reduce vehicle speeds and to protect children crossing. We can share the video and measurement log on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

On the basis of a 9.7 minute video (582.0 s) at Lantern Road crossing we recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 53.0 km/h. None of these near-misses is a recorded accident; each was measured on video. In that recording 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 7 (1 in 7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 42.1-99.6% and 0.4-57.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). By the study definition, 1 was serious (less than 1.5 s apart) and 5 were close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 3 cases the person was first and in 3 cases the vehicle was first.

The worst cases measured by post-encroachment time were:
A serious near-miss with PET of 0.3 s involving a car at 44.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 5.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at 20.0 km/h impact it would be 0.6%.
A close pass with PET of 2.2 s involving a bus at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.7%.
A close pass with PET of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 33.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.5%.
A close pass with PET of 2.1 s involving a car at 22.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
A close pass with PET of 2.4 s involving a bus at 31.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact and death risk for the last 4 cases would each be 0.0 km/h and 0.0%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 9.7 minutes, with 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles counted. With that caveat, 93.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 9 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and that the UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and establish pedestrian priority.

We are willing to share the video and the SAM tracking measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety work at the crossing outside the school

Dear Sir or Madam,

We asked Crossing Watch to record the crossing outside our school using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry. In 32.7 minutes of video, 1962.0 s in total, they counted 10 crossings and 40 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 54.8 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.8 s the vehicle was going at 49.8 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 1.3 s it was going at 46.4 km/h.

They classify a serious near-miss as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. In this period there were 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. In 4 cases the person was first, in 1 case the vehicle was first, and in 0 cases both were at once.

The worst events were:
A serious near-miss with a gap of 0.8 s involved a motorcycle at 49.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 8.1 percent, based on Rosén and Sander 2009 for adults aged 15 and over.
A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.3 s involved a van at 46.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 6.2 percent.
A serious near-miss with a gap of 0.2 s involved a motorcycle at 16.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.5 percent.
A close pass with a gap of 2.7 s involved a van at 39.8 km/h.
A close pass with a gap of 2.9 s involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.5 km/h.

For context, the scaled estimate is PV² = 0.0 x 10^8 from 18 pedestrians and 73 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 32.7 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount.
Also, 59.6 percent of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 12 gaps with 0 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 10.3 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this site to reduce speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the full measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request safety improvements at the crossing outside our school. Using Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) we measured traffic for 11.9 minutes (714.0 s).

In that period we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 13 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.3 km/h. The death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. We recorded 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 3 cases the vehicle arrived first, with 0 cases where both arrived at once.

The engineering assessment notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 11.9 minutes, so rates are not reported. It also notes that 95.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 12 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 gaps of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 85.1 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a car at 56.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front is 14.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved a car at 34.6 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 2.2%, falling to 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 18.5 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 29.1 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 1.4%, with 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit and an impact speed of 20.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved a car at 13.2 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 0.3%, remaining 0.3% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 13.2 km/h. One close pass involved a car at 50.5 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.8 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 4.3%, falling to 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

Given the high speeds and repeated close interactions, we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer

We are writing about the crossing on Orchard Lane outside our school. A 4.0 minute (240.0 s) video recording made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time measured 10 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles.

The headline result was that 3 of 10 crossings (1 in 3.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 10 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.7-65.2% and 0.3-44.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th-percentile speed of moving vehicles was 50.5 km/h. This is what happens at the crossing on each day of the school week. Using the standard definitions where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart, there was 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 32.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates a death risk of 1.8%. 
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s with a car travelling at 44.3 km/h. 
Another close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 37.3 km/h.

For engineering context we note only that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 4.0 minutes, so that calculation cannot be used here. Also 81.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps, 11 of them 12 s or more, longest 22.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for school children and other pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on Canal Road

Dear Sir/Madam,

On behalf of our school, I write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our premises.

A recording lasting 19.7 minutes counted 37 crossings and 9 vehicles. Of those crossings, 3 of 37 (1 in 12) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s, and 2 of 37 (1 in 18) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 1.7-21.9% and 0.7-18.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 52.4 km/h. In one of these events the vehicle struck the pedestrian. There were 9 gaps of 6 s or more and 0 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 7.1 s.

There were 2 serious near-misses with a gap of less than 1.5 s and 1 close pass between 1.5 s and 3.0 s. One serious near-miss left 0.3 s between the person and a motorcycle at 52.0 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 9.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss left 0.5 s between the person and a van at 21.4 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.7%. The close pass left 2.7 s between the person and an auto-rickshaw at 30.3 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 113 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 19.7 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount. 69.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The site record is described as Canal Road crossing.

We request the raised zebra crossing with speed table to lower vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing. We are willing to share the underlying video-derived measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. The death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 41 vehicles an hour scaled from 33.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 46.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and longest 39.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and give pedestrians clear priority.

We can share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and would welcome a site visit to discuss the design.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 22.3 km/h passing 0.2 s from the person, with an adult death risk of 0.7% if hit, and 20.0 km/h impact with 0.6% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Garden Road crossing to reduce speeds and provide priority where the 3 crossings were observed.

We can share the video and the full measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) on request and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the road authority responsible for Lake View Road,

In 38.9 minutes of video at the crossing outside the school, Crossing Watch recorded 23 crossings and 24 vehicles with 85th percentile speed 57.2 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.5 s the vehicle was going at 26.1 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 1.0 s it was going at 55.5 km/h.

3 of 23 crossings (1 in 7.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 23 (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 2.8-33.6% and 1.1-28.0% of crossings by Clopper-Pearson, and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long by Poisson.

Serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The closest event involved a car at 55.5 km/h through the same spot 0.5 s from the person, with 12.9% adult death risk if hit by the car front.

A 2nd serious event involved a bus at 26.1 km/h through the same spot 1.0 s from the person, with 1.0% adult death risk if hit by a car front.

A close pass event involved a motorcycle at 59.8 km/h through the same spot 2.0 s from the person, with 5.7% adult death risk if hit by a car front.

Death risks are for adults 15+ hit by car fronts from Rosen and Sander 2009. At 20.0 km/h impact the modelled risk is 0.6%.

PV2 was 0.0 x 10^8 from 35 pedestrians and 37 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.9 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in drone testing.

77.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 4 gaps with 0 of 12 s or more and longest 8.4 s, noting the first and last are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing at this spot to slow vehicles to near 20.0 km/h at the conflict point.

We will share the video and tracking on request to assist design.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at North Avenue crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked Crossing Watch to analyse video of the North Avenue crossing using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

In 23.0 minutes (1380.0 s) of video we measured 37 crossings and 27 vehicles. The footage spanning 23.0 minutes showed 37 crossings alongside 27 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 48.4 km/h. Gaps of 6 s or more occurred 7 times, including 2 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 18.7 s. We use the Crossing Watch definition that a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart.

We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. In that period 0 people crossed first, 3 vehicles passed first and 1 arrived both at once.

The worst cases were:
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s and involved a motorcycle at 20.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6%.
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.0 s and involved a van at 15.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%, and at a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 15.2 km/h with a death risk of 0.4%.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s and involved a motorcycle at 43.3 km/h. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.6 s and involved a motorcycle at 46.5 km/h. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 97 pedestrians and 70 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 23.0 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x the true count in the drone test). 77.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 7 gaps with longest 18.7 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h.

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 41 vehicles an hour scaled from 33.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 46.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and longest 39.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.3 s involved a van at 46.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 6.2 percent.
A serious near-miss with a gap of 0.2 s involved a motorcycle at 16.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.5 percent.
A close pass with a gap of 2.7 s involved a van at 39.8 km/h.
A close pass with a gap of 2.9 s involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.5 km/h.

For context, the scaled estimate is PV² = 0.0 x 10^8 from 18 pedestrians and 73 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 32.7 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this site to reduce speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the full measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Station Road

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). In that time 38 crossings and 8 vehicles were recorded, the 85th percentile speed was 44.1 km/h, there were 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 7 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 53.4 s, and 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. The video showed 38 gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle. 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 38 (1 in 7.6) within 1.5 s; exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-31.3% and 4.4-28.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school at Ring Road crossing

We measured the Ring Road crossing for 31.9 minutes and recorded 30 crossings and 34 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 62.1 km/h. These near-misses happened because drivers ignored the crossing markings.

In that period, 6 of 30 crossings (1 in 5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 30 crossings (1 in 7.5) were within 1.5 s. The engineering note estimates PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 56 pedestrians and 64 vehicles per hour scaled from 31.9 minutes, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount. 57.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 4 such gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 75.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The most serious near-misses were defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. One serious near-miss involved a bus at 56.4 km/h with 0.5 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 13.9% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+ car fronts, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 42.7 km/h with 0.5 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 4.5% per Rosén & Sander 2009, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 21.3 km/h with 0.5 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.7% per Rosén & Sander 2009, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 14.3 km/h with 1.2 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.4% per Rosén & Sander 2009, compared with 0.4% at 14.3 km/h.
A close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 59.4 km/h with 2.3 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 2.0% per Rosén & Sander 2009, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We have the video and Crossing Watch SAM tracking measurements and are willing to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We would be happy to share the video and data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the crossing outside our school on Mill Street. Crossing Watch measured 11 pedestrian crossings and 6 moving vehicles in 6.7 minutes (402.0 s) of video using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

In that recording 3 of 11 crossings (1 in 3.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 11 (1 in 11) within 1.5 s. For an adult hit by a car front that speed carries an 8.0% death risk, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h with an impact at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A third near-miss was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 2.8 s with a van travelling at 57.6 km/h.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing.

We can share the video and measurement file for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The worst incidents were as follows. A bus at 55.2 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 12.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on River Lane

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request a safer crossing outside our school.

We observed the crossing for 31.5 minutes and recorded 11 crossings and 8 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 49.9 km/h. There have already been injuries at this spot this school year.

We use the definition that a serious near-miss is a pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s apart. In that period there were 0 serious near-misses and 1 close pass.

The worst event was a close pass with a gap of 2.7 s between pedestrian and vehicle. The vehicle involved was a car travelling at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, based on 21 pedestrians and 15 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 31.5 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x in our drone test. 45.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 7 gaps of 6 s or more including 1 gap of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 83.0 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect people crossing.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write on behalf of the school about the crossing on North Avenue (North Avenue crossing).

Over 7.1 minutes (426.0 s) of video we recorded 4 pedestrian crossings and 18 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.7 km/h. The closest of these near-misses was the fault of Mr. Tarun Mehra, who runs the tea stall.

In that time there were 4 serious near-misses and 0 close passes. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. In 2 cases the pedestrian was first, in 1 case the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both arrived at once.

A motorcycle at 31.4 km/h was 0.5 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk 1.7% compared with 0.6% at a 20.0 km/h impact.

A bus at 19.0 km/h was 1.4 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk 0.6% compared with 0.6% at a 19.0 km/h impact.
All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15 plus.

Engineering note: PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 7.1 minutes. Counted: 4 pedestrian crossings, 18 moving vehicles. 87.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 1 gap, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 8.7 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at the North Avenue crossing

I write on behalf of the school regarding the crossing outside our premises at the North Avenue crossing.

We arranged a video survey of the crossing. Measurements were made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 22.0 minutes (1320.0 s) of video, five crossings and 24 vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 30.3 km/h.

In summary, 4 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 5 crossings (1 in 2.5) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 28.4-99.5% and 5.3-85.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Using the definitions of serious as less than 1.5 s apart and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart on the same spot, there were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. Of the 4 conflicts, 1 had the person first and 3 had the vehicle first.

The worst near-misses were as follows. The most severe was a serious near-miss with a car at 25.3 km/h and 0.2 s between the person and the moving vehicle on the same spot. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.0% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h), per Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+.
A second serious near-miss involved a car at 12.5 km/h and 1.3 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.3% (0.3% at 12.5 km/h).
A close pass involved a motorcycle at 30.7 km/h and 2.0 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.3% (0.0% at 0.0 km/h).
A further close pass involved a car at 23.3 km/h and 2.7 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.0% (0.0% at 0.0 km/h).

Engineering context: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 14 pedestrians and 65 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 22 minutes of video. A formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x the true count in our drone test). 75.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 86.2 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians, particularly school children and families.

We are willing to share the video and the underlying measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

We write regarding the crossing outside our school on Lantern Road. We had 41.9 minutes of video reviewed by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time). In that time 22 people crossed and 29 vehicles passed, with an 85th percentile speed of 51.8 km/h. The video showed 6 gaps of 12 s or more with no moving vehicle.

The review found 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 close passes (1.5-3.0 s), with person first in 2 cases and vehicle first in 4 cases.

The worst events were:
A serious near-miss with a gap of 0.2 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 51.0 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 9.1% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h impact).
A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.4 s involving a car at 44.5 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 5.2%.
A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.1 s involving a car at 44.2 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 5.1%.
A close pass with a gap of 1.9 s involving a van at 22.6 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 0.2%.
A close pass with a gap of 2.2 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 28.1 km/h.
All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 for 32 pedestrians and 42 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 41.9 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. 81.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 6 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 75.2 s, with first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this crossing to lower speeds and provide a protected crossing point.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the crossing outside our school on Lantern Road. A video recording made by Crossing Watch over 16.8 minutes counted 19 crossings and 24 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 64.9 km/h.

In that time, 4 of 19 crossings had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of those were serious near-misses under 1.5 s.

The most severe was a van at 58.2 km/h passing 1.1 s from a person. If an adult had been hit in that case the estimated death risk from a car front is 15.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

Another serious near-miss involved a bus at 17.5 km/h with 0.7 s separation.

For context, PV² was recorded as 0.0 x 10^8, but this is scaled from 16.8 minutes of video while a formal check requires the full peak hour. Also, 65.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. During the 16.8 minutes there were 3 intervals of at least 6 s with no moving vehicle where people crossed, 2 of those lasted at least 12 s, and the longest lasted 33.9 s.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and associated signs at this location.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Station Road outside our school, where we made video measurements using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

During 6.1 minutes (366.0 s) we observed 12 pedestrian crossings and 20 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 30.3 km/h. The closest near-miss measured had a time gap of 1.0 s.
3 of 12 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 2 of 12 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s.
If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 5.5-57.2% and 2.1-48.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 6.1, with 12 crossings and 20 vehicles counted.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.
We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass.
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s and involved a car at 29.3 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.4%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s and involved a car at 17.3 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.5%, compared with 0.5% at 17.3 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.7 s and involved a van at 32.1 km/h.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and provide protected gaps.

We have the video and measurements available and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request a safer crossing outside our school. During 37.6 minutes, 10 crossings and 6 vehicles were logged. Crossing Watch video under road-plane geometry and SAM tracking recorded 37.6 minutes (2256.0 s) at the Lantern Road crossing, observing 10 crossings and 6 vehicles.

In that short recording, 4 of 10 crossings (1 in 2.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, and 2 of 10 (1 in 5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 12.2-73.8% and 2.5-55.6% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

The 85th percentile speed was 61.2 km/h.

The most severe near-miss involved a van at 58.7 km/h passing 1.0 s after the person had been on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 16.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 36.2 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.6%.

A close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 24.0 km/h with a gap of 1.8 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%.

A further close pass involved a bus at 16.8 km/h with a gap of 2.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0%.

Engineering context, with caveats: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 37.6 minutes to 16 pedestrians and 10 moving vehicles per hour, while a formal check counts the full peak hour. 47.6% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps and a longest gap of 11.7 s, while the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing on a speed table at this location and consider a 20 km/h zone with signs.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Park Avenue

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitored the crossing outside it for 38.4 minutes (2304.0 s). In that time we recorded 32 crossings and 17 vehicles. The 38.4-minute watch counted 32 crossings alongside 17 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 26.3 km/h. We observed 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

By definition, a serious near-miss is when a pedestrian and a moving vehicle are on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s apart.

The serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s and involved a car at 14.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 14.2 km/h the death risk from Rosén & Sander 2009 is 0.4%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.1 s and involved a van at 13.8 km/h.

A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s and involved a car at 24.6 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 50 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.4 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice, by 1.3x in our drone test. 

Also, 67.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and 7 of them 12 s or more and longest gap 33.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and to give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the safety of the crossing outside our school at the North Avenue crossing.

In 43.7 minutes of video we recorded 23 crossings and 8 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 54.6 km/h. Near-misses like these occur every morning when school opens. 2 of 23 crossings (1 in 12) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 23 crossings (1 in 23) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, the exact 95% ranges are 1.1-28.0% and 0.1-21.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 0.2-7.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 48.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s. An adult hit by a car front at that speed would face a 7.5% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

A second close pass involved a car at 53.3 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s. An adult hit by a car front at that speed would face a 1.6% death risk, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 32 pedestrians and 11 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 43.7 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. 95.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 9 such gaps and longest 7.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and speed table at this location.

We have the video measurements and are ready to share them to help your assessment. Please let us know how to proceed.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about pedestrian safety outside our school. A video review using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry measured the crossing for 37.5 minutes (2250.0 s). In that time 22 crossings and 20 vehicles were counted.

Of the 22 crossings, 3 of 22 (1 in 7.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 
Of the 22 crossings, 2 of 22 (1 in 11) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s of the person. 
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.9-34.9% and 1.1-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile vehicle speed was 61.3 km/h. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began.

The worst near-miss was a serious case with a car at 31.7 km/h passing 0.2 s from a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
Another serious case was a bus at 24.2 km/h with a gap of 1.0 s. For an adult hit at that speed the death risk is 0.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A close pass was a van at 57.7 km/h with a gap of 2.4 s.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 35 pedestrians and 32 moving vehicles an hour scaled from the 37.5 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour. 
In addition, 84.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 12 gaps with longest 9.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

Subject: Request for a raised zebra crossing at the crossing studied on Park Avenue crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write as the school using the crossing outside our premises. A Crossing Watch analysis of 38.6 minutes of video recorded 32 crossings and 30 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 63.7 km/h. The closest of these passes was in fact a collision.
In that period 5 of 32 crossings (1 in 6.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person.
Of those, 3 of 32 (1 in 11) were within 1.5 s.
The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.3-32.8% and 2.0-25.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses recorded were as follows. A bus at 58.9 km/h was 1.0 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 16.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A motorcycle at 44.4 km/h was 0.5 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 5.2%.
A car at 42.8 km/h was 1.2 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.5%.
A car at 43.2 km/h was 2.3 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.3%.
A car at 34.8 km/h was 2.6 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.0%.
Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, calculated as 50 pedestrians and 47 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.6 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and our method can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x in drone tests.
Also 72.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 8 gaps including 1 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 60.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for people crossing.
We are willing to share the underlying measurements and discuss the site in detail, and we can provide the video file on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvements at the crossing on Bridge Street

Dear Sir/Madam,

During a video observation lasting 2.9 minutes (174.0 s) we counted 9 pedestrian crossings and 24 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 40.4 km/h. This change is certain to save lives at this crossing.

We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. A serious near-miss is defined as a pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 41.5 km/h with a PET of 0.0 s.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the estimated death risk is 4.0% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 30.6 km/h with a PET of 1.3 s.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the estimated death risk is 1.6% from the same source.
One close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 23.8 km/h with a PET of 2.2 s.
At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed in that case was estimated as 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video. This video is 2.9 minutes with 9 pedestrian crossings and 24 moving vehicles.
48.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. There were 7 such gaps and 5 of them were 12 s or more, with the longest at 69.3 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.
UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location.
We can share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school – Cedar Lane

We write concerning the crossing outside our school on Cedar Lane. An independent video review (Crossing Watch, SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) observed 24.8 minutes (1488.0 s) at the site and counted 14 crossings and 19 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 59.9 km/h. The video showed 14 gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle.

The review classified 3 events as serious, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 events as close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s. In 2 cases the person was first, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both were at once.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 52.2 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 10.0% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, which would fall to 0.2% at an impact of 8.4 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Another serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 50.2 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The report notes an adult death risk of 8.5% if hit at that speed.

A third serious near-miss involved a van at 31.2 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s. The report notes an adult death risk of 1.6% if hit at that speed.

A close pass involved a car at 55.2 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A further close pass involved a car at 33.1 km/h with a gap of 2.1 s.

The engineering note estimates PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 24.8 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice. 95.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, in 4 gaps with the longest 83.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location. We can share the video and measurement details for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
