LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school on Brook Street

We asked Crossing Watch to measure the crossing outside our school using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 36.1 minutes (2166.0 s) of video they counted 13 crossings and 26 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 km/h. The recording these figures come from lasted 36.1 minutes. There were 6 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 58.6 s.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 2 cases the vehicle arrived first.

The most serious near-miss left 0.4 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that near-miss was at 48.1 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 7.1% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss left 1.0 s between pedestrian and an auto-rickshaw.
The auto-rickshaw in that near-miss was at 28.7 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 1.3% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A close pass left 1.8 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that close pass was at 50.7 km/h.
A close pass left 2.1 s between pedestrian and a bus.
The bus in that close pass was at 33.4 km/h.
A close pass left 2.5 s between pedestrian and a van.
The van in that close pass was at 15.2 km/h.

For engineering context the scaled PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 22 pedestrians and 43 vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 36.1 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice.
43.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds.

We have retained the video measurements and can share the video files on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

On the basis of a 9.7 minute video (582.0 s) at Lantern Road crossing we recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 53.0 km/h. The first and last gaps of 6 s or more are cut short by the video. In that recording 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 7 (1 in 7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 42.1-99.6% and 0.4-57.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). By the study definition, 1 was serious (less than 1.5 s apart) and 5 were close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 3 cases the person was first and in 3 cases the vehicle was first.

The worst cases measured by post-encroachment time were:
A serious near-miss with PET of 0.3 s involving a car at 44.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 5.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at 20.0 km/h impact it would be 0.6%.
A close pass with PET of 2.2 s involving a bus at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.7%.
A close pass with PET of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 33.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.5%.
A close pass with PET of 2.1 s involving a car at 22.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
A close pass with PET of 2.4 s involving a bus at 31.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact and death risk for the last 4 cases would each be 0.0 km/h and 0.0%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 9.7 minutes, with 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles counted. With that caveat, 93.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 9 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and that the UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and establish pedestrian priority.

We are willing to share the video and the SAM tracking measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Of the timed encounters, 2 had the person first and 2 had the vehicle first.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). The most severe serious near-miss involved a car at 54.1 km/h with a time gap of 0.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 11.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss involved a van at 18.0 km/h with a time gap of 1.3 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.5%, which would remain 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 18.0 km/h. The close pass involved a car at 28.3 km/h with a time gap of 1.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h.

For context, engineering guidance notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, while this recording is only 6.6 minutes, and that 97.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more, 3 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 25.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Canal Road crossing to slow approaching traffic and give clear priority to people crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school – Cedar Lane

We write concerning the crossing outside our school on Cedar Lane. An independent video review (Crossing Watch, SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) observed 24.8 minutes (1488.0 s) at the site and counted 14 crossings and 19 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 59.9 km/h. The recording showed 2 serious near-misses in all.

The review classified 3 events as serious, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 events as close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s. In 2 cases the person was first, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both were at once.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 52.2 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 10.0% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, which would fall to 0.2% at an impact of 8.4 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Another serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 50.2 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The report notes an adult death risk of 8.5% if hit at that speed.

A third serious near-miss involved a van at 31.2 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s. The report notes an adult death risk of 1.6% if hit at that speed.

A close pass involved a car at 55.2 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A further close pass involved a car at 33.1 km/h with a gap of 2.1 s.

The engineering note estimates PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 24.8 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice. 95.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, in 4 gaps with the longest 83.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location. We can share the video and measurement details for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 mph.

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 41 vehicles an hour scaled from 33.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 46.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and longest 39.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the pedestrian crossing outside our school on River Lane. We arranged a Crossing Watch measurement of the crossing. In 7.0 minutes (420.0 s) it counted 11 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles, with an 85th-percentile speed of 54.4 km/h. By these figures the crossing already qualifies for a signal-controlled crossing. There were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes, defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Where order could be seen, 4 interactions were person-first and 1 was vehicle-first.

The most severe near-miss was 0.3 s apart with a car at 49.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled adult death risk is 7.9%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart with a bus at 48.7 km/h, with a modelled adult death risk of 7.5% if hit.

A third serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart with a car at 45.7 km/h, with a modelled adult death risk of 5.8% if hit.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 7.0, so results are indicative only. 48.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 8.8 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and give pedestrians clear priority.

We can share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and would welcome a site visit to discuss the design.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school

We measured activity at the crossing outside the school for 40.6 minutes (2436.0 s). In that time we recorded 22 crossings and 29 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 41.9 km/h. All of the pedestrians involved were children on their way home.

The most serious was a car at 40.2 km/h passing 1.0 s after the person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second event was a motorcycle at 31.3 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A third event was a van at 42.5 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A fourth event was a car at 23.0 km/h with a gap of 2.9 s.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled as 33 pedestrians and 43 moving vehicles an hour from 40.6 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. 67.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 4 such gaps including 1 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 60.8 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We can share the video and tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Another close pass involved a car at 13.9 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s. 36 people crossed while 25 vehicles passed and 12 gaps of at least 6 s were observed.
A further close pass involved a car at 24.2 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s.

For context, PV2 in the recording was 0.0 x 10^8, from 49 pedestrians and 34 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 44.1 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice, 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 56.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with high-visibility markings and curb build-outs at this crossing.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share it. Please let us know the next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The worst serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 47.4 km/h. A second serious near-miss was 0.2 s apart involving a van at 44.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss was 0.4 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 13.1 km/h. The close pass was 1.9 s apart involving a car at 50.1 km/h.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We write as the school using the crossing outside our gate. Crossing Watch video covering 25.6 minutes (1536.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 35 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.9 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.5 s the vehicle was going at 59.9 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 0.6 s it was going at 51.1 km/h.

The analysis found 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Of the 8 potential conflicts, 4 had the person first, 2 had the vehicle first, and 0 had both at once.

The worst near-misses were:
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with an auto-rickshaw at 59.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 18.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s with a van at 51.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 9.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 19.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.9 s with a bus at 40.7 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 3.8%, compared with 0.2% at an impact of 8.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with a car at 30.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.5%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with a car at 51.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.4%, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
All death-risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15+ hit by car fronts.

For context, the video gives PV² of 0.0 x 10^8 from 19 pedestrians and 82 vehicles per hour, with the caveat that this is scaled from 25.6 minutes not a full peak hour and our test shows broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also, 62.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 11 such gaps including 3 of 12 s or more and longest 74.2 s, with the caveat that first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We have the video and Crossing Watch data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The review found 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass of 1.5 to 3.0 s. In that period 3 crossings were person-first and 2 were vehicle-first.

One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 49.0 km/h with 1.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle.

For an adult hit by a car front at 49.0 km/h the death risk is 7.7% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

Another serious near-miss involved a car at 47.5 km/h with 0.5 s between pedestrian and vehicle.

For an adult hit by a car front at 47.5 km/h the death risk is 6.7%.

A further serious near-miss involved a van at 34.3 km/h with 1.0 s between pedestrian and vehicle.

For an adult hit by a car front at 34.3 km/h the death risk is 2.2%.

Another serious near-miss involved a car at 21.8 km/h with 0.5 s between pedestrian and vehicle.

For an adult hit by a car front at 21.8 km/h the death risk is 0.7%.

One close pass involved a bus at 38.3 km/h with 1.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle.

For an adult hit by a car front at 38.3 km/h the death risk is 1.4%.

Engineering notes from the same video show PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 57 pedestrians and 19 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 37.7 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x the true count in a drone test. The video also showed 93.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 12 such gaps and 5 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 13.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and provide priority for people crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about the River Lane crossing outside our school. In 42.9 minutes (2574.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 23 crossings and 25 vehicles.

Overall 5 of 23 crossings (1 in 4.6) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s, and 1 of 23 (1 in 23) within 1.5 s. The most serious near-miss was 0.7 s apart with a car at 57.6 km/h. For adults hit by a car front Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates 15.3% death risk if hit at that speed, and 0.0% death risk with impact at 0.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit.

A close pass was 1.7 s apart with a van at 42.0 km/h. For adults hit by a car front the estimate is 2.7% death risk if hit.

A close pass was 1.9 s apart with a bus at 41.2 km/h. For adults hit by a car front the estimate is 1.4% death risk if hit.

A close pass was 2.0 s apart with a car at 26.2 km/h. For adults hit by a car front the estimate is 0.2% death risk if hit.

A close pass was 2.6 s apart with a van at 28.6 km/h. For adults hit by a car front the estimate is 0.0% death risk if hit.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 32 pedestrians and 35 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 42.9 minutes of video. A formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in our drone test.

Also 68.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a raised table at this location to slow approaching speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the video and measurements and to meet on site.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the crossing on School Lane outside our school.

We measured traffic for 11.9 minutes and counted 7 pedestrian crossings and 40 moving vehicles.

The 85th percentile speed was 42.3 km/h. All of the pedestrians involved were children on their way home.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses and 3 close passes.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 34.8 km/h with 0.7 s between road users, with a 2.3% adult death risk if hit by a car front, which would fall to 0.6% adult death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Another serious near-miss involved a van at 27.0 km/h with 0.4 s between road users, with a 1.1% adult death risk if hit by a car front, which would fall to 0.6% adult death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

A third serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 24.4 km/h with 1.3 s between road users, with a 0.9% adult death risk if hit by a car front, which would fall to 0.5% adult death risk at an impact of 17.7 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 11.9 minutes.

Only 40.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to reduce speeds and provide a safe crossing point.

We are willing to share the video of the crossing for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We write concerning the crossing on Garden Road outside our school.

In 17.7 minutes of video we recorded 14 crossings and 6 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 62.3 km/h. Of the 14 crossings, 2 of 14 (1 in 7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 14 (1 in 14) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical the exact 95% ranges are 1.8-42.8% and 0.2-33.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s between the person and a car; the car was travelling at 56.5 km/h, which carries an adult death risk of 14.0% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed in that event would have been 14.3 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.4%. A second close pass had a gap of 2.6 s with a motorcycle at 17.5 km/h.

On engineering measures, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 for 47 pedestrians and 20 vehicles per hour, but this is scaled from only 17.7 minutes and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). Also 68.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and 7 of 12 s or more and the longest 84.3 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this crossing. We would be happy to share the video and the measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Bridge Street crossing

Our school has reviewed video measurements of the Bridge Street crossing undertaken with SAM tracking and road-plane geometry with post-encroachment time.

In 22.7 minutes (1362.0 s) there were 9 crossings and 29 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 50.1 km/h.

Of the 9 crossings, 5 of 9 (1 in 1.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 9 (1 in 3) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 21.2-86.3% and 7.5-70.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

By definition, serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s. There were 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes.

The most severe serious near-miss had a gap of 0.4 s with a motorcycle measured at 44.5 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 5.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact would be 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

A second serious near-miss had a gap of 1.0 s with a van measured at 28.0 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 1.2%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact would be 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a gap of 0.7 s with a car measured at 15.2 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.4%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact would be 15.2 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.4%.

One close pass had a gap of 1.6 s with a car measured at 44.0 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 4.0%.

The other close pass had a gap of 2.4 s with a car measured at 37.7 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.0%.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (24 pedestrians and 77 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 22.7 minutes of video, but a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x). 94.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and longest 60.2 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at the Bridge Street crossing.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Road Authority,

We write about safety at the Mill Street crossing outside our school.

In 5.3 minutes of video (318.0 s) we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 17 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 49.8 km/h. In total, 3 close passes were measured. There were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes by the definition of less than 1.5 s for serious and 1.5-3.0 s for close pass, with 3 events where the person was first and 1 where the vehicle was first and 0 where both arrived at once.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this video is 5.3 minutes with 6 crossings and 17 vehicles counted. 71.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 70.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

The worst events recorded were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a bus at 43.0 km/h with a time gap of 0.9 s, where the death risk for an adult hit by a car front would have been 4.6% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts. A second serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 34.5 km/h with a time gap of 1.1 s, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 2.2%. A close pass involved a car at 43.5 km/h with a time gap of 1.5 s, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 4.8%. Another close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 26.9 km/h with a time gap of 2.6 s, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 0.0%.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data to help your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

On the basis of a 9.7 minute video (582.0 s) at Lantern Road crossing we recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 53.0 km/h. In that recording 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 7 (1 in 7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 42.1-99.6% and 0.4-57.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). By the study definition, 1 was serious (less than 1.5 s apart) and 5 were close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 3 cases the person was first and in 3 cases the vehicle was first.

The worst cases measured by post-encroachment time were:
A serious near-miss with PET of 0.3 s involving a car at 44.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 5.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at 20.0 km/h impact it would be 0.6%.
A close pass with PET of 2.2 s involving a bus at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.7%.
A close pass with PET of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 33.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.5%.
A close pass with PET of 2.1 s involving a car at 22.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
A close pass with PET of 2.4 s involving a bus at 31.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact and death risk for the last 4 cases would each be 0.0 km/h and 0.0%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 9.7 minutes, with 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles counted. With that caveat, 93.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 9 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and that the UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and establish pedestrian priority. Children walking to the nearby school are at high risk of being killed at this crossing every week.

We are willing to share the video and the SAM tracking measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety at Brook Street crossing

We write concerning the Brook Street crossing outside our school. A Crossing Watch analysis of 8.6 minutes (516.0 s) of video recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 16 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow traffic and give pedestrians priority.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at Cedar Lane crossing

We measured the Cedar Lane crossing for 36.7 minutes (2202.0 s). In that time 37 people crossed and 16 vehicles passed. The 85th percentile speed was 62.8 mph.

We recorded 1 serious near-miss (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 5 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 1 case the person was first, in 5 cases the vehicle was first, and in 0 cases both were at once.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s and involved a car travelling at 59.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 17.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6%.

A second event was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 2.0 s and a car travelling at 56.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 4.1%.

A third event was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 1.5 s and a car travelling at 33.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 2.0%.

A fourth event was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 1.6 s and a motorcycle travelling at 30.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 1.2%.

A fifth event was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s and a motorcycle travelling at 48.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (60 pedestrians and 26 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.7 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test). In the video 93.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed (10 gaps, 10 of them 12 s or more, longest 65.8 s, first and last are cut short by the video).

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measurements.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school

We measured activity at the crossing outside the school for 40.6 minutes (2436.0 s). In that time we recorded 22 crossings and 29 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 41.9 km/h. With this measure in place there will be no more fatalities here.

Of the 22 crossings, 4 (1 in 5.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, and 1 of 22 (1 in 22) was within 1.5 s. We class serious as less than 1.5 s apart and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s. There was 1 serious near-miss and 3 close passes.

The most serious was a car at 40.2 km/h passing 1.0 s after the person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second event was a motorcycle at 31.3 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A third event was a van at 42.5 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A fourth event was a car at 23.0 km/h with a gap of 2.9 s.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled as 33 pedestrians and 43 moving vehicles an hour from 40.6 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. 67.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 4 such gaps including 1 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 60.8 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We can share the video and tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

A 3.8 minute recording (228.0 s) counted 10 pedestrian crossings and 24 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 28.8 km/h. We are happy to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school on Brook Street

We asked Crossing Watch to measure the crossing outside our school using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 36.1 minutes (2166.0 s) of video they counted 13 crossings and 26 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 km/h. Every person in these near-misses was a pupil of our school. There were 6 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 58.6 s.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 2 cases the vehicle arrived first.

The most serious near-miss left 0.4 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that near-miss was at 48.1 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 7.1% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss left 1.0 s between pedestrian and an auto-rickshaw.
The auto-rickshaw in that near-miss was at 28.7 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 1.3% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A close pass left 1.8 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that close pass was at 50.7 km/h.
A close pass left 2.1 s between pedestrian and a bus.
The bus in that close pass was at 33.4 km/h.
A close pass left 2.5 s between pedestrian and a van.
The van in that close pass was at 15.2 km/h.

For engineering context the scaled PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 22 pedestrians and 43 vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 36.1 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice.
43.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds.

We have retained the video measurements and can share the video files on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school on Brook Street

We asked Crossing Watch to measure the crossing outside our school using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. The most serious near-miss left 0.4 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that near-miss was at 48.1 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 7.1% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A close pass left 2.5 s between pedestrian and a van.
The van in that close pass was at 15.2 km/h.

For engineering context the scaled PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 22 pedestrians and 43 vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 36.1 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds.

We have retained the video measurements and can share the video files on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The auto-rickshaw in that near-miss was at 28.7 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 1.3% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about pedestrian safety outside our school. A video review using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry measured the crossing for 37.5 minutes (2250.0 s). In that time 22 crossings and 20 vehicles were counted.

Of the 22 crossings, 3 of 22 (1 in 7.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 
Of the 22 crossings, 2 of 22 (1 in 11) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s of the person. 
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.9-34.9% and 1.1-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile vehicle speed was 61.3 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.2 s the vehicle was going at 24.2 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 1.0 s it was going at 31.7 km/h.

The worst near-miss was a serious case with a car at 31.7 km/h passing 0.2 s from a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
Another serious case was a bus at 24.2 km/h with a gap of 1.0 s. For an adult hit at that speed the death risk is 0.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A close pass was a van at 57.7 km/h with a gap of 2.4 s.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 35 pedestrians and 32 moving vehicles an hour scaled from the 37.5 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour. 
In addition, 84.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 12 gaps with longest 9.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety of the pedestrian crossing on Cedar Lane

We write to request a raised zebra crossing outside our school.

Crossing Watch measurements over 4.7 minutes recorded 12 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 54.8 km/h.

2 serious near-misses and 4 close passes were recorded. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass is defined as 1.5 to 3.0 s apart.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 40.3 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 3.7%.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 35.1 km/h with a gap of 0.2 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 2.3%.

One close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 50.2 km/h with a gap of 1.8 s.

One close pass involved a car at 34.6 km/h with a gap of 1.9 s.

One close pass involved a van at 21.9 km/h with a gap of 2.4 s.

All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen and Sander 2009.

Engineering context with caveats: PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 4.7 minutes. 61.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 7 gaps, 7 of them 12 s or more, longest 19.4 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We therefore request that you provide a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children and adults crossing. These results prove the location meets the legal warrant for a signalised crossing.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The site record is described as Canal Road crossing.

We request the raised zebra crossing with speed table to lower vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing. We are willing to share the underlying video-derived measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school

We measured activity at the crossing outside the school for 40.6 minutes (2436.0 s). In that time we recorded 22 crossings and 29 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 41.9 km/h. The drivers involved were speeding because they were late for work.

Of the 22 crossings, 4 (1 in 5.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, and 1 of 22 (1 in 22) was within 1.5 s. We class serious as less than 1.5 s apart and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s. There was 1 serious near-miss and 3 close passes.

The most serious was a car at 40.2 km/h passing 1.0 s after the person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second event was a motorcycle at 31.3 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A third event was a van at 42.5 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A fourth event was a car at 23.0 km/h with a gap of 2.9 s.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled as 33 pedestrians and 43 moving vehicles an hour from 40.6 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. 67.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 4 such gaps including 1 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 60.8 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We can share the video and tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write to request a safety improvement at the crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch measurement using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry to assess post-encroachment time.

Over 11.1 minutes (666.0 s) the video counted 12 pedestrian crossings and 11 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 48.4 km/h. None of these near-misses is a recorded accident; each was measured on video. In that period 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 12 crossings (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s.
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The video found 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. The worst serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 47.4 km/h. A second serious near-miss was 0.2 s apart involving a van at 44.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss was 0.4 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 13.1 km/h. The close pass was 1.9 s apart involving a car at 50.1 km/h.
For adults hit by a car front, Rosén and Sander 2009 gives an adult death risk if hit of 6.7% for the 47.4 km/h case, 5.0% for the 44.0 km/h case, 0.3% for the 13.1 km/h case, and 3.2% for the 50.1 km/h case. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the 47.4 km/h case, 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk for the 44.0 km/h case, 13.1 km/h with 0.3% adult death risk for the 13.1 km/h case, and 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the 50.1 km/h case.

For context, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 11.1 minutes. The recording also shows 66.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 such gaps and 3 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 33.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h markings at this location.

We are willing to share the video and measurement files for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Lantern Road

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the crossing outside our school on Lantern Road. We had 41.9 minutes of video reviewed by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time). In that time 22 people crossed and 29 vehicles passed, with an 85th percentile speed of 51.8 km/h. 22 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video.

The review found 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 close passes (1.5-3.0 s), with person first in 2 cases and vehicle first in 4 cases.

The worst events were:
A serious near-miss with a gap of 0.2 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 51.0 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 9.1% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h impact).
A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.4 s involving a car at 44.5 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 5.2%.
A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.1 s involving a car at 44.2 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 5.1%.
A close pass with a gap of 1.9 s involving a van at 22.6 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 0.2%.
A close pass with a gap of 2.2 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 28.1 km/h.
All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 for 32 pedestrians and 42 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 41.9 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. 81.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 6 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 75.2 s, with first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this crossing to lower speeds and provide a protected crossing point.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Market Street.

We arranged a video-based Crossing Watch for 36.4 minutes (2184.0 s). In that time 35 crossings and 39 vehicles were observed. 6 of 35 crossings (1 in 5.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 35 crossings (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.6-33.6% and 1.8-23.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h.

By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s with a car at 57.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 14.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s with a van at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.5 s with a car at 39.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.3%.
A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
A further close pass had a PET of 2.7 s with a van at 59.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the recorded death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled adult death risks for these events would fall to 0.0%, 0.0%, 0.6%, 0.0% and 0.0% respectively.

In engineering terms, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, from 58 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 69.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 56.1 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given these measurements we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer

We are writing about the crossing on Orchard Lane outside our school. A 4.0 minute (240.0 s) video recording made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time measured 10 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles.

The headline result was that 3 of 10 crossings (1 in 3.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 10 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.7-65.2% and 0.3-44.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th-percentile speed of moving vehicles was 50.5 km/h. 10 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video. Using the standard definitions where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart, there was 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 32.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates a death risk of 1.8%. 
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s with a car travelling at 44.3 km/h. 
Another close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 37.3 km/h.

For engineering context we note only that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 4.0 minutes, so that calculation cannot be used here. Also 81.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps, 11 of them 12 s or more, longest 22.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for school children and other pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Hill View Road crossing. A Crossing Watch video of 1.8 minutes (108.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 48 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 44.0 mph.

Engineering assessment is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 1.8. One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 36.8 km/h with 1.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 35.9 km/h with 0.2 s between users.

A third serious near-miss involved a car at 22.5 km/h with 0.1 s between users.

A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 19.8 km/h with 1.0 s between users.

One close pass involved a car at 20.5 km/h with 2.0 s between users.

For adults hit by a car front, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates adult death risk rises with impact speed. At these speeds adult risk was 2.7% at 36.8 km/h, 2.5% at 35.9 km/h, 0.8% at 22.5 km/h and 0.6% at 19.8 km/h. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed and adult death risk would be lower, for example 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to slow vehicles and provide protected priority for pedestrians at this school crossing.

We are happy to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. These near-misses happened because drivers ignored the crossing markings.

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 41 vehicles an hour scaled from 33.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 46.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and longest 39.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Station Road

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). In that time 38 crossings and 8 vehicles were recorded, the 85th percentile speed was 44.1 km/h, there were 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 7 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 53.4 s, and 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. The video showed 7 gaps of 12 s or more with no moving vehicle. 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 38 (1 in 7.6) within 1.5 s; exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-31.3% and 4.4-28.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school on River Lane. Video measurements over 17.8 minutes recorded 5 crossings and 19 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 52.7 km/h. The closest of these passes was in fact a collision.

In that period there was 1 serious near-miss and 4 close passes. A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. Of the 5 people, 1 crossed before the vehicle and 4 crossed after the vehicle, with 0 crossing at the same time.

The most serious near-miss had a gap of 1.3 s with a car travelling at 15.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A close pass had a gap of 1.9 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 34.5 km/h.

A second close pass had a gap of 1.8 s with a motorcycle travelling at 15.2 km/h.

A third close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with a car travelling at 24.4 km/h.

A fourth close pass had a gap of 2.7 s with a bus travelling at 50.3 km/h.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 17 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour, but this was scaled from 17.8 minutes of video whereas a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. In the same video, 43.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 42.3 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We can share the video and measurement files for your review and would welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school on Lake View Road

We write regarding the crossing outside our school on Lake View Road. A Crossing Watch review of 21.4 minutes of video (1284.0 s) recorded 11 crossings and 22 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 50.9 km/h. The recording showed 1 serious near-miss in all.

The review found 4 of 11 crossings (1 in 2.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 11 (1 in 3.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 10.9-69.2% and 6.0-61.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 3 serious near-misses and 1 close pass as defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1.5-3.0 s respectively.

The worst near-misses were:
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s with a car at 51.3 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 9.2% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s with an auto-rickshaw at 42.7 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.5%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s with an auto-rickshaw at 37.7 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 2.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s with a car at 51.5 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 6.1%.

In engineering terms, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 31 pedestrians and 62 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 21.4 minutes of video, and a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice as 1.3x the true count in our drone test. Also 43.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more and longest 17.6 s, with the caveat that the first and last are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing on Park Avenue outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school arranged a Crossing Watch on the crossing on Park Avenue. In 6.9 minutes (414.0 s) we counted 7 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 47.9 km/h. To sum up, the recording showed 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass.

We record a serious near-miss as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart. We observed 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass, with 1 case where the person was first and 2 cases where the vehicle was first.

One serious near-miss involved a van at 45.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 5.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 44.2 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 5.1% (same source).

A close pass involved a car at 22.1 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s.

We note that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 6.9 minutes. In this short sample 50.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 7 gaps of 6 s or more and 6 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 79.0 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We can share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir / Madam,

Re: Safety at Lake View Road crossing

In a Crossing Watch video of 33.6 minutes (2016.0 s) we measured 6 pedestrian crossings and 33 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 43.6 km/h. Had a child been struck, the impact would almost certainly have been fatal.

5 of 6 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 6 (1 in 2) were within 1.5 s.
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 35.9-99.6% and 11.8-88.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes were:
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s and involved a car at 35.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 2.3% for a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s and involved a car at 33.4 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 2.0% for a car front, falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s and involved a car at 17.8 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.5% for a car front, remaining 0.5% at an impact of 17.8 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s and involved a car at 22.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.1% at an impact of 3.3 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.3 s and involved a bus at 44.8 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, but this is scaled from only 33.6 minutes of video and a formal check counts the full peak hour with caveats about broken tracks.
73.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 8 of 12 s or more and longest gap 76.8 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority.

We can share the full video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We write as the school using the crossing outside our gate. Crossing Watch video covering 25.6 minutes (1536.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 35 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.9 km/h.

The analysis found 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Of the 8 potential conflicts, 4 had the person first, 2 had the vehicle first, and 0 had both at once.

The worst near-misses were:
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with an auto-rickshaw at 59.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 18.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s with a van at 51.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 9.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 19.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.9 s with a bus at 40.7 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 3.8%, compared with 0.2% at an impact of 8.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with a car at 30.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.5%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with a car at 51.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.4%, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
All death-risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15+ hit by car fronts.

For context, the video gives PV² of 0.0 x 10^8 from 19 pedestrians and 82 vehicles per hour, with the caveat that this is scaled from 25.6 minutes not a full peak hour and our test shows broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also, 62.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 11 such gaps including 3 of 12 s or more and longest 74.2 s, with the caveat that first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We have the video and Crossing Watch data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Canal Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school arranged a video review of Canal Road crossing. In 44.9 minutes (2694.0 s) we observed 39 crossings and 7 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 30.4 km/h. Overall, 1 of 39 crossings (1 in 39) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 1 of 39 (1 in 39) within 1.5 s, defined as serious. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 0.1-13.5% and 0.1-13.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.0-5.6 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst serious near-miss involved a van. The time gap between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot was 0.4 s. The vehicle speed was 25.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+). At 20.0 km/h the death risk would be 0.6%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, based on 52 pedestrians and 9 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 44.9 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and counts in our method can be 1.3x the true count in our drone test. Also, 42.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 1 gap, longest 10.6 s, with first and last cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and improve pedestrian priority.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for verification.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety at North Avenue crossing

We are writing to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our school.

Measurements from a Crossing Watch survey over 6.9 minutes (414.0 s) recorded 11 pedestrian crossings and 7 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 50.5 km/h. We would be glad to walk the crossing with your engineers whenever it suits them.

In that short period there was 1 serious near-miss (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s apart).

The most serious event had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s and involved a car at 16.9 km/h.

A separate close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s and involved a motorcycle at 44.4 km/h.

A separate close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.6 s and involved a bus at 17.6 km/h.

For the car event, published figures for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+) give an adult death risk if hit of 0.5% at 16.9 km/h.

Engineering context carries caveats: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 6.9 minutes, and 81.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more (4 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 41.7 s) with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that the road authority install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and protect children crossing.

We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the road authority responsible for Lake View Road,

In 38.9 minutes of video at the crossing outside the school, Crossing Watch recorded 23 crossings and 24 vehicles with 85th percentile speed 57.2 km/h. Had a child been struck, the impact would almost certainly have been fatal.

3 of 23 crossings (1 in 7.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 23 (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 2.8-33.6% and 1.1-28.0% of crossings by Clopper-Pearson, and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long by Poisson.

Serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The closest event involved a car at 55.5 km/h through the same spot 0.5 s from the person, with 12.9% adult death risk if hit by the car front.

A 2nd serious event involved a bus at 26.1 km/h through the same spot 1.0 s from the person, with 1.0% adult death risk if hit by a car front.

A close pass event involved a motorcycle at 59.8 km/h through the same spot 2.0 s from the person, with 5.7% adult death risk if hit by a car front.

Death risks are for adults 15+ hit by car fronts from Rosen and Sander 2009. At 20.0 km/h impact the modelled risk is 0.6%.

PV2 was 0.0 x 10^8 from 35 pedestrians and 37 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.9 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in drone testing.

77.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 4 gaps with 0 of 12 s or more and longest 8.4 s, noting the first and last are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing at this spot to slow vehicles to near 20.0 km/h at the conflict point.

We will share the video and tracking on request to assist design.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 42 pedestrians and 69 vehicles an hour scaled from 20.1 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also 95.1% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, from 1 such gap, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We can share the video for your review and welcome a site inspection.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We are writing about the pedestrian crossing outside our school on River Lane. We arranged a Crossing Watch measurement of the crossing. The most severe near-miss was 0.3 s apart with a car at 49.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled adult death risk is 7.9%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and give pedestrians clear priority.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at North Avenue crossing

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at North Avenue crossing. Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry) for 18.2 minutes recorded 40 crossings and 28 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 45.1 km/h. The closest near-miss measured had a time gap of 1.4 s.

In that period 6 of 40 crossings (1 in 6.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 40 crossings (1 in 10) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 5.7-29.8% and 2.8-23.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 with 132 pedestrians and 92 moving vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 18.2 minutes while a formal check counts the full peak hour. 62.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The worst near-misses illustrate the risk. One serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 38.7 km/h with 1.3 s between road users. For an adult hit by a car front at 38.7 km/h the estimated death risk is 3.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk.

One serious near-miss involved a van at 32.9 km/h with 0.1 s between road users. For an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.9%.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 31.6 km/h with 0.7 s between road users. For an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.7%.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 26.9 km/h with 1.4 s between road users. For an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.1%.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 3.3 km/h with 0.1% adult death risk.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds to the 20 km/h limit. We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce speeds at the crossing.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
