Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school on River Lane. Video measurements over 17.8 minutes recorded 5 crossings and 19 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 52.7 km/h. The closest near-miss measured had a time gap of 1.8 s.

In that period there was 1 serious near-miss and 4 close passes. A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. Of the 5 people, 1 crossed before the vehicle and 4 crossed after the vehicle, with 0 crossing at the same time.

The most serious near-miss had a gap of 1.3 s with a car travelling at 15.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A close pass had a gap of 1.9 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 34.5 km/h.

A second close pass had a gap of 1.8 s with a motorcycle travelling at 15.2 km/h.

A third close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with a car travelling at 24.4 km/h.

A fourth close pass had a gap of 2.7 s with a bus travelling at 50.3 km/h.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 17 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour, but this was scaled from 17.8 minutes of video whereas a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. In the same video, 43.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 42.3 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We can share the video and measurement files for your review and would welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Garden Road outside our school. A Crossing Watch review of 174.0 s of video (2.9 minutes) counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 39 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.9 km/h. Parents see the same danger here at each school dismissal.

There were 3 serious near-misses defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 3 close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. Of the 6 crossings, 1 had the person enter first and 5 had the vehicle enter first.

The worst events were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a bus at 56.2 km/h with a gap of 0.4 s and an adult death risk of 13.7% if hit by a car front, which would be 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
Another serious near-miss involved a van at 49.0 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s and an adult death risk of 7.7% if hit by a car front, which would be 0.3% at an impact of 13.5 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
A further serious near-miss involved a car at 24.3 km/h with a gap of 0.5 s and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit by a car front, which would be 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
One close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 29.9 km/h with a gap of 1.9 s and an adult death risk of 0.5% if hit by a car front.
Another close pass involved a car at 15.0 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s and an adult death risk of 0.0% if hit by a car front.
Risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen & Sander 2009.

For context, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 2.9. 82.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps and 4 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.0 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We hold the video and measurement data and are willing to share them on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Market Street crossing

Dear Sir or Madam,

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at Market Street crossing following video measurements of pedestrian risk.

What was measured: Over 4.6 minutes (276.0 s) we recorded 6 pedestrian crossings and 33 moving vehicles. 6 of 6 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 5 of 6 (1 in 1.2) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 54.1% to 100.0% and 35.9% to 99.6% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2 to 13.1 and 1.6 to 11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 55.5 km/h. At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 1.2 s apart. There was 1 person-first and 5 vehicle-first interactions, with 0 both-at-once, comprising 5 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5 s to 3.0 s).

Worst near-misses (serious):
A bus at 51.3 km/h was 1.2 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 9.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.
A car at 51.1 km/h was 0.8 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 9.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.
A car at 46.3 km/h was 0.3 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 6.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 20.0 km/h.
An auto-rickshaw at 44.2 km/h was 0.7 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 5.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 18.8 km/h.
A bus at 42.7 km/h was 1.4 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 4.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.

Engineering context, briefly and with caveats: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, but this recording is 4.6 minutes with 6 crossings and 33 vehicles, so estimates are limited. 41.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 54.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4 s to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10 s to 12 s or longer.

We request that you install the raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We offer to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Lantern Road

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the crossing outside our school on Lantern Road. We had 41.9 minutes of video reviewed by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time). In that time 22 people crossed and 29 vehicles passed, with an 85th percentile speed of 51.8 km/h.

The review found 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 close passes (1.5-3.0 s), with person first in 2 cases and vehicle first in 4 cases.

The worst events were:
A serious near-miss with a gap of 0.2 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 51.0 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 9.1% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h impact).
A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.4 s involving a car at 44.5 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 5.2%.
A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.1 s involving a car at 44.2 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 5.1%.
A close pass with a gap of 1.9 s involving a van at 22.6 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 0.2%.

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on Hill View Road

We measured traffic at the crossing on Hill View Road for 39.3 minutes. In that time we observed 34 crossings and 21 vehicles. The 85th-percentile speed was 60.0 km/h. We would be glad to walk the crossing with your engineers whenever it suits them.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for children crossing. We are willing to share the video and measurement file for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Park Avenue

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitored the crossing outside it for 38.4 minutes (2304.0 s). In that time we recorded 32 crossings and 17 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 26.3 km/h. Traffic has grown sharply compared with last term. We observed 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

By definition, a serious near-miss is when a pedestrian and a moving vehicle are on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s apart.

The serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s and involved a car at 14.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 14.2 km/h the death risk from Rosén & Sander 2009 is 0.4%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.1 s and involved a van at 13.8 km/h.

A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s and involved a car at 24.6 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 50 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.4 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice, by 1.3x in our drone test. 

Also, 67.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and 7 of them 12 s or more and longest gap 33.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and to give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

We have the video and measurements and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A second serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart with a bus at 48.7 km/h, with a modelled adult death risk of 7.5% if hit.

A third serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart with a car at 45.7 km/h, with a modelled adult death risk of 5.8% if hit.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 7.0, so results are indicative only. 48.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 8.8 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and give pedestrians clear priority.

We can share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and would welcome a site visit to discuss the design.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Brook Street crossing

We write concerning the Brook Street crossing outside our school. A 20.3 minute video (1218.0 s) recorded 38 crossings and 45 vehicles. In that recording, 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 3 of 38 (1 in 13) were within 1.5 s.

If this recording is typical, the exact 95% ranges are 6.0-31.3% and 1.7-21.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 close passes (1.5-3.0 s) included:

1 serious case had a gap of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 49.8 km/h. A parent was injured here by a passing motorcycle earlier this year. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 8.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

1 serious case had a gap of 0.0 s with a car travelling at 36.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.7%.

1 serious case had a gap of 0.4 s with a car travelling at 21.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.7%.

1 close pass had a gap of 1.7 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 54.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 7.7%.

1 close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 25.7 km/h.

At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact speeds and adult death risks would be 0.0 km/h and 0.0%, 20.0 km/h and 0.6%, 20.0 km/h and 0.6%, 0.0 km/h and 0.0%, and 0.0 km/h and 0.0% respectively.

The 85th percentile speed was 56.3 km/h. For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (112 pedestrians and 133 moving vehicles an hour), but this is scaled from 20.3 minutes of video and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 70.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed (3 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 7.0 s), but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.

We will share the full video and tracking data on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

On behalf of our school I write about the River Lane crossing.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We will share the video and measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Park Avenue

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitored the crossing outside it for 38.4 minutes (2304.0 s). In that time we recorded 32 crossings and 17 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 26.3 km/h. The recording these figures come from lasted 38.4 minutes. We observed 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

By definition, a serious near-miss is when a pedestrian and a moving vehicle are on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s apart.

The serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s and involved a car at 14.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 14.2 km/h the death risk from Rosén & Sander 2009 is 0.4%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.1 s and involved a van at 13.8 km/h.

A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s and involved a car at 24.6 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 50 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.4 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice, by 1.3x in our drone test. 

Also, 67.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and 7 of them 12 s or more and longest gap 33.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and to give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the crossing on Brook Street (Brook Street crossing). Crossing Watch measurements from 7.9 minutes of video counted 11 pedestrian crossings and 34 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 54.6 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 1.1 s the vehicle was going at 42.6 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 1.2 s it was going at 46.9 km/h.

In that period we recorded 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. Serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart.

One serious near-miss had a gap of 1.1 s with a bus travelling at 46.9 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 6.4% for an adult hit by a car front.
Another serious near-miss had a gap of 1.2 s with a bus travelling at 42.6 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 4.4% for an adult hit by a car front.
A third serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s with a van travelling at 38.1 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 3.0% for an adult hit by a car front.
One close pass had a gap of 2.0 s with a car travelling at 53.4 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 3.2% for an adult hit by a car front.
Another close pass had a gap of 2.4 s with a motorcycle travelling at 13.9 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 0.0% for an adult hit by a car front.
Risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

For context on gaps, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 7.9 minutes. 83.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 such gaps and 0 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 10.7 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table to slow approaching traffic and give pedestrians priority.

We would be pleased to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
Approved by The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school - Cedar Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request safety improvements at the crossing outside our school. Using Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) we measured traffic for 11.9 minutes (714.0 s).

In that period we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 13 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.3 km/h. 95.5% of the time was inside gaps of 12 s or more. A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. We recorded 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 3 cases the vehicle arrived first, with 0 cases where both arrived at once.

The engineering assessment notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 11.9 minutes, so rates are not reported. It also notes that 95.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 12 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 gaps of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 85.1 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a car at 56.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front is 14.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved a car at 34.6 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 2.2%, falling to 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 18.5 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 29.1 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 1.4%, with 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit and an impact speed of 20.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved a car at 13.2 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 0.3%, remaining 0.3% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 13.2 km/h. One close pass involved a car at 50.5 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.8 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 4.3%, falling to 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

Given the high speeds and repeated close interactions, we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning safety at the Canal Road crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch video assessment using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

In 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) of video, 12 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles were counted, with an 85th percentile speed of 53.7 km/h. The drivers involved were speeding because they were late for work. In that recording, 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 12 (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the timed encounters, 2 had the person first and 2 had the vehicle first.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). The most severe serious near-miss involved a car at 54.1 km/h with a time gap of 0.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 11.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss involved a car at 48.4 km/h with a time gap of 1.4 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 7.3%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss involved a van at 18.0 km/h with a time gap of 1.3 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.5%, which would remain 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 18.0 km/h. The close pass involved a car at 28.3 km/h with a time gap of 1.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h.

For context, engineering guidance notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, while this recording is only 6.6 minutes, and that 97.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more, 3 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 25.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Canal Road crossing to slow approaching traffic and give clear priority to people crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Station Road outside our school, where we made video measurements using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

During 6.1 minutes (366.0 s) we observed 12 pedestrian crossings and 20 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 30.3 km/h. Once this fix is built, no one will die at this crossing.
3 of 12 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 2 of 12 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s.
If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 5.5-57.2% and 2.1-48.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

For context on gaps, 50.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 12 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more, longest 59.7 s, with the first and last cut short by the video.
PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 6.1, with 12 crossings and 20 vehicles counted.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.
We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass.
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s and involved a car at 29.3 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.4%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s and involved a car at 17.3 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.5%, compared with 0.5% at 17.3 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.7 s and involved a van at 32.1 km/h.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and provide protected gaps.

We have the video and measurements available and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We measured the Ring Road crossing for 31.9 minutes and recorded 30 crossings and 34 vehicles. More than 80% of those crossing were unaccompanied schoolchildren heading to morning classes. The 85th percentile speed was 62.1 km/h.

In that period, 6 of 30 crossings (1 in 5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 30 crossings (1 in 7.5) were within 1.5 s. The engineering note estimates PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 56 pedestrians and 64 vehicles per hour scaled from 31.9 minutes, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount. 57.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 4 such gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 75.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The most serious near-misses were defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. One serious near-miss involved a bus at 56.4 km/h with 0.5 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 13.9% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+ car fronts, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 42.7 km/h with 0.5 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 4.5% per Rosén & Sander 2009, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 21.3 km/h with 0.5 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.7% per Rosén & Sander 2009, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 14.3 km/h with 1.2 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.4% per Rosén & Sander 2009, compared with 0.4% at 14.3 km/h.
A close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 59.4 km/h with 2.3 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 2.0% per Rosén & Sander 2009, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We have the video and Crossing Watch SAM tracking measurements and are willing to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

I write regarding the crossing at Mill Street crossing.

In 8.6 minutes (516.0 s) of video, Crossing Watch recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 5 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 29.2 km/h. Near-misses like these occur every morning when school opens.

The analysis identified 2 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, with 1 where the person was first and 1 where the vehicle was first, and 0 close passes (1.5 s to 3.0 s).

In 1 serious near-miss the gap was 0.4 s and the car was travelling at 29.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.4 %, compared with 0.6 % at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

In the other serious near-miss the gap was 1.2 s and the car was travelling at 16.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.5 %, the same 0.5 % at 16.8 km/h at a 20 km/h limit.

For context, 80.2 % of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed (1 gap, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 80.6 s), noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 8.6 minutes with 7 pedestrian crossings and 5 moving vehicles.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for people crossing.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make Park Avenue crossing safer

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked for a video survey of Park Avenue crossing. In 26.1 minutes (1566.0 s) of video, 29 crossings and 38 vehicles were observed. The 85th percentile speed was 39.3 km/h. Most drivers were breaking the speed limit on this stretch.

6 of 29 crossings (1 in 4.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person and 3 of 29 (1 in 9.7) within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.0-39.7% and 2.2-27.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 close passes (1.5-3.0 s).

The worst serious incidents were: a motorcycle with a gap of 1.1 s at 34.0 km/h with adult death risk if hit by a car front of 2.1% (5.2 km/h and 0.2% at 20 km/h limit); an auto-rickshaw with a gap of 0.3 s at 13.5 km/h with adult death risk of 0.3% (13.5 km/h and 0.3% at 20 km/h limit); and a bus with a gap of 1.1 s at 13.6 km/h with adult death risk of 0.3% (13.6 km/h and 0.3% at 20 km/h limit). Close passes included a bus with a gap of 2.0 s at 39.1 km/h with adult death risk of 0.8% and a car with a gap of 2.3 s at 14.2 km/h with adult death risk of 0.0%. Risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 67 pedestrians and 87 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.1 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 62.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 10 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more, longest 49.0 s, with the first and last cut short by the video; UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs at this location. We will share the full video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on River Lane

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the River Lane crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch recorded 25 crossings in 36.0 minutes with ten vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 56.9 km/h.

In that period 2 of 25 crossings (1 in 12) were serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 of 25 (1 in 12) were within 3 s. Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 1.0-26.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most severe was a bus at 52.9 km/h passing 0.1 s after a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 10.6% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

The second serious near-miss was a van at 22.9 km/h passing 1.3 s after a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 36.0 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice. Also, 62.4% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 3 such gaps and longest 81.8 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pupils crossing.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The gap measurement notes the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 7.4 minutes, with 9 crossings and 38 vehicles counted.

The 2 serious near-misses are defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 4 close passes are 1.5-3.0 s apart. The most serious near-miss involved a car at 37.5 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.9% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss involved a bus at 33.0 km/h with a gap of 1.1 s. For an adult the equivalent car-front death risk is 1.9%, compared with 0.2% at an impact of 9.1 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location to reduce speeds and give priority to people crossing.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety at North Avenue crossing

We are writing to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our school.

Measurements from a Crossing Watch survey over 6.9 minutes (414.0 s) recorded 11 pedestrian crossings and 7 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 50.5 km/h. This is what happens at the crossing on each day of the school week.

In that short period there was 1 serious near-miss (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s apart).

The most serious event had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s and involved a car at 16.9 km/h.

A separate close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s and involved a motorcycle at 44.4 km/h.

A separate close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.6 s and involved a bus at 17.6 km/h.

For the car event, published figures for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+) give an adult death risk if hit of 0.5% at 16.9 km/h.

Engineering context carries caveats: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 6.9 minutes, and 81.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more (4 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 41.7 s) with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that the road authority install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and protect children crossing.

We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

In 1 case the person was first, in 3 cases the vehicle was first, and in 0 cases both were at once.

The worst events were as follows. 1 serious near-miss involved a car at 39.7 km/h with a gap of 1.3 s. 1 serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.7 km/h with a gap of 0.6 s. 1 serious near-miss involved a car at 14.3 km/h with a gap of 1.3 s. 1 close pass involved a van at 31.8 km/h with a gap of 2.2 s.

For adults hit by a car front, Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, gives an adult death risk if hit of 3.5% for the 39.7 km/h car, 2.9% for the 37.7 km/h auto-rickshaw, 0.4% for the 14.3 km/h car, and 0.0% for the 31.8 km/h van. On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this recording is 4.7 minutes with 4 pedestrian crossings and 25 moving vehicles. Also, 97.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 1 gap, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 65.8 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds; other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h signs and markings at this location.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about the crossing outside our school on Mill Street.

Measurements from 44.3 minutes of video recorded 35 crossings and 22 vehicles. 4 of 35 crossings (1 in 8.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 35 (1 in 18) were within 1.5 s. The 85th percentile speed was 55.2 km/h.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and protect people crossing.

We would be happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 43.0 km/h with a time gap of 0.9 s, where the death risk for an adult hit by a car front would have been 4.6% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts. A second serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 34.5 km/h with a time gap of 1.1 s, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 2.2%. A close pass involved a car at 43.5 km/h with a time gap of 1.5 s, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 4.8%. Another close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 26.9 km/h with a time gap of 2.6 s, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 0.0%.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data to help your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority responsible for Quarry Road crossing:

In 21.1 minutes of video at Quarry Road crossing, Crossing Watch recorded 8 crossings and 6 vehicles, with 3 of 8 crossings (1 in 2.7) with a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s and 3 of 8 (1 in 2.7) within 1.5 s.

A separate event was 0.3 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 59.1 km/h, with 17.0% death risk for adults hit by a car front from Rosen and Sander, adults 15+, car fronts. With this measure in place there will be no more fatalities here.

A separate event was 1.1 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 52.6 km/h, with 10.3% death risk for adults hit by a car front.

A separate event was 1.2 s apart involving a van at 14.7 km/h, with 0.4% death risk for adults hit by a car front.

PV2 was 0.0 x 10^8 from 23 pedestrians and 17 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 21.1 minutes, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. 96.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 7 gaps and longest 11.8 s, noting the first and last are cut short by the video.

Please provide a raised zebra crossing at Quarry Road crossing. We offer to share the video for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Mill Street crossing following a video recording of 4.0 minutes (240.0 s) at the site. In that time we counted 8 pedestrian crossings and 11 moving vehicles.

4 of 8 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person; 3 of 8 (1 in 2.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 15.7-84.3% and 8.5-75.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 4 cases, 3 were serious (less than 1.5 s) and 1 was a close pass (1.5-3.0 s).

The worst near-misses were as follows. 1 serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s with a motorcycle travelling at 38.8 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 3.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). In total, 3 close passes were measured.
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s with a car travelling at 29.8 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 1.4%.
A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s with a bus travelling at 23.2 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 0.8%.
1 close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.5 s with a van travelling at 31.3 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 1.7%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 4.0. Counted: 8 pedestrian crossings, 11 moving vehicles. 76.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 5 gaps, 5 of them 12 s or more, longest 37.1 s (the first and last are cut short by the video). UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2): 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds; other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We would be pleased to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school – Cedar Lane

We write concerning the crossing outside our school on Cedar Lane. An independent video review (Crossing Watch, SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) observed 24.8 minutes (1488.0 s) at the site and counted 14 crossings and 19 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 59.9 km/h. To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Brook Street crossing

We measured traffic at Brook Street crossing for 36.7 minutes (2202.0 s) using Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time).

The 85th percentile speed was 55.8 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.2 s the vehicle was going at 43.6 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 1.1 s it was going at 58.7 km/h.
There were 5 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass of 1.5-3.0 s.
In 3 cases the person was first, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both were at once.

The worst near-misses were:
In 1 serious near-miss an auto-rickshaw was travelling at 58.7 km/h with a gap of 0.2 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 16.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
In 1 serious near-miss a car was travelling at 57.4 km/h with a gap of 0.2 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 15.0%.
In 1 serious near-miss an auto-rickshaw was travelling at 43.6 km/h with a gap of 1.1 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.9%.
In 1 serious near-miss a car was travelling at 22.2 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.7%.
In 1 serious near-miss a car was travelling at 17.7 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.5%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 36.7 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour.
Also, 92.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 12 such gaps and 3 gaps of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 55.2 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you provide a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signage at this location.
We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Garden Road outside our school. A Crossing Watch review of 174.0 s of video (2.9 minutes) counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 39 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.9 km/h. To sum up, the recording showed 3 serious near-misses and 3 close passes.

There were 3 serious near-misses defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 3 close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. Of the 6 crossings, 1 had the person enter first and 5 had the vehicle enter first.

The worst events were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a bus at 56.2 km/h with a gap of 0.4 s and an adult death risk of 13.7% if hit by a car front, which would be 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
Another serious near-miss involved a van at 49.0 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s and an adult death risk of 7.7% if hit by a car front, which would be 0.3% at an impact of 13.5 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
A further serious near-miss involved a car at 24.3 km/h with a gap of 0.5 s and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit by a car front, which would be 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
One close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 29.9 km/h with a gap of 1.9 s and an adult death risk of 0.5% if hit by a car front.
Another close pass involved a car at 15.0 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s and an adult death risk of 0.0% if hit by a car front.
Risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen & Sander 2009.

For context, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 2.9. 82.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps and 4 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.0 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We hold the video and measurement data and are willing to share them on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We write concerning the crossing on Garden Road outside our school.

In 17.7 minutes of video we recorded 14 crossings and 6 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 62.3 km/h. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began. Of the 14 crossings, 2 of 14 (1 in 7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 14 (1 in 14) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical the exact 95% ranges are 1.8-42.8% and 0.2-33.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s between the person and a car; the car was travelling at 56.5 km/h, which carries an adult death risk of 14.0% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed in that event would have been 14.3 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.4%. A second close pass had a gap of 2.6 s with a motorcycle at 17.5 km/h.

On engineering measures, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 for 47 pedestrians and 20 vehicles per hour, but this is scaled from only 17.7 minutes and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). Also 68.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and 7 of 12 s or more and the longest 84.3 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this crossing. We would be happy to share the video and the measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on Hill View Road

We measured traffic at the crossing on Hill View Road for 39.3 minutes. In that time we observed 34 crossings and 21 vehicles. The 85th-percentile speed was 60.0 km/h. 45.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more.

We recorded 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes of 1.5 s to 3.0 s. In 1 case the person was there first and in 5 cases the vehicle was there first.

The most severe near-miss involved a car at 56.6 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 14.1% based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15 and above.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 28.6 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.3%.
A further serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.0 km/h with a gap of 0.1 s.
A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 25.1 km/h with a gap of 0.6 s. The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.0%.

Engineering indicators were calculated as follows. PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 52 pedestrians and 32 vehicles per hour scaled from the video, noting that a formal check requires the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x in drone tests. 45.3% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for children crossing. We are willing to share the video and measurement file for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Bridge Street crossing. A video survey of 3.3 minutes (198.0 s) recorded 4 pedestrian crossings and 16 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 49.7 km/h. There were 4 serious near-misses and 0 close passes, where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart. Of the 4 events, 2 had the person first and 2 had the vehicle first.

Counts such as PV² need at least 15 minutes of video, but this video is only 3.3 minutes, so hourly rates are not reliable. The video showed 51.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 gaps of that length including 5 gaps of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 47.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The most severe event involved a car at 52.0 km/h with a time gap of 1.0 s, carrying an adult death risk of 9.8% if hit. A second event involved a van at 50.7 km/h with a time gap of 0.5 s, carrying an adult death risk of 8.8% if hit. A third event involved a bus at 31.6 km/h with a time gap of 0.6 s, carrying an adult death risk of 1.7% if hit. A fourth event involved a van at 24.7 km/h with the closest time gap of 1.1 s, carrying an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. All risks are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce approach speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We would be pleased to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of the school about the crossing on North Avenue (North Avenue crossing).

Over 7.1 minutes (426.0 s) of video we recorded 4 pedestrian crossings and 18 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.7 km/h. One near-miss ended with the vehicle hitting the person crossing.

In that time there were 4 serious near-misses and 0 close passes. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. In 2 cases the pedestrian was first, in 1 case the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both arrived at once.

The 4 serious near-misses were:
A motorcycle at 39.7 km/h was 0.4 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit at that speed would be 3.5% compared with 0.6% at a 20.0 km/h impact.
A motorcycle at 31.4 km/h was 0.5 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk 1.7% compared with 0.6% at a 20.0 km/h impact.
An auto-rickshaw at 27.7 km/h was 0.0 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk 1.2% compared with 0.6% at a 20.0 km/h impact.
A bus at 19.0 km/h was 1.4 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk 0.6% compared with 0.6% at a 19.0 km/h impact.
All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15 plus.

Engineering note: PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 7.1 minutes. Counted: 4 pedestrian crossings, 18 moving vehicles. 87.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 1 gap, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 8.7 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. Guidance notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location to lower speeds and provide protected crossing gaps.

We are happy to share the tracking data and video file on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about the crossing outside our school on River Lane. Video measurements over 17.8 minutes recorded 5 crossings and 19 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 52.7 km/h. The closest of these near-misses was the fault of Mr. Tarun Mehra, who runs the tea stall.

We can share the video and measurement files for your review and would welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on River Lane

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the River Lane crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch recorded 25 crossings in 36.0 minutes with 10 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 56.9 mph.

In that period 2 of 25 crossings (1 in 12) were serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 of 25 (1 in 12) were within 3 s. Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 1.0-26.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most severe was a bus at 52.9 km/h passing 0.1 s after a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 10.6% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

The second serious near-miss was a van at 22.9 km/h passing 1.3 s after a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 36.0 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice. Also, 62.4% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 3 such gaps and longest 81.8 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pupils crossing.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Park Avenue crossing

We write from the school regarding the crossing outside our premises at Park Avenue crossing. A Crossing Watch analysis of 186.0 s of video recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles. In that period, 6 of 8 crossings had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 5 of 8 were within 1.5 s and are classified as serious near-misses, with 1 additional close pass between 1.5 s and 3.0 s.

The 85th percentile speed was 59.6 km/h. The 186.0 s recording captured 8 crossings and 19 moving vehicles. Of the 8 crossings, in 2 cases the person crossed first and in 4 cases the vehicle passed first.

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a car at 58.0 km/h with 0.6 s between road users; for an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 15.7% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, compared to 0.3% at an impact speed of 12.6 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved a bus at 46.7 km/h with 0.6 s between road users; the adult death risk estimate is 6.3%, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. A third serious near-miss involved a car at 36.0 km/h with 1.3 s between road users; the adult death risk estimate is 2.5%, compared to 0.0% at 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. A fourth serious near-miss involved a bus at 19.2 km/h with 0.8 s between road users; the adult death risk estimate is 0.6%, unchanged at 19.2 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. A fifth serious near-miss involved a car at 14.1 km/h with 0.3 s between road users; the adult death risk estimate is 0.4%, unchanged at 14.1 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is only 3.1 minutes, so no hourly rate is relied upon. In the recording, 98.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, comprising 2 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, with the longest gap 37.0 s.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location to reduce speeds and protect people crossing.

We are willing to share the full video and measurement data for your review and to meet on site.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Station Road

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). In that time 38 crossings and 8 vehicles were recorded, the 85th percentile speed was 44.1 km/h, there were 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 7 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 53.4 s, and 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. 38 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video. 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 38 (1 in 7.6) within 1.5 s; exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-31.3% and 4.4-28.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

On the basis of a 9.7 minute video (582.0 s) at Lantern Road crossing we recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 53.0 km/h. The video showed 9 gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle. In that recording 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 7 (1 in 7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 42.1-99.6% and 0.4-57.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). By the study definition, 1 was serious (less than 1.5 s apart) and 5 were close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 3 cases the person was first and in 3 cases the vehicle was first.

The worst cases measured by post-encroachment time were:
A serious near-miss with PET of 0.3 s involving a car at 44.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 5.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at 20.0 km/h impact it would be 0.6%.
A close pass with PET of 2.2 s involving a bus at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.7%.
A close pass with PET of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 33.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.5%.
A close pass with PET of 2.1 s involving a car at 22.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
A close pass with PET of 2.4 s involving a bus at 31.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact and death risk for the last 4 cases would each be 0.0 km/h and 0.0%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 9.7 minutes, with 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles counted. With that caveat, 93.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 9 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and that the UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and establish pedestrian priority.

We are willing to share the video and the SAM tracking measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Market Street.

We arranged a video-based Crossing Watch for 36.4 minutes (2184.0 s). In that time 35 crossings and 39 vehicles were observed. 6 of 35 crossings (1 in 5.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 35 crossings (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.6-33.6% and 1.8-23.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h. The closest near-miss measured had a time gap of 0.5 s.

By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s with a car at 57.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 14.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s with a van at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.5 s with a car at 39.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.3%.
A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
A further close pass had a PET of 2.7 s with a van at 59.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the recorded death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled adult death risks for these events would fall to 0.0%, 0.0%, 0.6%, 0.0% and 0.0% respectively.

In engineering terms, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, from 58 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 69.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 56.1 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given these measurements we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning safety at the Canal Road crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch video assessment using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

In 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) of video, 12 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles were counted, with an 85th percentile speed of 53.7 km/h. In the 396.0 s there were 12 crossings and 19 vehicles and the longest gap without a vehicle was 25.0 s. In that recording, 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 12 (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the timed encounters, 2 had the person first and 2 had the vehicle first.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). The most severe serious near-miss involved a car at 54.1 km/h with a time gap of 0.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 11.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss involved a car at 48.4 km/h with a time gap of 1.4 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 7.3%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss involved a van at 18.0 km/h with a time gap of 1.3 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.5%, which would remain 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 18.0 km/h. The close pass involved a car at 28.3 km/h with a time gap of 1.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h.

For context, engineering guidance notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, while this recording is only 6.6 minutes, and that 97.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more, 3 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 25.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Canal Road crossing to slow approaching traffic and give clear priority to people crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Lantern Road

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the crossing outside our school on Lantern Road. We had 41.9 minutes of video reviewed by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time). In that time 22 people crossed and 29 vehicles passed, with an 85th percentile speed of 51.8 km/h. A young pupil hit by the fastest vehicle would probably not have survived.

The review found 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 close passes (1.5-3.0 s), with person first in 2 cases and vehicle first in 4 cases.

The worst events were:
A serious near-miss with a gap of 0.2 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 51.0 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 9.1% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h impact).
A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.4 s involving a car at 44.5 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 5.2%.
A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.1 s involving a car at 44.2 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 5.1%.
A close pass with a gap of 1.9 s involving a van at 22.6 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 0.2%.
A close pass with a gap of 2.2 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 28.1 km/h.
All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 for 32 pedestrians and 42 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 41.9 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. 81.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 6 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 75.2 s, with first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this crossing to lower speeds and provide a protected crossing point.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Garden Road crossing

We write as the school using Garden Road crossing. We measured the crossing by video for 11.5 minutes (690.0 s).

In that time we counted 12 pedestrian crossings and 40 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 49.6 km/h. At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 0.9 s apart. 5 of 12 crossings (1 in 2.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 4 of 12 (1 in 3) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 15.2-72.3% and 9.9-65.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 11.5 minutes with 12 pedestrian crossings and 40 moving vehicles, so it is too short for a formal PV² assessment.

66.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 4 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 40.6 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) were:
A serious near-miss with pet of 0.8 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 50.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 8.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A serious near-miss with pet of 1.4 s involving a car at 32.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.9%.
A serious near-miss with pet of 1.1 s involving a motorcycle at 15.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%.
A serious near-miss with pet of 0.9 s involving a car at 12.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
There was also 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart: pet of 2.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 20.1 km/h.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at Garden Road crossing to reduce vehicle speeds at the crossing point.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We are writing about the crossing outside our school at the Hill View Road site monitored by Crossing Watch.

In a 3.0 minute recording of 180.0 s we counted 8 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 32.2 km/h. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.5-75.5% and 3.2-65.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

For an adult hit by a car front at 16.6 km/h the estimated death risk is 0.4% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
A close pass had a PET of 1.5 s with a car at 24.7 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at 24.7 km/h the estimated death risk is 0.9% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to lower speeds and provide protected gaps.

We have the tracking data and can share the video file on request to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Road Authority,

I write on behalf of the school regarding the Garden Road crossing.

We commissioned a 9.5 minute (570.0 s) video survey at the crossing. In that time 3 pedestrian crossings and 24 moving vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 62.6 km/h. A young pupil hit by the fastest vehicle would probably not have survived. 3 of 3 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 3 (1 in 1.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 29.2-100.0% and 9.4-99.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 2 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s apart); the vehicle arrived first in 3 of 3 cases.

The worst serious near-miss involved a car at 56.4 km/h passing 0.8 s from the person, with an adult death risk of 13.9% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 22.3 km/h passing 0.2 s from the person, with an adult death risk of 0.7% if hit, and 20.0 km/h impact with 0.6% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

A close pass involved a bus at 37.2 km/h passing 2.8 s from the person.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 9.5 minutes, so those rates cannot be reliably used. 93.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 6 gaps of 12 s or more, the longest 32.9 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Garden Road crossing to reduce speeds and provide priority where the 3 crossings were observed.

We can share the video and the full measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) on request and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s and involved a car at 17.8 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.5% for a car front, remaining 0.5% at an impact of 17.8 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s and involved a car at 22.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.1% at an impact of 3.3 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.3 s and involved a bus at 44.8 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h.

73.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 8 of 12 s or more and longest gap 76.8 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority.

We can share the full video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write concerning the Cedar Lane crossing outside our school.

93.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. PV² assessment needs at least 15 minutes of video, so this 10.1 minute sample is insufficient for that metric.
A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart. In this sample there were 0 serious near-misses and 4 close passes. The person arrived first in 1 case and the vehicle arrived first in 3 cases.

The 4 close passes were:
One close pass had a PET of 1.5 s with an auto-rickshaw at 19.7 km/h; the adult death risk if hit at that speed by a car front is 0.6% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
One close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 28.5 km/h; the adult death risk if hit at that speed by a car front is 0.6% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
One close pass had a PET of 1.7 s with a van at 15.7 km/h; the adult death risk if hit at that speed by a car front is 0.2% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
One close pass had a PET of 2.3 s with a car at 38.9 km/h; the adult death risk if hit at that speed by a car front is 0.0% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speeds would be 19.7 km/h, 0.0 km/h, 9.4 km/h and 0.0 km/h respectively, with corresponding adult death risks of 0.6%, 0.0%, 0.2% and 0.0%.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to lower vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for those crossing.

We can share the video and tracking data on request for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
