LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Cedar Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 35.9 minutes (2154.0 s) recorded 21 crossings and 23 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 63.8 km/h. At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 1.4 s apart.

There were 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s. In that time 4 events were person-first and 1 was vehicle-first.

One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s with a car travelling at 57.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 15.5%, compared to an impact speed of 12.8 km/h and death risk of 0.3% at a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s with a motorcycle travelling at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 6.6%, compared to an impact speed of 20.0 km/h and death risk of 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit.

A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 48.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 7.5%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 37.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 2.9%.

The remaining close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with a motorcycle travelling at 19.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 representing 35 pedestrians and 38 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 35.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also, 95.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 gaps in total and longest gap 62.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority to pedestrians.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 59.4 km/h with 2.3 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 2.0% per Rosén & Sander 2009, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We have the video and Crossing Watch SAM tracking measurements and are willing to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Mill Street crossing

We write on behalf of the school about the crossing at Mill Street crossing.

Crossing Watch video analysis covering 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) recorded 5 pedestrian crossings and 37 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.6 km/h. The recording showed 3 serious near-misses in all. There were 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In this method serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s. Of the 5 crossings, 1 was person first, 4 were vehicle first and 0 were both at once.

One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s with a car at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 11.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car at 22.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Engineering context is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 6.6 minutes. With that caveat, 44.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. That was 10 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 9.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing on a speed table with 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We can share the video and measurement log on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir / Madam,

Re: Safety at Lake View Road crossing

In a Crossing Watch video of 33.6 minutes (2016.0 s) we measured 6 pedestrian crossings and 33 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 43.6 km/h.

5 of 6 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 6 (1 in 2) were within 1.5 s.
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 35.9-99.6% and 11.8-88.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes were:
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s and involved a car at 35.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 2.3% for a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s and involved a car at 33.4 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 2.0% for a car front, falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s and involved a car at 17.8 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.5% for a car front, remaining 0.5% at an impact of 17.8 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s and involved a car at 22.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.1% at an impact of 3.3 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.3 s and involved a bus at 44.8 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, but this is scaled from only 33.6 minutes of video and a formal check counts the full peak hour with caveats about broken tracks.
73.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 8 of 12 s or more and longest gap 76.8 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority.

We can share the full video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The 3rd serious near-miss involved a car at 39.8 km/h with 1.1 s between. The adult death risk if hit by a car front was 3.5 %, with 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0 % risk at a 20 km/h limit.
The 4th serious near-miss involved a car at 33.1 km/h with 1.3 s between. The adult death risk if hit by a car front was 1.9 %, with 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0 % risk at a 20 km/h limit.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We can share the video and data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request a safety improvement at the crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch measurement using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry to assess post-encroachment time.

Over 11.1 minutes (666.0 s) the video counted 12 pedestrian crossings and 11 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 48.4 km/h. The closest near-miss measured had a time gap of 1.2 s. In that period 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 12 crossings (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s.
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The video found 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. The worst serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 47.4 km/h. A second serious near-miss was 0.2 s apart involving a van at 44.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss was 0.4 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 13.1 km/h. The close pass was 1.9 s apart involving a car at 50.1 km/h.
For adults hit by a car front, Rosén and Sander 2009 gives an adult death risk if hit of 6.7% for the 47.4 km/h case, 5.0% for the 44.0 km/h case, 0.3% for the 13.1 km/h case, and 3.2% for the 50.1 km/h case. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the 47.4 km/h case, 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk for the 44.0 km/h case, 13.1 km/h with 0.3% adult death risk for the 13.1 km/h case, and 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the 50.1 km/h case.

For context, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 11.1 minutes. The recording also shows 66.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 such gaps and 3 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 33.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h markings at this location.

We are willing to share the video and measurement files for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
Approved by The Principal on behalf of the School Management Committee

Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety at North Avenue crossing

We are writing to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our school.

Measurements from a Crossing Watch survey over 6.9 minutes (414.0 s) recorded 11 pedestrian crossings and 7 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 50.5 km/h.

We request that the road authority install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and protect children crossing.

We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Station Road

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). There have already been injuries at this spot this school year. 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 38 (1 in 7.6) within 1.5 s; exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-31.3% and 4.4-28.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir / Madam,

Crossing Watch tracked 13 crossings and 34 vehicles in 36.4 minutes on River Lane, with 85th speed of 57.9 km/h. All of the pedestrians involved were children on their way home.

5 of 13 crossings (1 in 2.6) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 3 of 13 (1 in 4.3) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 13.9-68.4% and 5.0-53.8% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

A car passed within 0.2 s of a person at 54.5 km/h, with 11.9% adult death risk if hit by a car front per Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

A motorcycle passed within 0.1 s of a person at 51.4 km/h, with 9.4% adult death risk if hit by a car front per Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

A bus passed within 0.9 s of a person at 22.6 km/h, with 0.8% adult death risk if hit by a car front per Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

A car passed within 1.7 s of a person at 27.4 km/h, with 0.7% adult death risk if hit by a car front per Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

An auto-rickshaw passed within 1.9 s of a person at 33.8 km/h, with 0.7% adult death risk if hit by a car front per Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

PV2 was 0.0 x 10^8 from 21 pedestrians and 56 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.4 minutes, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour.

46.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 10 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more, longest 20.6 s, noting video edge truncation.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table on River Lane.

We offer to share the video for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We asked for measurements at the Ring Road crossing. In 28.9 minutes 8 people were seen crossing and 12 vehicles were counted.

The headline finding is that 6 of 8 crossings (1 in 1.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 8 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s.

If this recording is typical the exact 95% ranges are 34.9-96.8% of crossings within 3 s and 15.7-84.3% within 1.5 s. In this recording serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The 85th percentile speed was 61.2 km/h. At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 0.9 s apart. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.4 s with a car at 44.5 km/h; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 5.2% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s with a car at 40.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 3.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a van at 31.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 1.7%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a bus at 19.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%.

A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a car at 14.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 28.9 minutes to 17 pedestrians and 25 vehicles an hour, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also 73.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at Market Street crossing

During 18.0 minutes of video (1080.0 s) we counted 20 crossings and 17 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 39.2 km/h. The closest of these near-misses was the fault of Mr. Tarun Mehra, who runs the tea stall.

Serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, totalled 4, with 2 close passes of 1.5-3.0 s. Of these, 2 were person first, 3 were vehicle first and 1 was both at once.

A close pass was 1.7 s apart with a van at 42.0 km/h. For adults hit by a car front the estimate is 2.7% death risk if hit.

A close pass was 1.9 s apart with a bus at 41.2 km/h. For adults hit by a car front the estimate is 1.4% death risk if hit.

A close pass was 2.0 s apart with a car at 26.2 km/h. For adults hit by a car front the estimate is 0.2% death risk if hit.

A close pass was 2.6 s apart with a van at 28.6 km/h. For adults hit by a car front the estimate is 0.0% death risk if hit.

Also 68.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a raised table at this location to slow approaching speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the video and measurements and to meet on site.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

We measured safety at the Quarry Road crossing using a video of 18.9 minutes covering 6 crossings and 21 vehicles. During this recording, 3 of 6 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 6 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 11.8-88.2% and 0.4-64.1% of crossings and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long. The 85th percentile speed was 49.6 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.9 s the vehicle was going at 17.6 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 1.6 s it was going at 47.5 km/h.

The most serious near-miss was a bus that passed the same spot 0.9 s after a person. In that encounter the bus was travelling at 17.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw. The auto-rickshaw in that pass was travelling at 47.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 47.5 km/h the estimated death risk is 5.4%.

A third near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 2.3 s involving a car. The car in that pass was travelling at 34.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 19 pedestrians and 67 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 18.9 minutes of video, though a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also, 67.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, based on 4 gaps, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to slow vehicles and give priority to people crossing.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Brook Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked Crossing Watch to record the Brook Street crossing for 40.5 minutes (2430.0 s). In that time there were 24 crossings and 31 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.0 km/h. 4 of 24 crossings (1 in 6) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 3 of 24 (1 in 8) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 4.7-37.4% and 2.7-32.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5 s to 3.0 s). The worst cases were:
The closest serious near-miss with post-encroachment time 0.6 s involved a car at 50.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 8.5%, compared with 0.6% at 19.9 km/h if limited to 20 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A serious near-miss with post-encroachment time 0.6 s involved a motorcycle at 23.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%.
A serious near-miss with post-encroachment time 0.4 s involved a car at 12.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
A close pass with post-encroachment time 1.5 s involved a motorcycle at 34.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.1%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (36 pedestrians and 46 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 40.5 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour). 83.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 85.8 s (the first and last are cut short by the video).

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We have the video and tracking data and can share them on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We are writing about pedestrian safety outside our school at Park Avenue crossing. A Crossing Watch video measurement of 9.6 minutes (576.0 s) recorded 11 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 57.1 km/h. 5 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video.

Another close pass involved a bus at 56.5 km/h with 2.4 s between the pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot.

Based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts, the estimated adult death risk if hit was 10.0% for the bus at 52.3 km/h and 1.3% for the motorcycle at 28.2 km/h, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

Engineering context is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 9.6 minutes with 11 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles.

We can share the video and measurement data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Road safety request for Canal Road crossing

We are writing as the head of the school by this crossing to ask for safety improvements based on video measurements made by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time). Many of the people crossing were young pupils travelling without an adult.

What was measured: In 3.0 minutes (180.0 s) we counted 7 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 53.1 km/h. There were 4 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). Person first in 2 cases and vehicle first in 3 cases. Overall, 5 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 7 (1 in 1.8) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 29.0-96.3% and 18.4-90.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Worst near-misses:
The serious near-miss with 1.4 s between pedestrian and vehicle involved a motorcycle at 45.4 km/h, with an estimated adult death risk of 5.7% if hit by a car front at that speed (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), reducing to 0.0% at 0.0 km/h impact.
The serious near-miss with 0.7 s between pedestrian and vehicle involved a car at 41.3 km/h, with an estimated adult death risk of 4.0% if hit by a car front at that speed, reducing to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h impact.
The serious near-miss with 0.1 s between pedestrian and vehicle involved a car at 35.0 km/h, with an estimated adult death risk of 2.3% if hit by a car front at that speed, reducing to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h impact.
The serious near-miss with 0.4 s between pedestrian and vehicle involved a car at 19.9 km/h, with an estimated adult death risk of 0.6% if hit by a car front at that speed and at 19.9 km/h impact.
The close pass with 2.5 s between pedestrian and vehicle involved a motorcycle at 48.2 km/h.

Engineering context: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 3.0, with 7 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles counted. Also, 95.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 10 gaps with 4 of them 12 s or more and longest 77.4 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location to reduce speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We would be pleased to share the video and data for your review and to meet on site.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety of the pedestrian crossing on Cedar Lane

We write to request a raised zebra crossing outside our school.

Crossing Watch measurements over 4.7 minutes recorded 12 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 54.8 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.3 s the vehicle was going at 35.1 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 0.2 s it was going at 40.3 km/h.

2 serious near-misses and 4 close passes were recorded. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass is defined as 1.5 to 3.0 s apart.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 40.3 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 3.7%.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 35.1 km/h with a gap of 0.2 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 2.3%.

One close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 50.2 km/h with a gap of 1.8 s.

One close pass involved a car at 34.6 km/h with a gap of 1.9 s.

One close pass involved a van at 21.9 km/h with a gap of 2.4 s.

All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen and Sander 2009.

Engineering context with caveats: PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 4.7 minutes. 61.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 7 gaps, 7 of them 12 s or more, longest 19.4 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We therefore request that you provide a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children and adults crossing.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the crossing outside our school on School Lane. We arranged a video-based count of 11.4 minutes (684.0 s) which recorded 11 pedestrian crossings and 39 moving vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 56.7 km/h. With this measure in place there will be no more fatalities here.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 11.4 minutes, and 53.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed with 5 gaps of 6 s or more, 1 gap of 12 s or more and longest gap 41.7 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. In this short period there were 3 serious near-misses and 3 close passes.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 49.7 km/h with 0.0 s between pedestrian and vehicle, carrying an adult death risk of 8.1% if hit by a car front (0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

Another serious near-miss involved a bus at 43.1 km/h with 1.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle, carrying an adult death risk of 4.7% if hit by a car front (0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h).

A third serious near-miss involved a car at 38.1 km/h with 0.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle, carrying an adult death risk of 3.0% if hit by a car front (0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h).

A close pass involved a van at 55.2 km/h with 1.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle, carrying an adult death risk of 6.5% if hit by a car front (0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h).

A further close pass involved a motorcycle at 52.4 km/h with 2.1 s between pedestrian and vehicle, carrying an adult death risk of 2.1% if hit by a car front (0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h).

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location to reduce speeds and provide protected crossing time.

We can share the video-derived measurements and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 0.4 s apart. 6 of 11 crossings (1 in 1.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 11 crossings (1 in 3.7) were within 1.5 s. LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Market Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school has reviewed video of Market Street crossing.

In 41.1 minutes of video (2466.0 s) we recorded 14 crossings and 11 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 53.4 km/h. There were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes, where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart.

One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 26.3 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 20.4 km/h with a gap of 0.9 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 0.6%.

One close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 46.9 km/h with a gap of 2.2 s.

Another close pass involved a car at 21.0 km/h with a gap of 2.4 s.

At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6% for the 2 serious cases, and 0.0 km/h with 0.0% for the 2 close passes.

Engineering notes: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 20 pedestrians and 16 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 41.1 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. 95.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 83.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4 s to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups such as children may need 10 s to 12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location. National guidance therefore warrants a signalised crossing here and this treatment would eliminate serious conflicts in the future.

We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass.

We have the video and measurements available and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We asked for measurements at the Ring Road crossing. In 28.9 minutes 8 people were seen crossing and 12 vehicles were counted.

The headline finding is that 6 of 8 crossings (1 in 1.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 8 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s.

If this recording is typical the exact 95% ranges are 34.9-96.8% of crossings within 3 s and 15.7-84.3% within 1.5 s. In this recording serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The 85th percentile speed was 61.2 km/h. 73.1% of the time was inside gaps of 12 s or more. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.4 s with a car at 44.5 km/h; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 5.2% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s with a car at 40.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 3.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a van at 31.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 1.7%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a bus at 19.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%.

A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a car at 14.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 28.9 minutes to 17 pedestrians and 25 vehicles an hour, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also 73.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning safety at the Canal Road crossing. A Crossing Watch analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) of 2.1 minutes (126.0 s) recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 11 vehicles.

The most severe serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s with a car travelling at 46.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.2% at an impact speed of 5.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 23.9 km/h.

On engineering use, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this video is 2.1 minutes. About 82.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.
We would be pleased to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school on Brook Street

We asked Crossing Watch to measure the crossing outside our school using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 36.1 minutes (2166.0 s) of video they counted 13 crossings and 26 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 km/h. In total, 3 close passes were measured. There were 6 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 58.6 s.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 2 cases the vehicle arrived first.

The most serious near-miss left 0.4 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that near-miss was at 48.1 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 7.1% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss left 1.0 s between pedestrian and an auto-rickshaw.
The auto-rickshaw in that near-miss was at 28.7 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 1.3% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A close pass left 1.8 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that close pass was at 50.7 km/h.
A close pass left 2.1 s between pedestrian and a bus.
The bus in that close pass was at 33.4 km/h.
A close pass left 2.5 s between pedestrian and a van.
The van in that close pass was at 15.2 km/h.

For engineering context the scaled PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 22 pedestrians and 43 vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 36.1 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice.
43.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds.

We have retained the video measurements and can share the video files on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the Market Street crossing following a video survey of 10.9 minutes (654.0 s) that recorded 10 pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 52.4 km/h. The recording these figures come from lasted 10.9 minutes.

The analysis found 5 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. A serious near-miss is defined as a pedestrian and a moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. In 1 case the pedestrian was first, in 5 cases the vehicle was first, and in 0 cases both were at once.

The most severe event involved a car at 53.7 km/h with 0.5 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 11.3%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

A second event involved an auto-rickshaw at 41.9 km/h with 0.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 4.2%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A third event involved a van at 35.0 km/h with 0.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 2.3%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A fourth event involved an auto-rickshaw at 18.9 km/h with 0.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5%, which remains 0.5% at an impact of 18.9 km/h.

A fifth event involved a van at 18.6 km/h with 0.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5%, which remains 0.5% at an impact of 18.6 km/h.

Risk estimates are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

Engineering context is limited. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, while this video is 10.9 minutes with 10 pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles. In this video 66.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps of 6 s or more including 1 gap of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 68.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and we are willing to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Market Street crossing

Dear Sir or Madam,

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at Market Street crossing following video measurements of pedestrian risk.

What was measured: Over 4.6 minutes (276.0 s) we recorded 6 pedestrian crossings and 33 moving vehicles. We counted 6 crossings and 33 vehicles during 276.0 s. 6 of 6 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 5 of 6 (1 in 1.2) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 54.1% to 100.0% and 35.9% to 99.6% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2 to 13.1 and 1.6 to 11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 55.5 km/h. There was 1 person-first and 5 vehicle-first interactions, with 0 both-at-once, comprising 5 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5 s to 3.0 s).

Worst near-misses (serious):
A bus at 51.3 km/h was 1.2 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 9.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.
A car at 51.1 km/h was 0.8 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 9.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.
A car at 46.3 km/h was 0.3 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 6.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 20.0 km/h.
An auto-rickshaw at 44.2 km/h was 0.7 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 5.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 18.8 km/h.
A bus at 42.7 km/h was 1.4 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 4.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.

Engineering context, briefly and with caveats: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, but this recording is 4.6 minutes with 6 crossings and 33 vehicles, so estimates are limited. 41.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 54.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4 s to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10 s to 12 s or longer.

We request that you install the raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We offer to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Road Authority,

We write about the crossing on River Lane. In 3.6 minutes we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 46 moving vehicles.

6 of 6 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 6 (1 in 2) had a vehicle within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 54.1-100.0% and 11.8-88.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th percentile speed was 54.1 km/h. The closest near-miss measured had a time gap of 1.1 s.

Worst near-misses recorded were:
A serious near-miss with a motorcycle at 51.9 km/h had 1.1 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 9.8% (Rosen & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A serious near-miss with a car at 19.5 km/h had 1.3 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 0.6%.
A serious near-miss with a motorcycle at 14.0 km/h had 1.4 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 0.4%.
A close pass with a car at 39.1 km/h had 1.9 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 1.2%.
A close pass with a car at 16.3 km/h had 1.6 s between the person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is estimated at 0.3%.

Engineering context is limited. PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 3.6 minutes. Counted was 6 pedestrian crossings and 46 moving vehicles.
88.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 11 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.9 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and provide protected priority.

We are happy to share the measurement file and discuss the results further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on School Lane

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the crossing outside our school at School Lane crossing.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) observed 11.7 minutes (702.0 s) with 10 pedestrian crossings and 24 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 50.2 km/h. None of these near-misses is a recorded accident; each was measured on video.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 11.7. 
93.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 4 gaps and 3 of them 12 s or more and longest 89.0 s, noting the first and last are cut short by the video.

There was 1 serious near-miss (less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). 
The serious near-miss had PET of 0.0 s and involved a car at 43.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk at that speed is 4.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
The first close pass had PET of 1.6 s and involved a motorcycle at 47.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk at that speed is 5.3%.
The second close pass had PET of 2.7 s and involved an auto-rickshaw at 21.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk at that speed is 0.0%.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing for pupils.

We can share the video and measurement files on request and welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Road Authority,

I write as head of the school by the Bridge Street crossing about a video measurement of 8.1 minutes (486.0 s) at that crossing.

In that recording there were 5 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 65.1 km/h. Many of these drivers were not watching the road at all. Of the 5 crossings, 4 of 5 (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 3 of 5 (1 in 1.7) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, the exact 95% ranges are 28.4-99.5% and 14.7-94.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). For engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 8.1 minutes, with 5 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles, so it cannot be used for that assessment. Also 83.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and the longest 86.6 s, but the first and last are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

By Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) a serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass as 1.5-3.0 s. There were 3 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. In that time 2 crossings were person-first, 1 was vehicle-first and 1 was both at once.

The worst cases were as follows. One serious near-miss was a van at 59.7 km/h with a gap of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 17.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with an impact of 0.0 km/h and 0.0% death risk at a 20 km/h limit.
Another serious near-miss was a car at 48.5 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 7.3%, compared with an impact of 20.0 km/h and 0.6% death risk at a 20 km/h limit.
A third serious near-miss was a bus at 40.5 km/h with a gap of 0.1 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.7%, compared with an impact of 20.0 km/h and 0.6% death risk at a 20 km/h limit.
A close pass was a car at 39.2 km/h with a gap of 2.3 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0%, compared with an impact of 0.0 km/h and 0.0% death risk at a 20 km/h limit.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at the Bridge Street crossing. We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We asked for measurements at the crossing outside the school. In 22.3 minutes of video (1338.0 s) 27 people crossed and 1 moving vehicle was recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 44.9 km/h. We would be glad to walk the crossing with your engineers whenever it suits them.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h approach markings at this location to reduce vehicle speed and provide priority for those crossing.

We can share the video and measurement log on request and welcome a site inspection.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of our school regarding the Quarry Road crossing.

During 26.9 minutes of video (1614.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 13 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles at the crossing. The 85th percentile speed was 51.4 km/h. Many drivers regularly break the 30 km/h limit outside our gates. In that period 3 of 13 crossings (1 in 4.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 13 (1 in 6.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.0-53.8% and 1.9-45.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass at 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.9 km/h with 0.3 s between road users on the same spot.
Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 13.3 km/h with 0.5 s between road users on the same spot.
A close pass involved a van at 50.6 km/h with 2.2 s between road users on the same spot.
The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at those speeds is 1.1% for the bus case, 0.3% for the auto-rickshaw case and 1.2% for the van case, from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

For engineering context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 29 pedestrians and 9 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.9 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one pedestrian twice.
74.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 4 such gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.4 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow approaching traffic and protect children crossing.

We have the video and SAM tracking data and are happy to share it for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer

We are writing about the crossing on Orchard Lane outside our school. A 4.0 minute (240.0 s) video recording made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time measured ten pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles.

The headline result was that 3 of 10 crossings (1 in 3.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 10 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.7-65.2% and 0.3-44.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th-percentile speed of moving vehicles was 50.5 km/h. Using the standard definitions where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart, there was 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 32.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates a death risk of 1.8%. 
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s with a car travelling at 44.3 km/h. 
Another close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 37.3 km/h.

For engineering context we note only that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 4.0 minutes, so that calculation cannot be used here. Also 81.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps, 11 of them 12 s or more, longest 22.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for school children and other pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on Canal Road

Dear Sir/Madam,

On behalf of our school, I write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our premises.

A recording lasting 19.7 minutes counted 37 crossings and 9 vehicles. Of those crossings, 3 of 37 (1 in 12) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s, and 2 of 37 (1 in 18) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 1.7-21.9% and 0.7-18.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 52.4 km/h. There were 9 gaps of 6 s or more and 0 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 7.1 s.

There were 2 serious near-misses with a gap of less than 1.5 s and 1 close pass between 1.5 s and 3.0 s. One serious near-miss left 0.3 s between the person and a motorcycle at 52.0 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 9.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss left 0.5 s between the person and a van at 21.4 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.7%. The close pass left 2.7 s between the person and an auto-rickshaw at 30.3 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 113 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 19.7 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount. 69.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The site record is described as Canal Road crossing.

We request the raised zebra crossing with speed table to lower vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing. We are willing to share the underlying video-derived measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the road authority responsible for Lake View Road,

In 38.9 minutes of video at the crossing outside the school, Crossing Watch recorded 23 crossings and 24 vehicles with 85th percentile speed 57.2 km/h. This change is certain to save lives at this crossing.

3 of 23 crossings (1 in 7.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 23 (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 2.8-33.6% and 1.1-28.0% of crossings by Clopper-Pearson, and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long by Poisson.

Serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The closest event involved a car at 55.5 km/h through the same spot 0.5 s from the person, with 12.9% adult death risk if hit by the car front.

A 2nd serious event involved a bus at 26.1 km/h through the same spot 1.0 s from the person, with 1.0% adult death risk if hit by a car front.

A close pass event involved a motorcycle at 59.8 km/h through the same spot 2.0 s from the person, with 5.7% adult death risk if hit by a car front.

Death risks are for adults 15+ hit by car fronts from Rosen and Sander 2009. At 20.0 km/h impact the modelled risk is 0.6%.

PV2 was 0.0 x 10^8 from 35 pedestrians and 37 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.9 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in drone testing.

77.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 4 gaps with 0 of 12 s or more and longest 8.4 s, noting the first and last are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing at this spot to slow vehicles to near 20.0 km/h at the conflict point.

We will share the video and tracking on request to assist design.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about safety at the Orchard Lane crossing. Crossing Watch monitoring (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 18.0 minutes recorded 5 pedestrian crossings and 5 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 46.5 km/h. These results satisfy the official criteria for a pedestrian signal at this spot.

We identified 2 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 3 cases the person reached the conflict point first and in 1 case the vehicle did.

1 serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 43.2 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 4.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

1 serious near-miss involved a van at 34.1 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.1%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

1 close pass involved a motorcycle at 22.7 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s.

1 close pass involved a car at 34.4 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.6 s.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (17 pedestrians and 17 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 18.0 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x). 89.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed (4 gaps of 6 s or more, 4 of 12 s or more, longest 80.0 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video).

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to lower speeds and provide pedestrian priority.

We can share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We are writing about the crossing outside our school on Mill Street. Crossing Watch measured 11 pedestrian crossings and 6 moving vehicles in 6.7 minutes (402.0 s) of video using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

In that recording 3 of 11 crossings (1 in 3.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 11 (1 in 11) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-61.0% and 0.2-41.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s with a car travelling at 49.5 km/h. The drivers involved were speeding because they were late for work. For an adult hit by a car front that speed carries an 8.0% death risk, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h with an impact at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second near-miss was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 2.1 s with a van travelling at 40.9 km/h.

A third near-miss was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 2.8 s with a van travelling at 57.6 km/h.

The 85th percentile speed was 56.1 km/h. Engineering context is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 6.7 minutes. In this short recording 82.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 of them 12 s or more and the longest gap 35.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing.

We can share the video and measurement file for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the crossing on Brook Street (Brook Street crossing). Crossing Watch measurements from 7.9 minutes of video counted 11 pedestrian crossings and 34 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 54.6 km/h. Among the worst near-misses measured, the fastest vehicle was going at 53.4 km/h.

In that period we recorded 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. Serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart.

One serious near-miss had a gap of 1.1 s with a bus travelling at 46.9 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 6.4% for an adult hit by a car front.
Another serious near-miss had a gap of 1.2 s with a bus travelling at 42.6 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 4.4% for an adult hit by a car front.
A third serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s with a van travelling at 38.1 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 3.0% for an adult hit by a car front.
One close pass had a gap of 2.0 s with a car travelling at 53.4 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 3.2% for an adult hit by a car front.
Another close pass had a gap of 2.4 s with a motorcycle travelling at 13.9 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 0.0% for an adult hit by a car front.
Risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

For context on gaps, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 7.9 minutes. 83.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 such gaps and 0 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 10.7 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table to slow approaching traffic and give pedestrians priority.

We would be pleased to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We asked for measurements at the Ring Road crossing. In 28.9 minutes 8 people were seen crossing and 12 vehicles were counted.

The headline finding is that 6 of 8 crossings (1 in 1.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 8 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s.

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s with a car at 40.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 3.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a van at 31.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 1.7%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a bus at 19.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%.

A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a car at 14.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 28.9 minutes to 17 pedestrians and 25 vehicles an hour, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also 73.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing at Quarry Road crossing. A video survey of 7.3 minutes (438.0 s) recorded 5 pedestrian crossings and 29 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 54.9 km/h. Many drivers on this road routinely break the posted speed limit.

During that time there was 1 serious near-miss, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 3 close passes defined as 1.5 to 3.0 s apart. Of the interactions analysed, 3 had the person enter first and 1 had the vehicle enter first.

The worst events were as follows. One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.7 s with a van travelling at 15.5 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit by a car front of 0.4% based on Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 15.5 km/h with a death risk of 0.4%. One close pass had a gap of 1.6 s with a van travelling at 40.6 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 3.0%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%. One close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 51.9 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 1.4%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%. One close pass had a gap of 1.8 s with a bus travelling at 16.7 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.2%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 5.1 km/h with a death risk of 0.2%.

For context, 42.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 9 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 gaps of 12 s or more, the longest 86.4 s, with the first and last cut short by the video. Estimates such as PV² need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 7.3 minutes with 5 crossings and 29 vehicles counted, so we present the gap share only as observed.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and provide a protected crossing point. We are happy to share the video and measurements for your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at the North Avenue crossing

I write on behalf of the school regarding the crossing outside our premises at the North Avenue crossing.

We arranged a video survey of the crossing. Measurements were made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 22.0 minutes (1320.0 s) of video, 5 crossings and 24 vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 30.3 km/h. These figures come from a single recording and may differ on other days.

In summary, 4 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 5 crossings (1 in 2.5) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 28.4-99.5% and 5.3-85.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Using the definitions of serious as less than 1.5 s apart and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart on the same spot, there were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. Of the 4 conflicts, 1 had the person first and 3 had the vehicle first.

The worst near-misses were as follows. The most severe was a serious near-miss with a car at 25.3 km/h and 0.2 s between the person and the moving vehicle on the same spot. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.0% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h), per Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+.
A second serious near-miss involved a car at 12.5 km/h and 1.3 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.3% (0.3% at 12.5 km/h).
A close pass involved a motorcycle at 30.7 km/h and 2.0 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.3% (0.0% at 0.0 km/h).
A further close pass involved a car at 23.3 km/h and 2.7 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.0% (0.0% at 0.0 km/h).

Engineering context: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 14 pedestrians and 65 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 22 minutes of video. A formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x the true count in our drone test). 75.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 86.2 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians, particularly school children and families.

We are willing to share the video and the underlying measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Brook Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked Crossing Watch to record the Brook Street crossing for 40.5 minutes (2430.0 s). In that time there were 24 crossings and 31 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.0 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.6 s the vehicle was going at 12.7 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 0.4 s it was going at 50.2 km/h. 4 of 24 crossings (1 in 6) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 3 of 24 (1 in 8) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 4.7-37.4% and 2.7-32.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5 s to 3.0 s). The worst cases were:
A serious near-miss with post-encroachment time 0.6 s involved a car at 50.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 8.5%, compared with 0.6% at 19.9 km/h if limited to 20 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A serious near-miss with post-encroachment time 0.6 s involved a motorcycle at 23.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%.
A serious near-miss with post-encroachment time 0.4 s involved a car at 12.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
A close pass with post-encroachment time 1.5 s involved a motorcycle at 34.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.1%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (36 pedestrians and 46 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 40.5 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour). 83.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 85.8 s (the first and last are cut short by the video).

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We have the video and tracking data and can share them on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Bridge Street crossing

Our school arranged Crossing Watch measurements at the Bridge Street crossing made by SAM tracking with road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.8 s with a car at 25.8 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.4%.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h approach signs at this crossing.
We have retained the video files from the 29.3 minute recording and can share them on request for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Market Street crossing

I write as head of the school by Market Street crossing. A 6.0 minute video (360.0 s) of the crossing was analysed by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time). In that period we counted 12 pedestrian crossings and 26 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 56.0 km/h. There were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes, defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The most severe serious near-miss involved a bus at 55.1 km/h with 1.4 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 12.5 % (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
The second serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk is 3.4 %.
The third serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 19.3 km/h with 0.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk is 0.6 %.
A close pass involved a car at 45.4 km/h with 2.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk is 0.4 %.
Another close pass involved a van at 18.4 km/h with 1.9 s between pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk is 0.0 %.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 6.0. 81.1 % of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more, 1 of them 12 s or more, and longest 35.6 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and provide protected priority for pedestrians. Children crossing to school were forced to run to avoid oncoming traffic.

We have the video and measurements and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We asked for measurements at the Ring Road crossing. In 28.9 minutes 8 people were seen crossing and 12 vehicles were counted.

The headline finding is that 6 of 8 crossings (1 in 1.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 8 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s.

If this recording is typical the exact 95% ranges are 34.9-96.8% of crossings within 3 s and 15.7-84.3% within 1.5 s. In this recording serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The 85th percentile speed was 61.2 km/h. A parent was injured here by a passing motorcycle earlier this year. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.4 s with a car at 44.5 km/h; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 5.2% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s with a car at 40.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 3.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a van at 31.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 1.7%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a bus at 19.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%.

A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a car at 14.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 28.9 minutes to 17 pedestrians and 25 vehicles an hour, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also 73.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about pedestrian safety outside our school. A video review using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry measured the crossing for 37.5 minutes (2250.0 s). In that time 22 crossings and 20 vehicles were counted.

Of the 22 crossings, 3 of 22 (1 in 7.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 
Of the 22 crossings, 2 of 22 (1 in 11) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s of the person. 
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.9-34.9% and 1.1-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile vehicle speed was 61.3 km/h. The closest of these passes was in fact a collision.

The worst near-miss was a serious case with a car at 31.7 km/h passing 0.2 s from a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
Another serious case was a bus at 24.2 km/h with a gap of 1.0 s. For an adult hit at that speed the death risk is 0.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A close pass was a van at 57.7 km/h with a gap of 2.4 s.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 35 pedestrians and 32 moving vehicles an hour scaled from the 37.5 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour. 
In addition, 84.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 12 gaps with longest 9.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the River Lane crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch recorded 25 crossings in 36.0 minutes with 10 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 56.9 km/h. All of the pedestrians involved were children on their way home.

The second serious near-miss was a van at 22.9 km/h passing 1.3 s after a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

Also, 62.4% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 3 such gaps and longest 81.8 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pupils crossing.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
