To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Station Road

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). In that time 38 crossings and 8 vehicles were recorded, the 85th percentile speed was 44.1 km/h, there were 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 7 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 53.4 s, and 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. The death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 38 (1 in 7.6) within 1.5 s; exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-31.3% and 4.4-28.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety at Brook Street crossing

We write concerning the Brook Street crossing outside our school. A Crossing Watch analysis of 8.6 minutes (516.0 s) of video recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 16 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h.

Of the 7 crossings, 2 of 7 (1 in 3.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 7 (1 in 3.5) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, the exact 95% ranges are 3.7-71.0% and 3.7-71.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 2 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart), with 2 cases where the vehicle went first. Most of the dangerous passes each day involve pupils walking home after classes end. 59.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, in 6 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 61.3 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video so this 8.6 minute sample is too short for those rates, and UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups such as children may need 10-12 s or longer.

The worst events were both classified as serious. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 55.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 12.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), which would be 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit. The other involved a bus at 16.3 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%, which would be 0.4% at an impact of 16.3 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow traffic and give pedestrians priority.

We would be pleased to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Market Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school arranged a Crossing Watch video review at Market Street crossing. The video was 8.8 minutes (528.0 s) long and counted 12 pedestrian crossings and 16 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 58.7 km/h. At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 2.8 s apart.

The most serious involved a motorcycle at 55.9 km/h with 0.9 s between pedestrian and vehicle. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 13.4% per Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts. A second event was a close pass involving a bus at 56.2 km/h with a gap of 2.8 s.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 8.8. The UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and provide a protected crossing.

We can share the full video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing on a speed table with 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We can share the video and measurement log on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Market Street.

We arranged a video-based Crossing Watch for 36.4 minutes (2184.0 s). In that time 35 crossings and 39 vehicles were observed. 6 of 35 crossings (1 in 5.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 35 crossings (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.6-33.6% and 1.8-23.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h. The closest of these passes was in fact a collision.

By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s with a car at 57.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 14.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s with a van at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.5 s with a car at 39.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.3%.
A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
A further close pass had a PET of 2.7 s with a van at 59.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the recorded death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled adult death risks for these events would fall to 0.0%, 0.0%, 0.6%, 0.0% and 0.0% respectively.

In engineering terms, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, from 58 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 69.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 56.1 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given these measurements we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We asked for measurements at the Ring Road crossing. In 28.9 minutes 8 people were seen crossing and 12 vehicles were counted.

The headline finding is that 6 of 8 crossings (1 in 1.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 8 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s.

If this recording is typical the exact 95% ranges are 34.9-96.8% of crossings within 3 s and 15.7-84.3% within 1.5 s. In this recording serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The 85th percentile speed was 61.2 km/h. Among the worst near-misses measured, the fastest vehicle was going at 44.5 km/h. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.4 s with a car at 44.5 km/h; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 5.2% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s with a car at 40.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 3.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a van at 31.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 1.7%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a bus at 19.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%.

A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a car at 14.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 28.9 minutes to 17 pedestrians and 25 vehicles an hour, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also 73.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

We measured safety at the Quarry Road crossing using a video of 18.9 minutes covering 6 crossings and 21 vehicles. During this recording, 3 of 6 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 6 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 11.8-88.2% and 0.4-64.1% of crossings and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long. The 85th percentile speed was 49.6 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.9 s the vehicle was going at 47.5 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 1.6 s it was going at 17.6 km/h.

The most serious near-miss was a bus that passed the same spot 0.9 s after a person. In that encounter the bus was travelling at 17.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw. The auto-rickshaw in that pass was travelling at 47.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 47.5 km/h the estimated death risk is 5.4%.

A third near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 2.3 s involving a car. The car in that pass was travelling at 34.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 19 pedestrians and 67 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 18.9 minutes of video, though a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also, 67.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, based on 4 gaps, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to slow vehicles and give priority to people crossing.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Park Avenue

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitored the crossing outside it for 38.4 minutes (2304.0 s). In that time we recorded 32 crossings and 17 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 26.3 km/h. The recording showed 1 serious near-miss in all. We observed 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

By definition, a serious near-miss is when a pedestrian and a moving vehicle are on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s apart.

The serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s and involved a car at 14.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 14.2 km/h the death risk from Rosén & Sander 2009 is 0.4%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.1 s and involved a van at 13.8 km/h.

A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s and involved a car at 24.6 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 50 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.4 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice, by 1.3x in our drone test. 

Also, 67.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and 7 of them 12 s or more and longest gap 33.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and to give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We write as the school using the crossing outside our gate. Crossing Watch video covering 25.6 minutes (1536.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 35 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.9 km/h. The van that came closest is driven by Mr. Ashok Varghese of the corner shop.

The analysis found 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Of the 8 potential conflicts, 4 had the person first, 2 had the vehicle first, and 0 had both at once.

The worst near-misses were:
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with an auto-rickshaw at 59.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 18.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s with a van at 51.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 9.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 19.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.9 s with a bus at 40.7 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 3.8%, compared with 0.2% at an impact of 8.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with a car at 30.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.5%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with a car at 51.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.4%, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
All death-risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15+ hit by car fronts.

For context, the video gives PV² of 0.0 x 10^8 from 19 pedestrians and 82 vehicles per hour, with the caveat that this is scaled from 25.6 minutes not a full peak hour and our test shows broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also, 62.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 11 such gaps including 3 of 12 s or more and longest 74.2 s, with the caveat that first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We have the video and Crossing Watch data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Hill View Road crossing. A Crossing Watch video of 1.8 minutes (108.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 48 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 44.0 km/h.

Engineering assessment is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 1.8. Within the recording, 43.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 9 gaps, 8 of them 12 s or more, longest 52.6 s (the first and last are cut short by the video).

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 35.9 km/h with 0.2 s between users.

A third serious near-miss involved a car at 22.5 km/h with 0.1 s between users.

A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 19.8 km/h with 1.0 s between users.

One close pass involved a car at 20.5 km/h with 2.0 s between users.

For adults hit by a car front, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates adult death risk rises with impact speed. At these speeds adult risk was 2.7% at 36.8 km/h, 2.5% at 35.9 km/h, 0.8% at 22.5 km/h and 0.6% at 19.8 km/h. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed and adult death risk would be lower, for example 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to slow vehicles and provide protected priority for pedestrians at this school crossing.

We are happy to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. Parents see the same danger here at each school dismissal.

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 41 vehicles an hour scaled from 33.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 46.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and longest 39.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Mill Street crossing

We write on behalf of the school about the crossing at Mill Street crossing.

Crossing Watch video analysis covering 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) recorded 5 pedestrian crossings and 37 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.6 km/h. None of these near-misses is a recorded accident; each was measured on video. There were 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In this method serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s. Of the 5 crossings, 1 was person first, 4 were vehicle first and 0 were both at once.

One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s with a car at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 11.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car at 22.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Engineering context is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 6.6 minutes. With that caveat, 44.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. That was 10 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 9.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing on a speed table with 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We can share the video and measurement log on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Re: Safety improvements at the Brook Street crossing

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Brook Street crossing. Crossing Watch video of this location covered 114.0 s of observation over 1.9 minutes. In that period 6 pedestrian crossings and 1 moving vehicle was counted. The 85th percentile speed was 64.2 km/h.

The review recorded 1 serious near-miss, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. The worst case involved a car with a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s. The vehicle speed was 57.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 14.6% based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15 years and older.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 1.9 minutes. The share of time inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed was 97.5%, comprising 11 gaps of 6 s or more and 3 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap at 82.2 s, noting that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce approach speeds and provide priority for pedestrians. We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the River Lane crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch measurements over 44.8 minutes recorded 12 crossings and 13 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 44.3 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 1.1 s the vehicle was going at 46.9 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 1.7 s it was going at 36.1 km/h. There was 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes, defined as a pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart for serious and 1.5 s to 3.0 s for a close pass.

PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 44.8 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test.

68.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 7 such gaps and 1 gap of 12 s or more, the longest 23.7 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 36.1 km/h, carrying an adult death risk of 2.5% if hit by a car front per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s with a car at 46.9 km/h, carrying an adult death risk of 4.1% if hit by a car front per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

Another close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.5 s with a car at 37.3 km/h, carrying an adult death risk of 2.8% if hit by a car front per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for those crossing.

We can share the video and measurement files on request and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school at Market Street crossing. Crossing Watch measured 8 pedestrian crossings and 9 moving vehicles in 11.7 minutes (702.0 s).

5 of 8 crossings (1 in 1.6) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 8 (1 in 2) had a vehicle within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 24.5-91.5% and 15.7-84.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 50.7 mph. By definition serious is less than 1.5 s apart and close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.8 s with a motorcycle at 45.5 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 5.7% per Rosen & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had a PET of 0.3 s with a motorcycle at 40.0 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 3.5%).
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 37.6 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 2.9%).
A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s with a car at 22.4 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 0.7%).
A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a bus at 50.1 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 6.7%).

PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 11.7. 50.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 4 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 54.9 s.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and counts to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of our school regarding the Quarry Road crossing.

During 26.9 minutes of video (1614.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 13 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles at the crossing. The 85th percentile speed was 51.4 km/h. Mrs. Leela Fernandes, who drives the morning bus, caused the worst of these events. In that period 3 of 13 crossings (1 in 4.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 13 (1 in 6.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.0-53.8% and 1.9-45.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass at 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.9 km/h with 0.3 s between road users on the same spot.
Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 13.3 km/h with 0.5 s between road users on the same spot.
A close pass involved a van at 50.6 km/h with 2.2 s between road users on the same spot.
The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at those speeds is 1.1% for the bus case, 0.3% for the auto-rickshaw case and 1.2% for the van case, from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

For engineering context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 29 pedestrians and 9 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.9 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one pedestrian twice.
74.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 4 such gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.4 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow approaching traffic and protect children crossing.

We have the video and SAM tracking data and are happy to share it for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

From the Head of the School, Ring Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We request that you make the crossing outside our school safer by installing a raised zebra crossing with speed table.

Crossing Watch made measurements from video of the crossing using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. The video covered 6.7 minutes (402.0 s). In that time there were 6 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 57.1 km/h. The closest of these passes was in fact a collision.

There were 3 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s. Of the interactions, 3 were person first, 1 was vehicle first and 0 were both at once.

The worst incidents were as follows. A bus at 55.2 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 12.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.
A car at 37.3 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 2.8%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.
A van at 18.0 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 0.5%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 18.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.5%.
A car at 47.4 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 2.7 s in the close pass category. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video. This video is 6.7 minutes with 6 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles, so PV² cannot be assessed. 44.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. There were 5 such gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 47.1 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4 to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10 to 12 s or longer.

We ask you to install the raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and to consider a 20 km/h zone with signs. We are ready to share the video and the measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school – Cedar Lane

We write concerning the crossing outside our school on Cedar Lane. An independent video review (Crossing Watch, SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) observed 24.8 minutes (1488.0 s) at the site and counted 14 crossings and 19 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 59.9 km/h. There have already been injuries at this spot this school year.

The review classified 3 events as serious, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 events as close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s. In 2 cases the person was first, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both were at once.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 52.2 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 10.0% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, which would fall to 0.2% at an impact of 8.4 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Another serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 50.2 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The report notes an adult death risk of 8.5% if hit at that speed.

A third serious near-miss involved a van at 31.2 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s. The report notes an adult death risk of 1.6% if hit at that speed.

A close pass involved a car at 55.2 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A further close pass involved a car at 33.1 km/h with a gap of 2.1 s.

The engineering note estimates PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 24.8 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice. 95.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, in 4 gaps with the longest 83.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location. We can share the video and measurement details for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the crossing outside our school on Mill Street. Crossing Watch measured 11 pedestrian crossings and 6 moving vehicles in 6.7 minutes (402.0 s) of video using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

In that recording 3 of 11 crossings (1 in 3.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 11 (1 in 11) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-61.0% and 0.2-41.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s with a car travelling at 49.5 km/h. A young pupil hit by the fastest vehicle would probably not have survived. For an adult hit by a car front that speed carries an 8.0% death risk, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h with an impact at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second near-miss was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 2.1 s with a van travelling at 40.9 km/h.

A third near-miss was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 2.8 s with a van travelling at 57.6 km/h.

The 85th percentile speed was 56.1 km/h. Engineering context is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 6.7 minutes. In this short recording 82.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 of them 12 s or more and the longest gap 35.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing.

We can share the video and measurement file for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvements at Cedar Lane crossing

We measured the Cedar Lane crossing for 36.7 minutes (2202.0 s). In that time 37 people crossed and 16 vehicles passed. The 85th percentile speed was 62.8 km/h.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s and involved a car travelling at 59.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 17.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). A fourth event was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 1.6 s and a motorcycle travelling at 30.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 1.2%.

A fifth event was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s and a motorcycle travelling at 48.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (60 pedestrians and 26 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.7 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test). We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measurements.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding safety outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. A video survey of 25.7 minutes recorded 8 crossings and 38 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 38.5 km/h.

The review found 0 serious near-misses and 5 close passes, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Of these, 3 were person-first and 2 were vehicle-first.

The worst close passes were:
The fastest close pass with a gap of 1.5 s involved a car at 29.4 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 1.4%.
A close pass with a gap of 2.0 s involved a car at 35.4 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 0.6%.
A close pass with a gap of 1.7 s involved a bus at 20.4 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 0.4%.
A close pass with a gap of 1.9 s involved a car at 22.6 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 0.2%.
A close pass with a gap of 2.0 s involved a bus at 18.9 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 0.0%.
Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen & Sander 2009.

For context, PV2 was scaled as 0.0 x 10^8 from 19 pedestrians and 89 vehicles per hour, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3 times. Also, 53.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 8 such gaps and 8 gaps of 12 s or more and longest gap 58.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We have the 25.7 minute video and tracking data available and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Lantern Road

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the crossing outside our school on Lantern Road. We had 41.9 minutes of video reviewed by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time). In that time 22 people crossed and 29 vehicles passed, with an 85th percentile speed of 51.8 km/h. To sum up, the recording showed 3 serious near-misses and 3 close passes.

The review found 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 close passes (1.5-3.0 s), with person first in 2 cases and vehicle first in 4 cases.

The worst events were:
A serious near-miss with a gap of 0.2 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 51.0 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 9.1% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h impact).
A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.4 s involving a car at 44.5 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 5.2%.
A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.1 s involving a car at 44.2 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 5.1%.
A close pass with a gap of 1.9 s involving a van at 22.6 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 0.2%.
A close pass with a gap of 2.2 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 28.1 km/h.
All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 for 32 pedestrians and 42 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 41.9 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. 81.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 6 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 75.2 s, with first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this crossing to lower speeds and provide a protected crossing point.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of our school regarding the Quarry Road crossing.

During 26.9 minutes of video (1614.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 13 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles at the crossing. The 85th percentile speed was 51.4 km/h. A parent was injured here by a passing motorcycle earlier this year. In that period 3 of 13 crossings (1 in 4.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 13 (1 in 6.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.0-53.8% and 1.9-45.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass at 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.9 km/h with 0.3 s between road users on the same spot.
Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 13.3 km/h with 0.5 s between road users on the same spot.
A close pass involved a van at 50.6 km/h with 2.2 s between road users on the same spot.
The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at those speeds is 1.1% for the bus case, 0.3% for the auto-rickshaw case and 1.2% for the van case, from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

For engineering context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 29 pedestrians and 9 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.9 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one pedestrian twice.
74.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 4 such gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.4 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow approaching traffic and protect children crossing.

We have the video and SAM tracking data and are happy to share it for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Another serious near-miss had a time gap of 1.3 s with a van at 16.5 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%, compared with 0.4% at 16.5 km/h. 
One close pass had a time gap of 1.9 s with a car at 24.5 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Market Street.

We arranged a video-based Crossing Watch for 36.4 minutes (2184.0 s). In that time 35 crossings and 39 vehicles were observed. 6 of 35 crossings (1 in 5.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 35 crossings (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.6-33.6% and 1.8-23.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h. Mrs. Leela Fernandes, who drives the morning bus, caused the worst of these events.

By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s with a car at 57.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 14.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s with a van at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.5 s with a car at 39.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.3%.
A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
A further close pass had a PET of 2.7 s with a van at 59.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the recorded death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled adult death risks for these events would fall to 0.0%, 0.0%, 0.6%, 0.0% and 0.0% respectively.

In engineering terms, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, from 58 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 69.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 56.1 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given these measurements we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

We write about the crossing outside our school at Garden Road crossing. Crossing Watch analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 2.1 minutes (126.0 s) of video with 7 pedestrian crossings and 1 moving vehicles. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 2.1, so rates are only indicative.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to reduce speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A fifth event involved a van at 18.6 km/h with 0.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5%, which remains 0.5% at an impact of 18.6 km/h.

Risk estimates are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on Hill View Road

We measured traffic at the crossing on Hill View Road for 39.3 minutes. In that time we observed 34 crossings and 21 vehicles. The 85th-percentile speed was 60.0 km/h. The video showed 12 gaps of 12 s or more with no moving vehicle.

We recorded 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes of 1.5 s to 3.0 s. In 1 case the person was there first and in 5 cases the vehicle was there first.

The most severe near-miss involved a car at 56.6 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 14.1% based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15 and above.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 28.6 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.3%.
A further serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.0 km/h with a gap of 0.1 s.
A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 25.1 km/h with a gap of 0.6 s. The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.0%.

Engineering indicators were calculated as follows. PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 52 pedestrians and 32 vehicles per hour scaled from the video, noting that a formal check requires the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x in drone tests. 45.3% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for children crossing. We are willing to share the video and measurement file for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request to make Park Avenue crossing safer

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked for a video survey of Park Avenue crossing. In 26.1 minutes (1566.0 s) of video, 29 crossings and 38 vehicles were observed. The 85th percentile speed was 39.3 km/h. These results satisfy the official criteria for a pedestrian signal at this spot.

6 of 29 crossings (1 in 4.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person and 3 of 29 (1 in 9.7) within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.0-39.7% and 2.2-27.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 close passes (1.5-3.0 s).

The worst serious incidents were: a motorcycle with a gap of 1.1 s at 34.0 km/h with adult death risk if hit by a car front of 2.1% (5.2 km/h and 0.2% at 20 km/h limit); an auto-rickshaw with a gap of 0.3 s at 13.5 km/h with adult death risk of 0.3% (13.5 km/h and 0.3% at 20 km/h limit); and a bus with a gap of 1.1 s at 13.6 km/h with adult death risk of 0.3% (13.6 km/h and 0.3% at 20 km/h limit). Close passes included a bus with a gap of 2.0 s at 39.1 km/h with adult death risk of 0.8% and a car with a gap of 2.3 s at 14.2 km/h with adult death risk of 0.0%. Risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 67 pedestrians and 87 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.1 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 62.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 10 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more, longest 49.0 s, with the first and last cut short by the video; UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs at this location. We will share the full video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

We measured safety at the Quarry Road crossing using a video of 18.9 minutes covering 6 crossings and 21 vehicles. Local residents report that vehicles regularly jump the signal here late at night. During this recording, 3 of 6 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 6 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 11.8-88.2% and 0.4-64.1% of crossings and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long. The 85th percentile speed was 49.6 km/h.

The most serious near-miss was a bus that passed the same spot 0.9 s after a person. In that encounter the bus was travelling at 17.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw. The auto-rickshaw in that pass was travelling at 47.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 47.5 km/h the estimated death risk is 5.4%.

A third near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 2.3 s involving a car. The car in that pass was travelling at 34.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 19 pedestrians and 67 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 18.9 minutes of video, though a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also, 67.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, based on 4 gaps, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to slow vehicles and give priority to people crossing.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety at North Avenue crossing

We are writing to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our school.

Measurements from a Crossing Watch survey over 6.9 minutes (414.0 s) recorded 11 pedestrian crossings and 7 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 50.5 km/h. All of the pedestrians involved were children on their way home.

In that short period there was 1 serious near-miss (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s apart).

The most serious event had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s and involved a car at 16.9 km/h.

A separate close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s and involved a motorcycle at 44.4 km/h.

A separate close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.6 s and involved a bus at 17.6 km/h.

For the car event, published figures for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+) give an adult death risk if hit of 0.5% at 16.9 km/h.

Engineering context carries caveats: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 6.9 minutes, and 81.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more (4 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 41.7 s) with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that the road authority install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and protect children crossing.

We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at North Avenue crossing

Our school arranged a video measurement at North Avenue crossing for 3.7 minutes (222.0 s).

In that recording 12 pedestrian crossings and 41 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 61.3 km/h. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began. 6 of 12 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 21.1-78.9% and 9.9-65.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Serious near-misses were defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s) were recorded.

The worst incidents were as follows. One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car at 58.3 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 16.1%. One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s with a car at 23.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.8%. One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s with an auto-rickshaw at 16.5 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4%. One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s with a car at 12.6 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.3%. One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.5 s with a bus at 35.7 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 2.4%. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front per Rosen & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, 83.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more, 0 of them 12 s or more and longest gap 10.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 3.7 minutes, so counts are limited to 12 pedestrian crossings and 41 moving vehicles.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h speed table and warning signs at this location to lower approach speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We can share the video and measurement data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow approaching traffic and protect children crossing.

We have the video and SAM tracking data and are happy to share it for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.8 s with a car at 25.8 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.4%.
A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s with a motorcycle at 21.5 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.2%.

For context, PV2 was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 25 pedestrians and 59 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 29.3 minutes of video, but a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in our drone test.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h approach signs at this crossing.
We have retained the video files from the 29.3 minute recording and can share them on request for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We can share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Lantern Road

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the crossing outside our school on Lantern Road. We had 41.9 minutes of video reviewed by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time). In that time 22 people crossed and 29 vehicles passed, with an 85th percentile speed of 51.8 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.2 s the vehicle was going at 44.5 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 1.4 s it was going at 51.0 km/h.

The review found 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 close passes (1.5-3.0 s), with person first in 2 cases and vehicle first in 4 cases.

The worst events were:
A serious near-miss with a gap of 0.2 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 51.0 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 9.1% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h impact).
A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.4 s involving a car at 44.5 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 5.2%.
A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.1 s involving a car at 44.2 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 5.1%.
A close pass with a gap of 1.9 s involving a van at 22.6 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 0.2%.
A close pass with a gap of 2.2 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 28.1 km/h.
All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 for 32 pedestrians and 42 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 41.9 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. 81.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 6 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 75.2 s, with first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this crossing to lower speeds and provide a protected crossing point.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about pedestrian safety at the Canal Road crossing outside our school.

We arranged a video survey of 11.8 minutes (708.0 s). It recorded 11 pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 17.9 km/h. 11 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video. 3 of 11 crossings (1 in 3.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person and 2 of 11 (1 in 5.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-61.0% and 2.3-51.8% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Serious was defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, close pass as 1.5-3.0 s. There were 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. In 1 case the person was first and in 2 cases the vehicle was first.

The worst serious near-miss involved a car at 18.9 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+). At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 18.9 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 15.7 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.4%. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 15.7 km/h with 0.4% adult death risk.

A close pass involved a motorcycle at 18.1 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 11.8 minutes. 57.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 85.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Hill View Road crossing. A Crossing Watch video of 1.8 minutes (108.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 48 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 44.0 km/h. Many of these drivers were not watching the road at all.

Engineering assessment is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 1.8. Within the recording, 43.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 9 gaps, 8 of them 12 s or more, longest 52.6 s (the first and last are cut short by the video).

In that same 1.8 minutes there were 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 36.8 km/h with 1.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 35.9 km/h with 0.2 s between users.

A third serious near-miss involved a car at 22.5 km/h with 0.1 s between users.

A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 19.8 km/h with 1.0 s between users.

One close pass involved a car at 20.5 km/h with 2.0 s between users.

For adults hit by a car front, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates adult death risk rises with impact speed. At these speeds adult risk was 2.7% at 36.8 km/h, 2.5% at 35.9 km/h, 0.8% at 22.5 km/h and 0.6% at 19.8 km/h. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed and adult death risk would be lower, for example 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to slow vehicles and provide protected priority for pedestrians at this school crossing.

We are happy to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We can share the video and tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Request for safety improvements at the Brook Street crossing

We write following a 4.5 minute (270.0 s) video recording at the Brook Street crossing, which captured 6 pedestrian crossings and 24 moving vehicles.

Headline findings were that 4 of 6 crossings (1 in 1.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 6 (1 in 3) were within 1.5 s. The recording also showed 2 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5 to 3.0 s).

In that recording the 85th percentile speed was 56.6 km/h. There have already been injuries at this spot this school year.

Our most serious near-miss involved a van at 17.4 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 13.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.

A close pass involved a car at 51.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s.

Another close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 29.3 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.8 s.

On engineering context, we note that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 4.5. Also, 74.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 9 such gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 23.5 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given the speeds and the proportion of crossings with close vehicle interactions, we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We would be happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make Park Avenue crossing safer

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked for a video survey of Park Avenue crossing. In 26.1 minutes (1566.0 s) of video, 29 crossings and 38 vehicles were observed. The 85th percentile speed was 39.3 km/h. 29 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video.

6 of 29 crossings (1 in 4.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person and 3 of 29 (1 in 9.7) within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.0-39.7% and 2.2-27.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 close passes (1.5-3.0 s).

The worst serious incidents were: a motorcycle with a gap of 1.1 s at 34.0 km/h with adult death risk if hit by a car front of 2.1% (5.2 km/h and 0.2% at 20 km/h limit); an auto-rickshaw with a gap of 0.3 s at 13.5 km/h with adult death risk of 0.3% (13.5 km/h and 0.3% at 20 km/h limit); and a bus with a gap of 1.1 s at 13.6 km/h with adult death risk of 0.3% (13.6 km/h and 0.3% at 20 km/h limit). Close passes included a bus with a gap of 2.0 s at 39.1 km/h with adult death risk of 0.8% and a car with a gap of 2.3 s at 14.2 km/h with adult death risk of 0.0%. Risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 67 pedestrians and 87 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.1 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 62.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 10 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more, longest 49.0 s, with the first and last cut short by the video; UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs at this location. We will share the full video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Station Road crossing outside our school.

A 10.9 minute video (654.0 s) of the crossing recorded 11 pedestrian crossings and 32 moving vehicles. 6 of 11 crossings (1 in 1.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person. 3 of 11 crossings (1 in 3.7) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 23.4-83.3% and 6.0-61.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 61.6 km/h.

Worst near-misses measured by post-encroachment time were:

The most severe serious near-miss had a PET of 0.3 s involving a car at 53.6 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 11.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit. A child struck in the worst near-miss would have faced a 25% risk of death.

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s involving a bus at 40.5 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 3.7%, falling to 0.2% at an impact of 8.8 km/h at a 20 km/h limit.

A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s involving a car at 13.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.3%, remaining 0.3% at an impact of 13.2 km/h at a 20 km/h limit.

A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s involving a car at 36.6 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 1.2%, falling to 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit.

A further close pass had a PET of 1.6 s involving a van at 28.3 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 1.0%, falling to 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 10.9 minutes, so rates are indicative only. 62.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps, 10 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.5 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request the raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce speeds and separate people and vehicles in time and space. We are happy to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write concerning safety outside our school at Bridge Street crossing.

A 5.0 minute (300.0 s) recording counted 5 pedestrian crossings and 20 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 55.4 km/h. To sum up, the recording showed 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes.

4 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person and 2 of 5 (1 in 2.5) within 1.5 s.

Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 28.4% to 99.5% and 5.3% to 85.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1 to 10.2 and 0.2 to 7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5 s to 3.0 s).

1 serious near-miss had PET of 0.0 s with a car at 53.0 km/h where adult death risk if hit is 10.7% compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

1 serious near-miss had PET of 0.1 s with a van at 48.7 km/h where adult death risk if hit is 7.5% compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

1 close pass had PET of 2.7 s with a car at 38.4 km/h.

1 close pass had PET of 2.7 s with a car at 33.3 km/h.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 5.0 minutes.

67.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 11 gaps, 7 of them 12 s or more, longest 33.7 s (first and last cut short by video).

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h speed table and signs at this location.

We are happy to share the recording data and video for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Station Road

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). In that time 38 crossings and 8 vehicles were recorded, the 85th percentile speed was 44.1 km/h, there were 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 7 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 53.4 s, and 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. Every person in these near-misses was a pupil of our school. 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 38 (1 in 7.6) within 1.5 s; exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-31.3% and 4.4-28.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Orchard Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about safety at Orchard Lane crossing. A video recording of 10.1 minutes (606.0 s) measured 5 pedestrian crossings and 10 vehicles, with 85th percentile speed 58.8 km/h. The video showed 5 gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle.

Headline result: 3 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 3 of 5 (1 in 1.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 14.7-94.7% and 14.7-94.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Within that time there were 3 serious near-misses and 0 close passes, where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a van at 52.0 km/h with 0.8 s between road users.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 48.5 km/h with 1.1 s between road users.

A third serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 22.9 km/h with 1.4 s between road users.

For adults hit by a car front the estimated death risks for those speeds are 9.8%, 7.3% and 0.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact speeds would be 0.0 km/h, 0.0 km/h and 17.3 km/h with death risks 0.0%, 0.0% and 0.5%.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 10.1 minutes with 5 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles. 50.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more, 0 gaps of 12 s or more and longest gap 11.3 s, with the main caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and measurement log for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a raised zebra crossing at the Park Avenue crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school on Park Avenue. During 43.9 minutes, cameras logged 37 crossings and 10 vehicles. We arranged a video review of 43.9 minutes (2634.0 s) which recorded 37 crossings and 10 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 56.6 km/h.

In that period 2 of 37 crossings (1 in 18) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 37 (1 in 37) was within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 0.7-18.2% and 0.1-14.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.2-7.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst serious near-miss involved a car at 59.5 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 17.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
The second event was a close pass with a gap of 2.3 s. It involved a car at 17.2 km/h.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 51 pedestrians and 14 vehicles per hour scaled from 43.9 minutes, noting a formal check requires a full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount by about 1.3x in tests. Also 75.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more (8 gaps, 5 of 12 s or more, longest 74.3 s), noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry) for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
