Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request a safety improvement at the crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch measurement using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry to assess post-encroachment time.

Over 11.1 minutes (666.0 s) the video counted 12 pedestrian crossings and 11 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 48.4 km/h. The death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). In that period 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 12 crossings (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s.
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The video found 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. The worst serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 47.4 km/h. A second serious near-miss was 0.2 s apart involving a van at 44.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss was 0.4 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 13.1 km/h. The close pass was 1.9 s apart involving a car at 50.1 km/h.
For adults hit by a car front, Rosén and Sander 2009 gives an adult death risk if hit of 6.7% for the 47.4 km/h case, 5.0% for the 44.0 km/h case, 0.3% for the 13.1 km/h case, and 3.2% for the 50.1 km/h case. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the 47.4 km/h case, 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk for the 44.0 km/h case, 13.1 km/h with 0.3% adult death risk for the 13.1 km/h case, and 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the 50.1 km/h case.

For context, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 11.1 minutes. The recording also shows 66.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 such gaps and 3 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 33.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h markings at this location.

We are willing to share the video and measurement files for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

A 3.8 minute recording (228.0 s) counted 10 pedestrian crossings and 24 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 28.8 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 18.0 km/h with a gap of 0.4 s. A close pass involved a bus at 17.1 km/h with a gap of 2.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at 29.5 km/h the death risk is 1.4%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

Assessment of PV² hourly rates needs at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 3.8 minutes. During the recording 80.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 7 gaps, 5 of them 12 s or more, longest 16.8 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to slow traffic and protect people crossing.

We are happy to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Quarry Road crossing.

Our Crossing Watch video recorded 4.0 minutes (240.0 s) with 8 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 53.7 km/h. 8 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video. In that time 4 of 8 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, and 3 of 8 (1 in 2.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 15.7-84.3% and 8.5-75.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the serious events 1 was person-first and 3 were vehicle-first, and 1 close pass was also recorded.

One serious near-miss was 0.2 s apart and involved an auto-rickshaw at 56.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 13.6%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss was 0.8 s apart and involved a car at 21.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.7%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A third serious near-miss was 1.4 s apart and involved an auto-rickshaw at 19.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.6%, compared with 0.6% at 19.6 km/h.

A close pass was 2.4 s apart and involved a motorcycle at 43.6 km/h.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 4.0 minutes with 8 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles counted, so we do not use that metric. About 72.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 59.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We ask for a raised zebra crossing to reduce speeds toward the 20.0 km/h limit and provide priority. We can share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school at Ring Road crossing

We measured the Ring Road crossing for 31.9 minutes and recorded 30 crossings and 34 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 62.1 km/h. The recording showed 2 serious near-misses in all.

In that period, 6 of 30 crossings (1 in 5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 30 crossings (1 in 7.5) were within 1.5 s. The engineering note estimates PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 56 pedestrians and 64 vehicles per hour scaled from 31.9 minutes, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount. 57.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 4 such gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 75.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The most serious near-misses were defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. One serious near-miss involved a bus at 56.4 km/h with 0.5 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 13.9% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+ car fronts, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 42.7 km/h with 0.5 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 4.5% per Rosén & Sander 2009, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 21.3 km/h with 0.5 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.7% per Rosén & Sander 2009, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 14.3 km/h with 1.2 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.4% per Rosén & Sander 2009, compared with 0.4% at 14.3 km/h.
A close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 59.4 km/h with 2.3 s between person and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 2.0% per Rosén & Sander 2009, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We have the video and Crossing Watch SAM tracking measurements and are willing to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on River Lane

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the River Lane crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch recorded 25 crossings in 36.0 minutes with 10 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 56.9 km/h. The recording these figures come from lasted 36.0 minutes.

In that period 2 of 25 crossings (1 in 12) were serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 of 25 (1 in 12) were within 3 s. Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 1.0-26.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most severe was a bus at 52.9 km/h passing 0.1 s after a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 10.6% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

The second serious near-miss was a van at 22.9 km/h passing 1.3 s after a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 36.0 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice. Also, 62.4% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 3 such gaps and longest 81.8 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pupils crossing.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry) for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Park Avenue

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitored the crossing outside it for 38.4 minutes (2304.0 s). In that time we recorded 32 crossings and 17 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 26.3 km/h. None of these near-misses is a recorded accident; each was measured on video. We observed 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

By definition, a serious near-miss is when a pedestrian and a moving vehicle are on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s apart.

The serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s and involved a car at 14.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 14.2 km/h the death risk from Rosén & Sander 2009 is 0.4%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.1 s and involved a van at 13.8 km/h.

A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s and involved a car at 24.6 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 50 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.4 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice, by 1.3x in our drone test. 

Also, 67.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and 7 of them 12 s or more and longest gap 33.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and to give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir / Madam,

Re: Safety at Lake View Road crossing

In a Crossing Watch video of 33.6 minutes (2016.0 s) we measured 6 pedestrian crossings and 33 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 43.6 km/h. The closest near-miss measured had a time gap of 2.3 s.

5 of 6 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 6 (1 in 2) were within 1.5 s.
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 35.9-99.6% and 11.8-88.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes were:
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s and involved a car at 35.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 2.3% for a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s and involved a car at 33.4 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 2.0% for a car front, falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s and involved a car at 17.8 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.5% for a car front, remaining 0.5% at an impact of 17.8 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s and involved a car at 22.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.1% at an impact of 3.3 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.3 s and involved a bus at 44.8 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, but this is scaled from only 33.6 minutes of video and a formal check counts the full peak hour with caveats about broken tracks.
73.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 8 of 12 s or more and longest gap 76.8 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority.

We can share the full video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A bus at 51.3 km/h was 1.2 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 9.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.
A car at 51.1 km/h was 0.8 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 9.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.

An auto-rickshaw at 44.2 km/h was 0.7 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 5.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 18.8 km/h.
A bus at 42.7 km/h was 1.4 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 4.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.

We request that you install the raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We offer to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Garden Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of the school beside Garden Road crossing to request a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h approach markings. Parents see the same danger here at each school dismissal.

Crossing Watch video analysis covered 2.0 minutes (120.0 s). In that time 7 pedestrian crossings and 30 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 54.0 km/h. A serious near-miss is defined as a pedestrian and a moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. A close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart.

We recorded 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. In 5 cases the pedestrian was first, in 1 case the vehicle was first.

The most severe serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 51.9 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts) would have been 9.7%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 9.1 km/h with a death risk of 0.2%.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 44.4 km/h with a gap of 1.0 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 5.2%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

A third serious near-miss involved a bus at 27.8 km/h with a gap of 0.6 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 1.2%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6%.

A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 20.6 km/h with a gap of 0.9 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 0.6%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6%.

A close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 46.1 km/h with a gap of 1.6 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 4.8%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video. This video is 2.0 minutes. Also, 96.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. There were 2 gaps of 6 s and 1 gap of 12 s or more. The longest gap was 69.1 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h approach markings to reduce approach speeds and protect pedestrians using the crossing.

We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Garden Road outside our school. A Crossing Watch review of 174.0 s of video (2.9 minutes) counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 39 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.9 km/h. The video showed 10 gaps of 12 s or more with no moving vehicle.

There were 3 serious near-misses defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 3 close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. Of the 6 crossings, 1 had the person enter first and 5 had the vehicle enter first.

The worst events were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a bus at 56.2 km/h with a gap of 0.4 s and an adult death risk of 13.7% if hit by a car front, which would be 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
Another serious near-miss involved a van at 49.0 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s and an adult death risk of 7.7% if hit by a car front, which would be 0.3% at an impact of 13.5 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
A further serious near-miss involved a car at 24.3 km/h with a gap of 0.5 s and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit by a car front, which would be 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
One close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 29.9 km/h with a gap of 1.9 s and an adult death risk of 0.5% if hit by a car front.
Another close pass involved a car at 15.0 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s and an adult death risk of 0.0% if hit by a car front.
Risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen & Sander 2009.

For context, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 2.9. 82.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps and 4 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.0 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We hold the video and measurement data and are willing to share them on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Request for safety improvements at the Brook Street crossing

We write following a 4.5 minute (270.0 s) video recording at the Brook Street crossing, which captured 6 pedestrian crossings and 24 moving vehicles.

Headline findings were that 4 of 6 crossings (1 in 1.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 6 (1 in 3) were within 1.5 s. The recording also showed 2 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5 to 3.0 s).

In that recording the 85th percentile speed was 56.6 km/h. 9 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video.

Our most serious near-miss involved a van at 17.4 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 13.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.

A close pass involved a car at 51.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s.

Another close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 29.3 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.8 s.

On engineering context, we note that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 4.5. Also, 74.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 9 such gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 23.5 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given the speeds and the proportion of crossings with close vehicle interactions, we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We would be happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir or Madam,

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at Market Street crossing following video measurements of pedestrian risk.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 54.1% to 100.0% and 35.9% to 99.6% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2 to 13.1 and 1.6 to 11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 55.5 km/h. A child hit at these speeds would face about a 9% chance of dying. There was 1 person-first and 5 vehicle-first interactions, with 0 both-at-once, comprising 5 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5 s to 3.0 s).

Worst near-misses (serious):
A bus at 51.3 km/h was 1.2 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 9.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.
A car at 51.1 km/h was 0.8 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 9.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.
A car at 46.3 km/h was 0.3 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 6.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 20.0 km/h.
An auto-rickshaw at 44.2 km/h was 0.7 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 5.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 18.8 km/h.
A bus at 42.7 km/h was 1.4 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 4.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.

Engineering context, briefly and with caveats: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, but this recording is 4.6 minutes with 6 crossings and 33 vehicles, so estimates are limited. 41.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 54.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4 s to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10 s to 12 s or longer.

We request that you install the raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We offer to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety at Brook Street crossing

We write concerning the Brook Street crossing outside our school. A Crossing Watch analysis of 8.6 minutes (516.0 s) of video recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 16 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h. The recording showed 0 serious near-misses in all.

Of the 7 crossings, 2 of 7 (1 in 3.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 7 (1 in 3.5) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, the exact 95% ranges are 3.7-71.0% and 3.7-71.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 2 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart), with 2 cases where the vehicle went first. 59.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, in 6 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 61.3 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video so this 8.6 minute sample is too short for those rates, and UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups such as children may need 10-12 s or longer.

The worst events were both classified as serious. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 55.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 12.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), which would be 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit. The other involved a bus at 16.3 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%, which would be 0.4% at an impact of 16.3 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow traffic and give pedestrians priority.

We would be pleased to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Our school asked Crossing Watch to analyse video of the North Avenue crossing using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

We use the Crossing Watch definition that a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart.

We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. In that period 0 people crossed first, 3 vehicles passed first and 1 arrived both at once.

The worst cases were:
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s and involved a motorcycle at 20.7 km/h. One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.6 s and involved a motorcycle at 46.5 km/h. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 97 pedestrians and 70 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 23.0 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x the true count in the drone test). 77.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 7 gaps with longest 18.7 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We asked for measurements at the Ring Road crossing. In 28.9 minutes 8 people were seen crossing and 12 vehicles were counted.

The headline finding is that 6 of 8 crossings (1 in 1.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 8 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s.

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s with a car at 40.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 3.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a van at 31.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 1.7%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a bus at 19.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%.

A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a car at 14.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.3%.

Also 73.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for a raised zebra crossing at the crossing studied on Park Avenue crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write as the school using the crossing outside our premises. A Crossing Watch analysis of 38.6 minutes of video recorded 32 crossings and 30 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 63.7 km/h. To sum up, the recording showed 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes.
In that period 5 of 32 crossings (1 in 6.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person.
Of those, 3 of 32 (1 in 11) were within 1.5 s.
The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.3-32.8% and 2.0-25.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses recorded were as follows. A bus at 58.9 km/h was 1.0 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 16.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A motorcycle at 44.4 km/h was 0.5 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 5.2%.
A car at 42.8 km/h was 1.2 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.5%.
A car at 43.2 km/h was 2.3 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.3%.
A car at 34.8 km/h was 2.6 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.0%.
Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, calculated as 50 pedestrians and 47 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.6 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and our method can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x in drone tests.
Also 72.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 8 gaps including 1 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 60.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for people crossing.
We are willing to share the underlying measurements and discuss the site in detail, and we can provide the video file on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Cedar Lane outside our school. Crossing Watch video for 23.1 minutes (1386.0 s) recorded 16 crossings and 20 vehicles, with 85th percentile speed 59.9 km/h.

In that recording, 4 of 16 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 16 (1 in 16) was within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 7.3-52.4% and 0.2-30.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.1-10.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. There was 1 serious near-miss and 3 close passes.

The worst serious near-miss had PET 0.0 s involving a car at 50.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 8.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at impact 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h limit.

Of the close passes, 1 had PET 1.7 s involving a car at 54.6 km/h. 1 had PET 1.5 s involving a bus at 30.4 km/h. 1 had PET 1.9 s involving a motorcycle at 23.2 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 52 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 23.1 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x. 90.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps and 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 87.5 s, with the caveat that first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We can share the video measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Garden Road outside our school. A Crossing Watch review of 174.0 s of video (2.9 minutes) counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 39 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.9 km/h. 82.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more.

There were 3 serious near-misses defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 3 close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. Of the 6 crossings, 1 had the person enter first and 5 had the vehicle enter first.

The worst events were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a bus at 56.2 km/h with a gap of 0.4 s and an adult death risk of 13.7% if hit by a car front, which would be 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
Another serious near-miss involved a van at 49.0 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s and an adult death risk of 7.7% if hit by a car front, which would be 0.3% at an impact of 13.5 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
A further serious near-miss involved a car at 24.3 km/h with a gap of 0.5 s and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit by a car front, which would be 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
One close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 29.9 km/h with a gap of 1.9 s and an adult death risk of 0.5% if hit by a car front.
Another close pass involved a car at 15.0 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s and an adult death risk of 0.0% if hit by a car front.
Risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen & Sander 2009.

For context, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 2.9. 82.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps and 4 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.0 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We hold the video and measurement data and are willing to share them on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. To sum up, the recording showed 3 serious near-misses and 3 close passes.

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 41 vehicles an hour scaled from 33.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 46.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and longest 39.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Market Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school has reviewed video of Market Street crossing.

In 41.1 minutes of video (2466.0 s) we recorded 14 crossings and 11 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 53.4 km/h. There were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes, where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart.

One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 26.3 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 20.4 km/h with a gap of 0.9 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 0.6%.

One close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 46.9 km/h with a gap of 2.2 s.

Another close pass involved a car at 21.0 km/h with a gap of 2.4 s.

At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact speed would have been 20.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.6% for the 2 serious cases, and 0.0 km/h with 0.0% for the 2 close passes.

Engineering notes: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 20 pedestrians and 16 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 41.1 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. 95.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 83.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4 s to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups such as children may need 10 s to 12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Brook Street crossing outside our school. In a video recording lasting 43.6 minutes we measured 14 crossings and 14 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 58.2 km/h. 14 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video.

Of the 14 crossings, 4 of 14 crossings (1 in 3.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 3 of 14 (1 in 4.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.4-58.1% and 4.7-50.8% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss was 1.0 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 54.5 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 11.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A second serious near-miss was 0.3 s apart involving a car at 50.5 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 8.7%.
A third serious near-miss was 0.4 s apart involving a motorcycle at 29.5 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.4%.
A close pass was 2.4 s apart involving a car at 46.1 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.2%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, being 19 pedestrians and 19 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 43.6 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test.
Also, 48.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 9 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 25.4 s, with the caveat that the first and last are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children crossing.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review and would welcome a site inspection.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

On behalf of our school, I write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our premises.

There were 9 gaps of 6 s or more and 0 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 7.1 s.

There were 2 serious near-misses with a gap of less than 1.5 s and 1 close pass between 1.5 s and 3.0 s. One serious near-miss left 0.3 s between the person and a motorcycle at 52.0 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 9.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss left 0.5 s between the person and a van at 21.4 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.7%. The site record is described as Canal Road crossing.

We request the raised zebra crossing with speed table to lower vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing. We are willing to share the underlying video-derived measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school has reviewed a video recording of the Quarry Road crossing. The recording lasted 11.8 minutes (708.0 s) and captured 6 pedestrian crossings and 32 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 61.1 km/h. Many drivers that morning were exceeding the posted speed limit near our school.

In that time 5 of 6 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 6 (1 in 1.5) were within 1.5 s, defined as serious. If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 35.9-99.6% and 22.3-95.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most severe incident was a serious near-miss with a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s involving a car at 53.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 11.1% per Rosen & Sander 2009, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A second serious near-miss had a gap of 0.3 s with a van at 21.4 km/h. For an adult the death risk at that speed is 0.7%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A third serious near-miss had a gap of 0.0 s with a motorcycle at 15.6 km/h. For an adult the death risk is 0.4% at 15.6 km/h and 0.4% at 15.6 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

A fourth serious near-miss had a gap of 0.3 s with a motorcycle at 16.1 km/h. For an adult the death risk is 0.4% at 16.1 km/h and 0.4% at 16.1 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

A further close pass had a gap of 2.3 s with a car at 15.2 km/h. For an adult the death risk is 0.0% at that speed and 0.0% at 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

We note PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 11.8. 73.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 3 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 6.2 s, with the first and last cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians. We are willing to share the video and measurements to support your assessment.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the Market Street crossing following a video survey of 10.9 minutes (654.0 s) that recorded 10 pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 52.4 km/h. Parents see the same danger here at each school dismissal.

The analysis found 5 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. A serious near-miss is defined as a pedestrian and a moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. In 1 case the pedestrian was first, in 5 cases the vehicle was first, and in 0 cases both were at once.

The most severe event involved a car at 53.7 km/h with 0.5 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 11.3%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

A second event involved an auto-rickshaw at 41.9 km/h with 0.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 4.2%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A third event involved a van at 35.0 km/h with 0.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 2.3%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A fourth event involved an auto-rickshaw at 18.9 km/h with 0.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5%, which remains 0.5% at an impact of 18.9 km/h.

A fifth event involved a van at 18.6 km/h with 0.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5%, which remains 0.5% at an impact of 18.6 km/h.

Risk estimates are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

Engineering context is limited. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, while this video is 10.9 minutes with 10 pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles. In this video 66.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps of 6 s or more including 1 gap of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 68.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and we are willing to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request a safety improvement at the crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch measurement using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry to assess post-encroachment time.

Over 11.1 minutes (666.0 s) the video counted 12 pedestrian crossings and 11 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 48.4 km/h. 66.6% of the time was inside gaps of 12 s or more. In that period 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 12 crossings (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s.
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The video found 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. The worst serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 47.4 km/h. A second serious near-miss was 0.2 s apart involving a van at 44.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss was 0.4 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 13.1 km/h. The close pass was 1.9 s apart involving a car at 50.1 km/h.
For adults hit by a car front, Rosén and Sander 2009 gives an adult death risk if hit of 6.7% for the 47.4 km/h case, 5.0% for the 44.0 km/h case, 0.3% for the 13.1 km/h case, and 3.2% for the 50.1 km/h case. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the 47.4 km/h case, 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk for the 44.0 km/h case, 13.1 km/h with 0.3% adult death risk for the 13.1 km/h case, and 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the 50.1 km/h case.

For context, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 11.1 minutes. The recording also shows 66.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 such gaps and 3 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 33.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h markings at this location.

We are willing to share the video and measurement files for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A bus at 51.3 km/h was 1.2 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 9.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.
A car at 51.1 km/h was 0.8 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 9.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit.
A car at 46.3 km/h was 0.3 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 6.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 20.0 km/h.

We offer to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about the crossing outside our school on Lantern Road. Crossing Watch measurements from 27.0 minutes of video (1620.0 s) recorded 8 crossings and 5 vehicles, with an 85th-percentile speed of 64.7 km/h. Had a child been struck, the impact would almost certainly have been fatal.

One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 58.6 km/h with 0.7 s between road users. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, would be 16.4%.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

We write concerning the crossing on Garden Road outside our school.

On engineering measures, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 for 47 pedestrians and 20 vehicles per hour, but this is scaled from only 17.7 minutes and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). Also 68.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and 7 of 12 s or more and the longest 84.3 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this crossing. We would be happy to share the video and the measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Ring Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school arranged video measurement at Ring Road crossing for 44.1 minutes (2646.0 s). In that time 36 people crossed and 25 moving vehicles passed. The 85th percentile speed was 42.1 km/h. All of the pedestrians involved were children on their way home.

4 of 36 crossings (1 in 9) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 36 (1 in 36) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 3.1-26.1% and 0.1-14.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst serious near-miss involved a van at 19.6 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A close pass involved a car at 42.7 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.0 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.2%.
Another close pass involved a car at 13.9 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s.
A further close pass involved a car at 24.2 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s.

For context, PV2 in the recording was 0.0 x 10^8, from 49 pedestrians and 34 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 44.1 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice, 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 56.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with high-visibility markings and curb build-outs at this crossing.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share it. Please let us know the next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing on Hill View Road

Our school monitored the Hill View Road crossing for 20.1 minutes (1206.0 s). We counted 14 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.9 km/h. Many of these drivers were not watching the road at all. There was 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 49.4 s.

In that time there were 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s apart). In 2 cases the person was first, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both were at once.

The worst incidents were as follows. 1 serious near-miss involved a van at 48.4 km/h with 1.0 s between road users; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 7.3% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). 1 serious near-miss involved a car at 21.8 km/h with 0.0 s between road users; the adult death risk is 0.7%. 1 serious near-miss involved a bus at 16.2 km/h with 0.9 s between road users; the adult death risk is 0.4%. 1 close pass involved a van at 47.8 km/h with 2.7 s between road users. 1 close pass involved a motorcycle at 26.6 km/h with 2.9 s between road users.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 42 pedestrians and 69 vehicles an hour scaled from 20.1 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also 95.1% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, from 1 such gap, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We can share the video for your review and welcome a site inspection.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority
Re: Safety at Garden Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the pedestrian crossing outside our school at Garden Road crossing.

Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) recorded 3.2 minutes (192.0 s) at the crossing. In that time there were 9 pedestrian crossings and 5 moving vehicles. The 192.0 s recording captured 9 crossings alongside 5 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 58.0 km/h.

5 of 9 crossings (1 in 1.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, and 2 of 9 (1 in 4.5) within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 21.2-86.3% and 2.8-60.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Of the near-misses, 2 were serious (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 were close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 3 cases the person was first, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 0 cases both were at once.

The worst events were:

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s. The vehicle was a bus at 59.4 km/h.
At that speed the risk of death for an adult hit by a car front is 17.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+). At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact speed would be 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s. The vehicle was a motorcycle at 33.3 km/h.
At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 2.0%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.0%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s. The vehicle was a van at 50.7 km/h.
At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.4%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.0%.

Another close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s. The vehicle was a bus at 33.4 km/h.
At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.0%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.0%.

A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.9 s. The vehicle was a car at 35.3 km/h.
At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.0%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.0%.

On engineering context: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, this recording is only 3.2 minutes with 9 pedestrian crossings and 5 moving vehicles. 80.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 6 gaps, 5 of them 12 s or more, longest 68.5 s (the first and last gaps are cut short by the video). UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request a raised zebra crossing on a speed table with 20 km/h zone signs and markings at Garden Road crossing to reduce speeds and provide priority for people crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and the full measurements for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We write as the school using the crossing outside our gate. Crossing Watch video covering 25.6 minutes (1536.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 35 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.9 km/h. The video showed 11 gaps of 12 s or more with no moving vehicle.

The analysis found 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Of the 8 potential conflicts, 4 had the person first, 2 had the vehicle first, and 0 had both at once.

The worst near-misses were:
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with an auto-rickshaw at 59.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 18.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s with a van at 51.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 9.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 19.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.9 s with a bus at 40.7 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 3.8%, compared with 0.2% at an impact of 8.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with a car at 30.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.5%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with a car at 51.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.4%, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
All death-risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15+ hit by car fronts.

For context, the video gives PV² of 0.0 x 10^8 from 19 pedestrians and 82 vehicles per hour, with the caveat that this is scaled from 25.6 minutes not a full peak hour and our test shows broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also, 62.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 11 such gaps including 3 of 12 s or more and longest 74.2 s, with the caveat that first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We have the video and Crossing Watch data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Park Avenue

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitored the crossing outside it for 38.4 minutes (2304.0 s). In that time we recorded 32 crossings and 17 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 26.3 km/h. These figures come from a single recording and may differ on other days. We observed 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

By definition, a serious near-miss is when a pedestrian and a moving vehicle are on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s apart.

The serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s and involved a car at 14.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 14.2 km/h the death risk from Rosén & Sander 2009 is 0.4%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.1 s and involved a van at 13.8 km/h.

A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s and involved a car at 24.6 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 50 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.4 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice, by 1.3x in our drone test. 

Also, 67.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and 7 of them 12 s or more and longest gap 33.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and to give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began.

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

LETTER:
Dear Road Authority,

I write as head of the school by the Bridge Street crossing about a video measurement of 8.1 minutes (486.0 s) at that crossing.

In that recording there were 5 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 65.1 km/h. The closest of these passes was in fact a collision. Of the 5 crossings, 4 of 5 (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 3 of 5 (1 in 1.7) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, the exact 95% ranges are 28.4-99.5% and 14.7-94.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). For engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 8.1 minutes, with 5 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles, so it cannot be used for that assessment. Also 83.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and the longest 86.6 s, but the first and last are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

By Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) a serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass as 1.5-3.0 s. There were 3 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. In that time 2 crossings were person-first, 1 was vehicle-first and 1 was both at once.

The worst cases were as follows. One serious near-miss was a van at 59.7 km/h with a gap of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 17.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with an impact of 0.0 km/h and 0.0% death risk at a 20 km/h limit.
Another serious near-miss was a car at 48.5 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 7.3%, compared with an impact of 20.0 km/h and 0.6% death risk at a 20 km/h limit.
A third serious near-miss was a bus at 40.5 km/h with a gap of 0.1 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.7%, compared with an impact of 20.0 km/h and 0.6% death risk at a 20 km/h limit.
A close pass was a car at 39.2 km/h with a gap of 2.3 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0%, compared with an impact of 0.0 km/h and 0.0% death risk at a 20 km/h limit.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at the Bridge Street crossing. We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Hill View Road crossing. A Crossing Watch video of 1.8 minutes (108.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 48 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 44.0 km/h. The van that came closest is driven by Mr. Ashok Varghese of the corner shop.

Engineering assessment is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 1.8. Within the recording, 43.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 9 gaps, 8 of them 12 s or more, longest 52.6 s (the first and last are cut short by the video).

In that same 1.8 minutes there were 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 36.8 km/h with 1.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 35.9 km/h with 0.2 s between users.

A third serious near-miss involved a car at 22.5 km/h with 0.1 s between users.

A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 19.8 km/h with 1.0 s between users.

One close pass involved a car at 20.5 km/h with 2.0 s between users.

For adults hit by a car front, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates adult death risk rises with impact speed. At these speeds adult risk was 2.7% at 36.8 km/h, 2.5% at 35.9 km/h, 0.8% at 22.5 km/h and 0.6% at 19.8 km/h. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed and adult death risk would be lower, for example 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to slow vehicles and provide protected priority for pedestrians at this school crossing.

We are happy to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

During 26.9 minutes of video (1614.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 13 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles at the crossing. The 85th percentile speed was 51.4 mph. One serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.9 km/h with 0.3 s between road users on the same spot.

A close pass involved a van at 50.6 km/h with 2.2 s between road users on the same spot.
The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at those speeds is 1.1% for the bus case, 0.3% for the auto-rickshaw case and 1.2% for the van case, from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow approaching traffic and protect children crossing.

We have the video and SAM tracking data and are happy to share it for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Garden Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school commissioned a video survey of the Garden Road crossing. In 16.9 minutes (1014.0 s) of video, 5 crossings and 8 vehicles were observed. 3 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 3 of 5 (1 in 1.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 14.7-94.7% and 14.7-94.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 45.6 km/h. The video showed 9 gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle.

There were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart.

One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.4 s with a car at 46.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

Another serious near-miss had a gap of 0.0 s with an auto-rickshaw at 22.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A third serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s with a car at 17.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.5%, compared with 0.5% at 17.5 km/h.

Engineering context from the survey, with caveats: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 18 pedestrians and 28 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 16.9 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour. 70.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 10 gaps, 9 of them 12 s or more, longest 23.5 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table to lower vehicle speeds and protect people crossing.

We are willing to share the full video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school at Canal Road crossing. Crossing Watch analysis of 34.6 minutes of video (2076.0 s) recorded 19 crossings and 23 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 56.5 km/h. Parents see the same danger here at each school dismissal.

In that recording 5 of 19 crossings (1 in 3.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 19 (1 in 19) within 1.5 s. The 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 9.1-51.2% and 0.1-26.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There was 1 serious near-miss and 4 close passes as defined by PET under 1.5 s and 1.5-3.0 s.

The serious near-miss had a PET of 0.9 s with a bus at 21.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk was 0.7%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A close pass had a PET of 2.0 s with a van at 55.2 km/h.

A close pass had a PET of 2.1 s with a bus at 49.3 km/h.

A close pass had a PET of 2.3 s with a car at 32.6 km/h.

A close pass had a PET of 2.4 s with a van at 39.5 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 34.6 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can double-count by 1.3x. Also 93.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 8 gaps of 12 s or more and longest gap 53.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. We are not stating that any standard is met.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to reduce approach speeds and give priority to pedestrians at this location.

We can share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

On the basis of a 9.7 minute video (582.0 s) at Lantern Road crossing we recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles. During the 9.7 minute recording at Lantern Road crossing, 28 moving vehicles and 7 pedestrian crossings were observed. The 85th percentile speed was 53.0 km/h. In that recording 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 7 (1 in 7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 42.1-99.6% and 0.4-57.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). By the study definition, 1 was serious (less than 1.5 s apart) and 5 were close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 3 cases the person was first and in 3 cases the vehicle was first.

The worst cases measured by post-encroachment time were:
A serious near-miss with PET of 0.3 s involving a car at 44.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 5.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at 20.0 km/h impact it would be 0.6%.
A close pass with PET of 2.2 s involving a bus at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.7%.
A close pass with PET of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 33.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.5%.
A close pass with PET of 2.1 s involving a car at 22.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
A close pass with PET of 2.4 s involving a bus at 31.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact and death risk for the last 4 cases would each be 0.0 km/h and 0.0%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 9.7 minutes, with 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles counted. With that caveat, 93.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 9 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and that the UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and establish pedestrian priority.

We are willing to share the video and the SAM tracking measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make Park Avenue crossing safer

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked for a video survey of Park Avenue crossing. In 26.1 minutes (1566.0 s) of video, 29 crossings and 38 vehicles were observed. The 85th percentile speed was 39.3 km/h.

6 of 29 crossings (1 in 4.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person and 3 of 29 (1 in 9.7) within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.0-39.7% and 2.2-27.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 close passes (1.5-3.0 s).

The worst serious incidents were: a motorcycle with a gap of 1.1 s at 34.0 km/h with adult death risk if hit by a car front of 2.1% (5.2 km/h and 0.2% at 20 km/h limit); an auto-rickshaw with a gap of 0.3 s at 13.5 km/h with adult death risk of 0.3% (13.5 km/h and 0.3% at 20 km/h limit); and a bus with a gap of 1.1 s at 13.6 km/h with adult death risk of 0.3% (13.6 km/h and 0.3% at 20 km/h limit). Close passes included a bus with a gap of 2.0 s at 39.1 km/h with adult death risk of 0.8% and a car with a gap of 2.3 s at 14.2 km/h with adult death risk of 0.0%. Risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 67 pedestrians and 87 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.1 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 62.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 10 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more, longest 49.0 s, with the first and last cut short by the video; UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs at this location. We will share the full video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school

We measured activity at the crossing outside the school for 40.6 minutes (2436.0 s). In that time we recorded 22 crossings and 29 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 41.9 km/h.

A third event was a van at 42.5 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A fourth event was a car at 23.0 km/h with a gap of 2.9 s.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We can share the video and tracking data on request.

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

We measured safety at the Quarry Road crossing using a video of 18.9 minutes covering 6 crossings and 21 vehicles. During this recording, 3 of 6 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 6 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 11.8-88.2% and 0.4-64.1% of crossings and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long. The 85th percentile speed was 49.6 km/h. This is what happens at the crossing on each day of the school week.

The most serious near-miss was a bus that passed the same spot 0.9 s after a person. In that encounter the bus was travelling at 17.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw. The auto-rickshaw in that pass was travelling at 47.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 47.5 km/h the estimated death risk is 5.4%.

A third near-miss was a close pass with a gap of 2.3 s involving a car. The car in that pass was travelling at 34.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 19 pedestrians and 67 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 18.9 minutes of video, though a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also, 67.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, based on 4 gaps, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to slow vehicles and give priority to people crossing.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write on behalf of the school about the crossing on North Avenue (North Avenue crossing).

A bus at 19.0 km/h was 1.4 s from a pedestrian. Adult death risk 0.6% compared with 0.6% at a 19.0 km/h impact.
All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15 plus.

Engineering note: PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 7.1 minutes. We are happy to share the tracking data and video file on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
