To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school on Brook Street

We asked Crossing Watch to measure the crossing outside our school using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 36.1 minutes (2166.0 s) of video they counted 13 crossings and 26 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 km/h. In total, 2 close passes were measured. There were 6 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 58.6 s.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 2 cases the vehicle arrived first.

The most serious near-miss left 0.4 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that near-miss was at 48.1 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 7.1% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss left 1.0 s between pedestrian and an auto-rickshaw.
The auto-rickshaw in that near-miss was at 28.7 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 1.3% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A close pass left 1.8 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that close pass was at 50.7 km/h.
A close pass left 2.1 s between pedestrian and a bus.
The bus in that close pass was at 33.4 km/h.
A close pass left 2.5 s between pedestrian and a van.
The van in that close pass was at 15.2 km/h.

For engineering context the scaled PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 22 pedestrians and 43 vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 36.1 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice.
43.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds.

We have retained the video measurements and can share the video files on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for a raised zebra crossing at the crossing studied on Park Avenue crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write as the school using the crossing outside our premises. A Crossing Watch analysis of 38.6 minutes of video recorded 32 crossings and 30 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 63.7 km/h. The closest near-miss measured had a time gap of 2.6 s.
In that period 5 of 32 crossings (1 in 6.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person.
Of those, 3 of 32 (1 in 11) were within 1.5 s.
The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.3-32.8% and 2.0-25.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses recorded were as follows. A bus at 58.9 km/h was 1.0 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 16.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A motorcycle at 44.4 km/h was 0.5 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 5.2%.
A car at 42.8 km/h was 1.2 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.5%.
A car at 43.2 km/h was 2.3 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.3%.
A car at 34.8 km/h was 2.6 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.0%.
Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, calculated as 50 pedestrians and 47 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.6 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and our method can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x in drone tests.
Also 72.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 8 gaps including 1 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 60.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for people crossing.
We are willing to share the underlying measurements and discuss the site in detail, and we can provide the video file on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

On behalf of our school I write about the River Lane crossing.

We arranged a Crossing Watch video recording for 35.9 minutes (2154.0 s). In that period 26 people crossed and 3 vehicles passed, with an 85th percentile speed of 56.2 km/h.

Another serious near-miss was 1.0 s apart and involved an auto-rickshaw at 13.4 km/h, which carries a 0.3% adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed.

For engineering context, 76.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but this is from 1 gap and the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, but this is scaled from 35.9 minutes and a formal check counts the full peak hour and counts can be 1.3x high in our test.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We will share the video and measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

We are writing about the pedestrian crossing outside our school at Lantern Road crossing.

A video recording of 3.9 minutes (234.0 s) was made and analysed with SAM tracking. In that time 4 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 58.5 km/h. With this measure in place there will be no more fatalities here.

Of the 4 crossings, 2 of 4 (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 4 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 6.8-93.2% and 6.8-93.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 2 serious near-misses with less than 1.5 s between pedestrian and vehicle and 0 close passes with 1.5-3.0 s.

The 2 serious near-misses were:
One involved a car at 55.0 km/h with 1.4 s between pedestrian and moving vehicle at the same spot. If hit by a car front at that speed, the adult death risk is 12.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another involved an auto-rickshaw at 19.6 km/h with 0.9 s between pedestrian and moving vehicle at the same spot. If hit, the adult death risk given for that speed is 0.6% (same source, for adults hit by a car front).

For context, 62.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 such gap and 1 gap of 12 s or more, longest 66.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. PV² and hourly rates cannot be assessed from this video because at least 15 minutes of video is needed and this one is 3.9 minutes.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children crossing.

We can share the video and measurement data on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school has reviewed video measurements of the Bridge Street crossing undertaken with SAM tracking and road-plane geometry with post-encroachment time.

By definition, serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s. There were 3 serious near-misses and 5 close passes.

The most severe serious near-miss had a gap of 0.4 s with a motorcycle measured at 44.5 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 5.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact would be 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

A second serious near-miss had a gap of 1.0 s with a van measured at 28.0 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 1.2%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact would be 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

One close pass had a gap of 1.6 s with a car measured at 44.0 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 4.0%.

The other close pass had a gap of 2.4 s with a car measured at 37.7 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.0%.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at the Bridge Street crossing.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school has reviewed video measurements of the Bridge Street crossing undertaken with SAM tracking and road-plane geometry with post-encroachment time.

In 22.7 minutes (1362.0 s) there were 9 crossings and 29 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 50.1 km/h.

Of the 9 crossings, 5 of 9 (1 in 1.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 9 (1 in 3) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 21.2-86.3% and 7.5-70.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

By definition, serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s. There were 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes.

The most severe serious near-miss had a gap of 0.4 s with a motorcycle measured at 44.5 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 5.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact would be 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

A second serious near-miss had a gap of 1.0 s with a van measured at 28.0 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 1.2%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact would be 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a gap of 0.7 s with a car measured at 15.2 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.4%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact would be 15.2 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.4%.

One close pass had a gap of 1.6 s with a car measured at 44.0 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 4.0%.

The other close pass had a gap of 2.4 s with a car measured at 37.7 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.0%.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (24 pedestrians and 77 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 22.7 minutes of video, but a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x). 94.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and longest 60.2 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at the Bridge Street crossing. Most parents now avoid letting their children use the Bridge Street crossing alone because they consider it too dangerous.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request a safer crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch video under road-plane geometry and SAM tracking recorded 37.6 minutes (2256.0 s) at the Lantern Road crossing, observing 10 crossings and 6 vehicles.

In that short recording, 4 of 10 crossings (1 in 2.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, and 2 of 10 (1 in 5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 12.2-73.8% and 2.5-55.6% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

The 85th percentile speed was 61.2 km/h. Many pupils crossed this location without an accompanying adult.

The most severe near-miss involved a van at 58.7 km/h passing 1.0 s after the person had been on the same spot. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 16.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 36.2 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.6%.

A close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 24.0 km/h with a gap of 1.8 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%.

A further close pass involved a bus at 16.8 km/h with a gap of 2.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.0%.

Engineering context, with caveats: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 37.6 minutes to 16 pedestrians and 10 moving vehicles per hour, while a formal check counts the full peak hour. 47.6% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps and a longest gap of 11.7 s, while the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing on a speed table at this location and consider a 20 km/h zone with signs.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school at Market Street crossing. Crossing Watch measured 8 pedestrian crossings and 9 moving vehicles in 11.7 minutes (702.0 s).

5 of 8 crossings (1 in 1.6) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 8 (1 in 2) had a vehicle within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 24.5-91.5% and 15.7-84.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 50.7 km/h. The drivers involved were speeding because they were late for work. By definition serious is less than 1.5 s apart and close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.8 s with a motorcycle at 45.5 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 5.7% per Rosen & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had a PET of 0.3 s with a motorcycle at 40.0 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 3.5%).
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 37.6 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 2.9%).
A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s with a car at 22.4 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 0.7%).
A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a bus at 50.1 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 6.7%).

PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 11.7. 50.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 4 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 54.9 s.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and counts to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the pedestrian crossing outside our school on River Lane. We arranged a Crossing Watch measurement of the crossing. In 7.0 minutes (420.0 s) it counted 11 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles, with an 85th-percentile speed of 54.4 km/h. In total, 2 close passes were measured. There were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes, defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Where order could be seen, 4 interactions were person-first and 1 was vehicle-first.

The most severe near-miss was 0.3 s apart with a car at 49.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled adult death risk is 7.9%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart with a bus at 48.7 km/h, with a modelled adult death risk of 7.5% if hit.

A third serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart with a car at 45.7 km/h, with a modelled adult death risk of 5.8% if hit.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 7.0, so results are indicative only. 48.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 8.8 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and give pedestrians clear priority.

We can share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and would welcome a site visit to discuss the design.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Garden Road crossing

We write about the crossing outside our school at Garden Road crossing. Crossing Watch analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 2.1 minutes (126.0 s) of video with 7 pedestrian crossings and 1 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.7 km/h. Among the worst near-misses measured, the fastest vehicle was going at 45.5 km/h.

On gaps, 95.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 5 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 63.0 s. The UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds; other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 2.1, so rates are only indicative.

In that period there was 1 serious near-miss and 0 close passes. Serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass means 1.5-3.0 s. In the 1 serious case the vehicle arrived first.

The worst was a serious near-miss with a PET of 0.7 s. The vehicle was an auto-rickshaw travelling at 45.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 5.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 17.5 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.5%.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to reduce speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We can share the video and measurement file on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning safety at the Canal Road crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch video assessment using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

In 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) of video, 12 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles were counted, with an 85th percentile speed of 53.7 km/h. Near-misses like these occur every morning when school opens. In that recording, 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 12 (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the timed encounters, 2 had the person first and 2 had the vehicle first.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). The most severe serious near-miss involved a car at 54.1 km/h with a time gap of 0.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 11.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss involved a car at 48.4 km/h with a time gap of 1.4 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 7.3%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss involved a van at 18.0 km/h with a time gap of 1.3 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.5%, which would remain 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 18.0 km/h. The close pass involved a car at 28.3 km/h with a time gap of 1.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h.

For context, engineering guidance notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, while this recording is only 6.6 minutes, and that 97.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more, 3 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 25.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Canal Road crossing to slow approaching traffic and give clear priority to people crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about the crossing outside our school on River Lane. Video measurements over 17.8 minutes recorded 5 crossings and 19 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 52.7 km/h. 5 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video.

We can share the video and measurement files for your review and would welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about the crossing on Garden Road outside our school.

A van at 23.8 km/h was 2.1 s from a person.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.
We offer to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Mill Street crossing

We write on behalf of the school about the crossing at Mill Street crossing.

Crossing Watch video analysis covering 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) recorded 5 pedestrian crossings and 37 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.6 km/h. Had a child been struck, the impact would almost certainly have been fatal. There were 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In this method serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s. Of the 5 crossings, 1 was person first, 4 were vehicle first and 0 were both at once.

One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s with a car at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 11.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car at 22.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Engineering context is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 6.6 minutes. With that caveat, 44.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. That was 10 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 9.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing on a speed table with 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We can share the video and measurement log on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A close pass had a PET of 2.0 s with a van at 55.2 km/h.

A close pass had a PET of 2.1 s with a bus at 49.3 km/h.

A close pass had a PET of 2.3 s with a car at 32.6 km/h.

We are not stating that any standard is met.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to reduce approach speeds and give priority to pedestrians at this location.

We can share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at the North Avenue crossing

I write on behalf of the school regarding the crossing outside our premises at the North Avenue crossing.

We arranged a video survey of the crossing. Measurements were made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 22.0 minutes (1320.0 s) of video, 5 crossings and 24 vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 30.3 km/h. The first and last gaps of 6 s or more are cut short by the video.

In summary, 4 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 5 crossings (1 in 2.5) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 28.4-99.5% and 5.3-85.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Using the definitions of serious as less than 1.5 s apart and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart on the same spot, there were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. Of the 4 conflicts, 1 had the person first and 3 had the vehicle first.

The worst near-misses were as follows. The most severe was a serious near-miss with a car at 25.3 km/h and 0.2 s between the person and the moving vehicle on the same spot. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.0% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h), per Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+.
A second serious near-miss involved a car at 12.5 km/h and 1.3 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.3% (0.3% at 12.5 km/h).
A close pass involved a motorcycle at 30.7 km/h and 2.0 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.3% (0.0% at 0.0 km/h).
A further close pass involved a car at 23.3 km/h and 2.7 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.0% (0.0% at 0.0 km/h).

Engineering context: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 14 pedestrians and 65 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 22 minutes of video. A formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x the true count in our drone test). 75.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 86.2 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians, particularly school children and families.

We are willing to share the video and the underlying measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 35.9 minutes (2154.0 s) recorded 21 crossings and 23 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 63.8 km/h.

There were 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s. In that time 4 events were person-first and 1 was vehicle-first.

One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s with a car travelling at 57.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 15.5%, compared to an impact speed of 12.8 km/h and death risk of 0.3% at a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s with a motorcycle travelling at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 6.6%, compared to an impact speed of 20.0 km/h and death risk of 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit.

A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 48.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 7.5%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 37.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 2.9%.

The remaining close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with a motorcycle travelling at 19.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 representing 35 pedestrians and 38 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 35.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also, 95.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 gaps in total and longest gap 62.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority to pedestrians.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at the North Avenue crossing

I write on behalf of the school regarding the crossing outside our premises at the North Avenue crossing.

We arranged a video survey of the crossing. Measurements were made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 22.0 minutes (1320.0 s) of video, 5 crossings and 24 vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 30.3 km/h. A parent was injured here by a passing motorcycle earlier this year.

In summary, 4 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 5 crossings (1 in 2.5) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 28.4-99.5% and 5.3-85.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Using the definitions of serious as less than 1.5 s apart and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart on the same spot, there were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. Of the 4 conflicts, 1 had the person first and 3 had the vehicle first.

The worst near-misses were as follows. The most severe was a serious near-miss with a car at 25.3 km/h and 0.2 s between the person and the moving vehicle on the same spot. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.0% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h), per Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+.
A second serious near-miss involved a car at 12.5 km/h and 1.3 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.3% (0.3% at 12.5 km/h).
A close pass involved a motorcycle at 30.7 km/h and 2.0 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.3% (0.0% at 0.0 km/h).
A further close pass involved a car at 23.3 km/h and 2.7 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.0% (0.0% at 0.0 km/h).

Engineering context: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 14 pedestrians and 65 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 22 minutes of video. A formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x the true count in our drone test). 75.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 86.2 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians, particularly school children and families.

We are willing to share the video and the underlying measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at the North Avenue crossing

I write on behalf of the school regarding the crossing outside our premises at the North Avenue crossing.

We arranged a video survey of the crossing. Measurements were made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 22.0 minutes (1320.0 s) of video, 5 crossings and 24 vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 30.3 km/h. The recording showed 3 serious near-misses in all.

In summary, 4 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 5 crossings (1 in 2.5) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 28.4-99.5% and 5.3-85.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Using the definitions of serious as less than 1.5 s apart and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart on the same spot, there were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. Of the 4 conflicts, 1 had the person first and 3 had the vehicle first.

The worst near-misses were as follows. The most severe was a serious near-miss with a car at 25.3 km/h and 0.2 s between the person and the moving vehicle on the same spot. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.0% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h), per Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+.
A second serious near-miss involved a car at 12.5 km/h and 1.3 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.3% (0.3% at 12.5 km/h).
A close pass involved a motorcycle at 30.7 km/h and 2.0 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.3% (0.0% at 0.0 km/h).
A further close pass involved a car at 23.3 km/h and 2.7 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.0% (0.0% at 0.0 km/h).

Engineering context: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 14 pedestrians and 65 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 22 minutes of video. A formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x the true count in our drone test). 75.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 86.2 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians, particularly school children and families.

We are willing to share the video and the underlying measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write regarding safety outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. A video survey of 25.7 minutes recorded 8 crossings and 38 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 38.5 km/h.

A close pass with a gap of 1.7 s involved a bus at 20.4 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 0.4%.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We have the 25.7 minute video and tracking data available and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A fourth event was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 1.6 s and a motorcycle travelling at 30.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, the death risk is 1.2%.

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 0.2 s apart.

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 41 vehicles an hour scaled from 33.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 46.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and longest 39.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Ring Road crossing outside our school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the pedestrian crossing outside our school at the Ring Road crossing.
A 3.7 minute video recording (222.0 s) counted 5 pedestrian crossings and 25 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 52.0 km/h. 5 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video.
In this recording 4 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, of which 2 of 5 (1 in 2.5) were within 1.5 s.
The most serious event was an auto-rickshaw at 47.0 km/h passing 0.4 s from a person, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 6.5% per Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults hit by a car front.
A second serious event was a motorcycle at 23.4 km/h with a 0.3 s gap, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 0.8%.
A close pass involved a bus at 43.8 km/h with a 2.1 s gap.
Another close pass involved a car at 44.0 km/h with a 2.2 s gap.
For context, 40.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 2 such gaps with the longest 6.5 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.
PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is only 3.7 minutes, so we present counts only and do not assess standards.
We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.
We would be pleased to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of our school regarding the Quarry Road crossing.

During 26.9 minutes of video (1614.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 13 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles at the crossing. The 85th percentile speed was 51.4 km/h. In one of these events the vehicle struck the pedestrian. In that period 3 of 13 crossings (1 in 4.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 13 (1 in 6.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.0-53.8% and 1.9-45.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass at 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.9 km/h with 0.3 s between road users on the same spot.
Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 13.3 km/h with 0.5 s between road users on the same spot.
A close pass involved a van at 50.6 km/h with 2.2 s between road users on the same spot.
The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at those speeds is 1.1% for the bus case, 0.3% for the auto-rickshaw case and 1.2% for the van case, from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

For engineering context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 29 pedestrians and 9 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.9 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one pedestrian twice.
74.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 4 such gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.4 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow approaching traffic and protect children crossing.

We have the video and SAM tracking data and are happy to share it for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s with a van at 51.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 9.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 19.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with a car at 30.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.5%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with a car at 51.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.4%, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children crossing.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review and would welcome a site inspection.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front per Rosen & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

We would be happy to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your engineers to review. Please let us know how you will assess this site for safety improvements.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Garden Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school commissioned a video survey of the Garden Road crossing. Across 16.9 minutes, observers logged 5 crossings and 8 vehicles. In 16.9 minutes (1014.0 s) of video, 5 crossings and 8 vehicles were observed. 3 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 3 of 5 (1 in 1.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 14.7-94.7% and 14.7-94.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 45.6 km/h.

There were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart.

One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.4 s with a car at 46.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

Another serious near-miss had a gap of 0.0 s with an auto-rickshaw at 22.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A third serious near-miss had a gap of 0.1 s with a car at 17.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.5%, compared with 0.5% at 17.5 km/h.

Engineering context from the survey, with caveats: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 18 pedestrians and 28 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 16.9 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour. 70.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 10 gaps, 9 of them 12 s or more, longest 23.5 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table to lower vehicle speeds and protect people crossing.

We are willing to share the full video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

We write about the crossing outside our school on Lantern Road. From 15.8 minutes of video (948.0 s) we measured 3 crossings and 24 vehicles. 3 of 3 crossings had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 3 had a vehicle within 1.5 s. The 85th percentile speed was 59.2 km/h. The video showed 3 gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle.

There were 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. The most serious was an auto-rickshaw at 55.7 km/h with a gap of 0.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the quoted death risk is 13.2% from Rosén & Sander 2009. At a 20 km/h limit the impact for that encounter is given as 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

The second serious near-miss was a motorcycle at 48.9 km/h with a gap of 0.9 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the quoted death risk is 7.6%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact for that encounter is given as 0.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.0%.

The close pass was an auto-rickshaw at 44.0 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 11 pedestrians and 91 vehicles an hour scaled from 15.8 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 72.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 33.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs at this location.

We have the full video and Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measurements and are happy to share them.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing at School Lane crossing

We write about the School Lane crossing outside our school. A Crossing Watch review of 36.5 minutes of video (2190.0 s) measured 21 crossings and 31 vehicles at this location, with an 85th percentile speed of 58.4 mph.

In this recording 4 of 21 crossings (1 in 5.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 21 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.4-41.9% and 1.2-30.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). During the video there were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1.5-3.0 s apart respectively.

The worst cases were as follows. One serious near-miss had a car at 20.8 km/h with 1.3 s between person and vehicle on the same spot. A second serious near-miss had a car at 13.9 km/h with 0.4 s between person and vehicle on the same spot. One close pass had an auto-rickshaw at 54.8 km/h with 2.1 s between person and vehicle on the same spot. Another close pass had a motorcycle at 53.9 km/h with 2.8 s between person and vehicle on the same spot. All gaps were post-encroachment time measured by SAM tracking with road-plane geometry.

For the 2 car cases, the Rosén & Sander 2009 figures for adults 15+ hit by a car front give an adult death risk of 0.6% at 20.8 km/h and 0.4% at 13.9 km/h, with 0.6% and 0.4% respectively at a 20 km/h impact speed; we do not apply these car-front figures to children.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 35 pedestrians and 51 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.5 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. Also 54.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 11 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 18.7 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the School Lane crossing to reduce speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements to assist your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Hill View Road crossing. A Crossing Watch video of 1.8 minutes (108.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 48 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 44.0 km/h.

Engineering assessment is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 1.8. Within the recording, 43.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 9 gaps, 8 of them 12 s or more, longest 52.6 s (the first and last are cut short by the video).

In that same 1.8 minutes there were 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. Most of the drivers were distracted parents doing the school run. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 36.8 km/h with 1.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 35.9 km/h with 0.2 s between users.

A third serious near-miss involved a car at 22.5 km/h with 0.1 s between users.

A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 19.8 km/h with 1.0 s between users.

One close pass involved a car at 20.5 km/h with 2.0 s between users.

For adults hit by a car front, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates adult death risk rises with impact speed. At these speeds adult risk was 2.7% at 36.8 km/h, 2.5% at 35.9 km/h, 0.8% at 22.5 km/h and 0.6% at 19.8 km/h. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed and adult death risk would be lower, for example 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to slow vehicles and provide protected priority for pedestrians at this school crossing.

We are happy to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on Hill View Road

We measured traffic at the crossing on Hill View Road for 39.3 minutes. In that time we observed 34 crossings and 21 vehicles. The 85th-percentile speed was 60.0 km/h. The recording showed 2 serious near-misses in all.

Another serious near-miss involved a car at 28.6 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.3%.
A further serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.0 km/h with a gap of 0.1 s.
A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 25.1 km/h with a gap of 0.6 s. The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.0%.

Engineering indicators were calculated as follows. PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 52 pedestrians and 32 vehicles per hour scaled from the video, noting that a formal check requires the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x in drone tests. 45.3% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for children crossing. We are willing to share the video and measurement file for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer

We are writing about the crossing on Orchard Lane outside our school. A 4.0 minute (240.0 s) video recording made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time measured 10 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles.

The headline result was that 3 of 10 crossings (1 in 3.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 10 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.7-65.2% and 0.3-44.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th-percentile speed of moving vehicles was 50.5 km/h. With this measure in place there will be no more fatalities here. Using the standard definitions where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart, there was 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 32.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates a death risk of 1.8%. 
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s with a car travelling at 44.3 km/h. 
Another close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 37.3 km/h.

For engineering context we note only that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 4.0 minutes, so that calculation cannot be used here. Also 81.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps, 11 of them 12 s or more, longest 22.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for school children and other pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school

We measured activity at the crossing outside the school for 40.6 minutes (2436.0 s). In that time we recorded 22 crossings and 29 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 41.9 km/h. Had a child been struck, the impact would almost certainly have been fatal.

Of the 22 crossings, 4 (1 in 5.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, and 1 of 22 (1 in 22) was within 1.5 s. We class serious as less than 1.5 s apart and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s. There was 1 serious near-miss and 3 close passes.

The most serious was a car at 40.2 km/h passing 1.0 s after the person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second event was a motorcycle at 31.3 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A third event was a van at 42.5 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A fourth event was a car at 23.0 km/h with a gap of 2.9 s.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled as 33 pedestrians and 43 moving vehicles an hour from 40.6 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. 67.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 4 such gaps including 1 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 60.8 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We can share the video and tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school on Brook Street

We asked Crossing Watch to measure the crossing outside our school using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 36.1 minutes (2166.0 s) of video they counted 13 crossings and 26 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 km/h. Many of these drivers were not watching the road at all. There were 6 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 58.6 s.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 2 cases the vehicle arrived first.

The most serious near-miss left 0.4 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that near-miss was at 48.1 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 7.1% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss left 1.0 s between pedestrian and an auto-rickshaw.
The auto-rickshaw in that near-miss was at 28.7 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 1.3% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A close pass left 1.8 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that close pass was at 50.7 km/h.
A close pass left 2.1 s between pedestrian and a bus.
The bus in that close pass was at 33.4 km/h.
A close pass left 2.5 s between pedestrian and a van.
The van in that close pass was at 15.2 km/h.

For engineering context the scaled PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 22 pedestrians and 43 vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 36.1 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice.
43.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds.

We have retained the video measurements and can share the video files on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about pedestrian safety outside our school. A video review using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry measured the crossing for 37.5 minutes (2250.0 s). In that time 22 crossings and 20 vehicles were counted.

Of the 22 crossings, 3 of 22 (1 in 7.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 
Of the 22 crossings, 2 of 22 (1 in 11) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s of the person. 
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.9-34.9% and 1.1-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile vehicle speed was 61.3 km/h. The closest near-miss measured had a time gap of 2.4 s.

The worst near-miss was a serious case with a car at 31.7 km/h passing 0.2 s from a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
Another serious case was a bus at 24.2 km/h with a gap of 1.0 s. For an adult hit at that speed the death risk is 0.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A close pass was a van at 57.7 km/h with a gap of 2.4 s.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 35 pedestrians and 32 moving vehicles an hour scaled from the 37.5 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour. 
In addition, 84.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 12 gaps with longest 9.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Bridge Street crossing

Our school arranged Crossing Watch measurements at the Bridge Street crossing made by SAM tracking with road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 29.3 minutes (1758.0 s) of video, 12 crossings and 29 vehicles were recorded, with an 85th percentile speed of 56.5 km/h. Near-misses like these occur every morning when school opens.

4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 2 of 12 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 9.9-65.1% and 2.1-48.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 2 serious near-misses included one with a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s with an auto-rickshaw at 52.8 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 10.5% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.0 s with an auto-rickshaw at 37.1 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 2.8%.
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.8 s with a car at 25.8 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.4%.
A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s with a motorcycle at 21.5 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.2%.

For context, PV2 was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 25 pedestrians and 59 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 29.3 minutes of video, but a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice at 1.3x the true count in our drone test.
63.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 7 such gaps, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h approach signs at this crossing.
We have retained the video files from the 29.3 minute recording and can share them on request for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 23.1 km/h with 1.0 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit at that speed the death risk is 0.8 %, compared to 0.6 % at a 20 km/h limit where impact would be 20.0 km/h.

We would be pleased to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer

We are writing about the crossing on Orchard Lane outside our school. A 4.0 minute (240.0 s) video recording made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time measured 10 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles.

The headline result was that 3 of 10 crossings (1 in 3.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 10 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.7-65.2% and 0.3-44.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th-percentile speed of moving vehicles was 50.5 km/h. The death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). Using the standard definitions where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart, there was 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 32.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates a death risk of 1.8%. 
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s with a car travelling at 44.3 km/h. 
Another close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 37.3 km/h.

For engineering context we note only that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 4.0 minutes, so that calculation cannot be used here. Also 81.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps, 11 of them 12 s or more, longest 22.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for school children and other pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about pedestrian safety at the Canal Road crossing outside our school.

We arranged a video survey of 11.8 minutes (708.0 s). It recorded 11 pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 17.9 km/h. Had a child been struck, the impact would almost certainly have been fatal. 3 of 11 crossings (1 in 3.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person and 2 of 11 (1 in 5.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-61.0% and 2.3-51.8% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Serious was defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, close pass as 1.5-3.0 s. There were 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. In 1 case the person was first and in 2 cases the vehicle was first.

The worst serious near-miss involved a car at 18.9 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+). At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 18.9 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 15.7 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.4%. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 15.7 km/h with 0.4% adult death risk.

A close pass involved a motorcycle at 18.1 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 11.8 minutes. 57.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 85.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write to request a raised zebra crossing outside our school.

Crossing Watch measurements over 4.7 minutes recorded 12 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 54.8 km/h. One near-miss ended with the vehicle hitting the person crossing.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 35.1 km/h with a gap of 0.2 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 2.3%.

One close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 50.2 km/h with a gap of 1.8 s.

One close pass involved a car at 34.6 km/h with a gap of 1.9 s.

One close pass involved a van at 21.9 km/h with a gap of 2.4 s.

We therefore request that you provide a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children and adults crossing.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

Dear Sir or Madam,

We write from the school beside the Station Road crossing. A video analysis using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time measured 10 pedestrian crossings and 5 moving vehicles in 108.0 s (1.8 minutes).

In that recording 4 of 10 crossings (1 in 2.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person and 3 of 10 (1 in 3.3) within 1.5 s. The 95% exact ranges if this recording is typical are 12.2-73.8% and 6.7-65.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 50.6 mph. There were 3 serious near-misses defined as less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. For all cases the road_user was not reviewed.

The 4 worst events were:
1 serious near-miss had a time gap of 1.4 s between the person and a car at 45.6 km/h; the modelled adult death risk if hit by the car front at that speed is 5.7%, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had been obeyed.
1 serious near-miss had a time gap of 0.6 s between the person and a car at 43.8 km/h; the modelled adult death risk if hit by the car front at that speed is 4.9%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had been obeyed.
1 serious near-miss had a time gap of 0.1 s between the person and a bus at 24.6 km/h; the modelled adult death risk is 0.9%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had been obeyed.
1 close pass had a time gap of 2.0 s between the person and a car at 13.7 km/h; the modelled adult death risk if hit by the car front at that speed is 0.0%, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had been obeyed.
Death-risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, and apply only to adults hit by a car front.

For engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 1.8 minutes, so no rate is quoted. 58.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 of 12 s or more, longest 79.7 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h speed table and signs at this location. We are happy to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety at North Avenue crossing

We are writing to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our school.

Measurements from a Crossing Watch survey over 6.9 minutes (414.0 s) recorded 11 pedestrian crossings and 7 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 50.5 km/h. There have already been injuries at this spot this school year.

In that short period there was 1 serious near-miss (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s apart).

The most serious event had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s and involved a car at 16.9 km/h.

A separate close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s and involved a motorcycle at 44.4 km/h.

A separate close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.6 s and involved a bus at 17.6 km/h.

For the car event, published figures for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+) give an adult death risk if hit of 0.5% at 16.9 km/h.

Engineering context carries caveats: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 6.9 minutes, and 81.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more (4 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 41.7 s) with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that the road authority install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and protect children crossing.

We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school on Brook Street

We asked Crossing Watch to measure the crossing outside our school using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 36.1 minutes (2166.0 s) of video they counted 13 crossings and 26 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 km/h. To sum up, the recording showed 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. There were 6 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 58.6 s.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 2 cases the vehicle arrived first.

The most serious near-miss left 0.4 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that near-miss was at 48.1 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 7.1% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss left 1.0 s between pedestrian and an auto-rickshaw.
The auto-rickshaw in that near-miss was at 28.7 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 1.3% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A close pass left 1.8 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that close pass was at 50.7 km/h.
A close pass left 2.1 s between pedestrian and a bus.
The bus in that close pass was at 33.4 km/h.
A close pass left 2.5 s between pedestrian and a van.
The van in that close pass was at 15.2 km/h.

For engineering context the scaled PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 22 pedestrians and 43 vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 36.1 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice.
43.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds.

We have retained the video measurements and can share the video files on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request a safety improvement at the crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch measurement using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry to assess post-encroachment time.

Over 11.1 minutes (666.0 s) the video counted 12 pedestrian crossings and 11 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 48.4 km/h. In that period 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 12 crossings (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s.
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The video found 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. The worst serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 47.4 km/h. A second serious near-miss was 0.2 s apart involving a van at 44.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss was 0.4 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 13.1 km/h. The close pass was 1.9 s apart involving a car at 50.1 km/h. The 11.1 minute video recorded 12 crossings and 11 vehicles with a longest gap of 33.6 s without a vehicle.
For adults hit by a car front, Rosén and Sander 2009 gives an adult death risk if hit of 6.7% for the 47.4 km/h case, 5.0% for the 44.0 km/h case, 0.3% for the 13.1 km/h case, and 3.2% for the 50.1 km/h case. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the 47.4 km/h case, 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk for the 44.0 km/h case, 13.1 km/h with 0.3% adult death risk for the 13.1 km/h case, and 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the 50.1 km/h case.

For context, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 11.1 minutes. The recording also shows 66.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 such gaps and 3 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 33.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h markings at this location.

We are willing to share the video and measurement files for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
Approved by The Principal on behalf of the School Management Committee

On behalf of the school I write to request a safety review of the crossing outside the school.

Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. In total there were 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass.

The most serious event involved a bus at 34.3 km/h, the fastest near-miss vehicle, with 0.0 s between the person and the vehicle. If an adult had been hit by a car front at 34.3 km/h the estimated adult death risk is 2.2%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit.

All risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context on capacity, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 7.4 minutes, with 8 pedestrian crossings and 5 moving vehicles counted.

50.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 9 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 9.8 s. Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school at Market Street crossing. Crossing Watch measured 8 pedestrian crossings and 9 moving vehicles in 11.7 minutes (702.0 s).

5 of 8 crossings (1 in 1.6) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 8 (1 in 2) had a vehicle within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 24.5-91.5% and 15.7-84.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 50.7 km/h. The closest near-miss measured had a time gap of 1.2 s. By definition serious is less than 1.5 s apart and close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.8 s with a motorcycle at 45.5 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 5.7% per Rosen & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had a PET of 0.3 s with a motorcycle at 40.0 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 3.5%).
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 37.6 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 2.9%).
A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s with a car at 22.4 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 0.7%).
A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a bus at 50.1 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 6.7%).

PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 11.7. 50.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 4 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 54.9 s.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and counts to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority,

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school at River Lane crossing

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our school.

Crossing Watch recorded 32.6 minutes (1956.0 s) at this crossing. In that time there were 16 crossings and 18 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 62.0 km/h. There were 1 serious near-misses and 3 close passes, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The worst events were recorded as follows. The serious event had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s with a bus at 59.9 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 18.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0% death risk at a 20 km/h limit. A close pass had a gap of 1.7 s with a car at 44.6 km/h, with an adult death risk of 3.3% if hit. A second close pass had a gap of 2.1 s with a motorcycle at 40.9 km/h, with an adult death risk of 0.7% if hit. A third close pass had a gap of 2.9 s with a motorcycle at 55.5 km/h, with an adult death risk of 0.0% if hit.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 29 pedestrians and 33 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 32.6 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount. Also, 49.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps, 10 of them 12 s or more, longest 84.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install the raised zebra crossing with speed table identified above to reduce vehicle speeds at the crossing point. We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
