To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

Dear Sir or Madam,

We write from the school beside the Station Road crossing. A video analysis using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time measured 10 pedestrian crossings and 5 moving vehicles in 108.0 s (1.8 minutes).

In that recording 4 of 10 crossings (1 in 2.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person and 3 of 10 (1 in 3.3) within 1.5 s. The 95% exact ranges if this recording is typical are 12.2-73.8% and 6.7-65.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 50.6 km/h. The closest near-miss measured had a time gap of 2.0 s. There were 3 serious near-misses defined as less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. For all cases the road_user was not reviewed.

The 4 worst events were:
1 serious near-miss had a time gap of 1.4 s between the person and a car at 45.6 km/h; the modelled adult death risk if hit by the car front at that speed is 5.7%, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had been obeyed.
1 serious near-miss had a time gap of 0.6 s between the person and a car at 43.8 km/h; the modelled adult death risk if hit by the car front at that speed is 4.9%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had been obeyed.
1 serious near-miss had a time gap of 0.1 s between the person and a bus at 24.6 km/h; the modelled adult death risk is 0.9%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had been obeyed.
1 close pass had a time gap of 2.0 s between the person and a car at 13.7 km/h; the modelled adult death risk if hit by the car front at that speed is 0.0%, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h if the 20 km/h limit had been obeyed.
Death-risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, and apply only to adults hit by a car front.

For engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 1.8 minutes, so no rate is quoted. 58.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 of 12 s or more, longest 79.7 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h speed table and signs at this location. We are happy to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Cedar Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 35.9 minutes (2154.0 s) recorded 21 crossings and 23 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 63.8 km/h.

There were 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s. In that time 4 events were person-first and 1 was vehicle-first.

One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s with a car travelling at 57.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 15.5%, compared to an impact speed of 12.8 km/h and death risk of 0.3% at a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s with a motorcycle travelling at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 6.6%, compared to an impact speed of 20.0 km/h and death risk of 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit.

A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 48.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 7.5%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 37.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 2.9%.

The remaining close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with a motorcycle travelling at 19.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 representing 35 pedestrians and 38 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 35.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also, 95.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 gaps in total and longest gap 62.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority to pedestrians. Many pupils have to run across because drivers rarely slow down.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Lantern Road crossing

During 43.6 minutes of video we counted 31 crossings and 19 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 54.0 km/h. The closest of these passes was in fact a collision. The worst near-miss was serious with a gap of 0.9 s and a car at 49.8 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 8.2% per Rosén & Sander 2009.
A second serious near-miss had a gap of 0.7 s and a car at 36.2 km/h.
A third serious near-miss had a gap of 0.4 s and a car at 35.4 km/h.
A fourth serious near-miss had a gap of 0.0 s and a car at 27.7 km/h.
A close pass had a gap of 1.9 s and a car at 36.4 km/h.
Person first was 3, vehicle first was 2 and both at once was 1.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 43 pedestrians and 26 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 43.6 minutes of video and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 41.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 5 gaps and longest 9.1 s and the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location. We are willing to share the measurement data and video excerpts for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Station Road

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). In that time 38 crossings and 8 vehicles were recorded, the 85th percentile speed was 44.1 km/h, there were 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 7 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 53.4 s, and 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 38 (1 in 7.6) within 1.5 s; exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-31.3% and 4.4-28.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safer crossing on Park Avenue outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school arranged a Crossing Watch on the crossing on Park Avenue. In 6.9 minutes (414.0 s) we counted 7 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 47.9 km/h. The first and last gaps of 6 s or more are cut short by the video.

We note that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 6.9 minutes. We request a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We can share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

We are writing about the crossing on Orchard Lane outside our school. A 4.0 minute (240.0 s) video recording made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time measured 10 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles.

The headline result was that 3 of 10 crossings (1 in 3.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 10 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.7-65.2% and 0.3-44.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th-percentile speed of moving vehicles was 50.5 km/h. The video showed 10 gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle. Using the standard definitions where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart, there was 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 32.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates a death risk of 1.8%. 
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s with a car travelling at 44.3 km/h. 
Another close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 37.3 km/h.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for school children and other pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school on Lake View Road

We write regarding the crossing outside our school on Lake View Road. A Crossing Watch review of 21.4 minutes of video (1284.0 s) recorded 11 crossings and 22 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 50.9 km/h. Near-misses like these occur every morning when school opens.

The review found 4 of 11 crossings (1 in 2.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 11 (1 in 3.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 10.9-69.2% and 6.0-61.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 3 serious near-misses and 1 close pass as defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1.5-3.0 s respectively.

The worst near-misses were:
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s with a car at 51.3 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 9.2% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s with an auto-rickshaw at 42.7 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.5%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s with an auto-rickshaw at 37.7 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 2.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s with a car at 51.5 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 6.1%.

In engineering terms, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 31 pedestrians and 62 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 21.4 minutes of video, and a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice as 1.3x the true count in our drone test. Also 43.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more and longest 17.6 s, with the caveat that the first and last are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing on Hill View Road

Our school monitored the Hill View Road crossing for 20.1 minutes (1206.0 s). We counted 14 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.9 mph. There was 1 gap of 6 s or more and 1 gap of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 49.4 s.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 42 pedestrians and 69 vehicles an hour scaled from 20.1 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also 95.1% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, from 1 such gap, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We can share the video for your review and welcome a site inspection.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at North Avenue crossing

Our school arranged a video measurement at North Avenue crossing for 3.7 minutes (222.0 s).

In that recording 12 pedestrian crossings and 41 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 61.3 km/h. Serious near-misses were defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s) were recorded.

One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s with a car at 23.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.8%. One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s with an auto-rickshaw at 16.5 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4%. One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s with a car at 12.6 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.3%. One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.5 s with a bus at 35.7 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 2.4%. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front per Rosen & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, 83.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more, 0 of them 12 s or more and longest gap 10.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 3.7 minutes, so counts are limited to 12 pedestrian crossings and 41 moving vehicles.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h speed table and warning signs at this location to lower approach speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We can share the video and measurement data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school on Brook Street

We asked Crossing Watch to measure the crossing outside our school using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 36.1 minutes (2166.0 s) of video they counted 13 crossings and 26 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 km/h. There were 6 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 58.6 s.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 2 cases the vehicle arrived first.

The most serious near-miss left 0.4 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that near-miss was at 48.1 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 7.1% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss left 1.0 s between pedestrian and an auto-rickshaw.
The auto-rickshaw in that near-miss was at 28.7 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 1.3% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A close pass left 1.8 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that close pass was at 50.7 km/h.
A close pass left 2.1 s between pedestrian and a bus.
The bus in that close pass was at 33.4 km/h.
A close pass left 2.5 s between pedestrian and a van.
The van in that close pass was at 15.2 km/h.

For engineering context the scaled PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 22 pedestrians and 43 vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 36.1 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice.
43.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds.

We have retained the video measurements and can share the video files on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to slow vehicles and give priority to people crossing.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

From the Head of the School, Ring Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We request that you make the crossing outside our school safer by installing a raised zebra crossing with speed table.

Crossing Watch made measurements from video of the crossing using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. The video covered 6.7 minutes (402.0 s). In that time there were 6 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 57.1 km/h. Once this fix is built, no one will die at this crossing.

There were 3 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s. Of the interactions, 3 were person first, 1 was vehicle first and 0 were both at once.

The worst incidents were as follows. A bus at 55.2 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 12.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.
A car at 37.3 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 2.8%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.
A van at 18.0 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 0.5%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 18.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.5%.
A car at 47.4 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 2.7 s in the close pass category. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video. This video is 6.7 minutes with 6 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles, so PV² cannot be assessed. 44.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. There were 5 such gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 47.1 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4 to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10 to 12 s or longer.

We ask you to install the raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and to consider a 20 km/h zone with signs. We are ready to share the video and the measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
Approved by The Principal as head of the school

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on Canal Road

Dear Sir/Madam,

On behalf of our school, I write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our premises.

A recording lasting 19.7 minutes counted 37 crossings and 9 vehicles. Of those crossings, 3 of 37 (1 in 12) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s, and 2 of 37 (1 in 18) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 1.7-21.9% and 0.7-18.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 52.4 km/h. A young pupil hit by the fastest vehicle would probably not have survived. There were 9 gaps of 6 s or more and 0 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 7.1 s.

There were 2 serious near-misses with a gap of less than 1.5 s and 1 close pass between 1.5 s and 3.0 s. One serious near-miss left 0.3 s between the person and a motorcycle at 52.0 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 9.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss left 0.5 s between the person and a van at 21.4 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.7%. The close pass left 2.7 s between the person and an auto-rickshaw at 30.3 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 113 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 19.7 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount. 69.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The site record is described as Canal Road crossing.

We request the raised zebra crossing with speed table to lower vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing. We are willing to share the underlying video-derived measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school at Market Street crossing. Crossing Watch measured 8 pedestrian crossings and 9 moving vehicles in 11.7 minutes (702.0 s).

5 of 8 crossings (1 in 1.6) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 8 (1 in 2) had a vehicle within 1.5 s. A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s with a car at 22.4 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 0.7%).
A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a bus at 50.1 km/h (adult death risk if hit by a car front 6.7%).

PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 11.7. 50.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 4 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 54.9 s.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the video and counts to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at the North Avenue crossing

I write on behalf of the school regarding the crossing outside our premises at the North Avenue crossing.

We arranged a video survey of the crossing. Measurements were made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 22.0 minutes (1320.0 s) of video, 5 crossings and 24 vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 30.3 km/h. These near-misses happened because drivers ignored the crossing markings.

In summary, 4 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 5 crossings (1 in 2.5) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 28.4-99.5% and 5.3-85.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Using the definitions of serious as less than 1.5 s apart and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart on the same spot, there were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. Of the 4 conflicts, 1 had the person first and 3 had the vehicle first.

The worst near-misses were as follows. The most severe was a serious near-miss with a car at 25.3 km/h and 0.2 s between the person and the moving vehicle on the same spot. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.0% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h), per Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+.
A second serious near-miss involved a car at 12.5 km/h and 1.3 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.3% (0.3% at 12.5 km/h).
A close pass involved a motorcycle at 30.7 km/h and 2.0 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.3% (0.0% at 0.0 km/h).

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning safety at the Canal Road crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch video assessment using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

In 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) of video, 12 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles were counted, with an 85th percentile speed of 53.7 km/h. 12 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video. In that recording, 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 12 (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the timed encounters, 2 had the person first and 2 had the vehicle first.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). The most severe serious near-miss involved a car at 54.1 km/h with a time gap of 0.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 11.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss involved a car at 48.4 km/h with a time gap of 1.4 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 7.3%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss involved a van at 18.0 km/h with a time gap of 1.3 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.5%, which would remain 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 18.0 km/h. The close pass involved a car at 28.3 km/h with a time gap of 1.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h.

For context, engineering guidance notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, while this recording is only 6.6 minutes, and that 97.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more, 3 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 25.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Canal Road crossing to slow approaching traffic and give clear priority to people crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at the Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school has reviewed video measurements of the Bridge Street crossing undertaken with SAM tracking and road-plane geometry with post-encroachment time.

In 22.7 minutes (1362.0 s) there were 9 crossings and 29 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 50.1 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.4 s the vehicle was going at 28.0 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 1.0 s it was going at 44.5 km/h.

Of the 9 crossings, 5 of 9 (1 in 1.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 9 (1 in 3) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 21.2-86.3% and 7.5-70.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

By definition, serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s. There were 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes.

The most severe serious near-miss had a gap of 0.4 s with a motorcycle measured at 44.5 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 5.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact would be 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

A second serious near-miss had a gap of 1.0 s with a van measured at 28.0 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 1.2%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact would be 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

A third serious near-miss had a gap of 0.7 s with a car measured at 15.2 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.4%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact would be 15.2 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.4%.

One close pass had a gap of 1.6 s with a car measured at 44.0 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 4.0%.

The other close pass had a gap of 2.4 s with a car measured at 37.7 km/h. At that speed the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.0%.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (24 pedestrians and 77 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 22.7 minutes of video, but a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount by 1.3x). 94.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and longest 60.2 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at the Bridge Street crossing.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school – Cedar Lane

We write concerning the crossing outside our school on Cedar Lane. An independent video review (Crossing Watch, SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) observed 24.8 minutes (1488.0 s) at the site and counted 14 crossings and 19 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 59.9 km/h. The review classified 3 events as serious, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 events as close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s. In 2 cases the person was first, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both were at once.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 52.2 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 10.0% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, which would fall to 0.2% at an impact of 8.4 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Another serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 50.2 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The report notes an adult death risk of 8.5% if hit at that speed.

A third serious near-miss involved a van at 31.2 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s. The report notes an adult death risk of 1.6% if hit at that speed.

A close pass involved a car at 55.2 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A further close pass involved a car at 33.1 km/h with a gap of 2.1 s.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location. We can share the video and measurement details for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school - Cedar Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request safety improvements at the crossing outside our school. Using Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) we measured traffic for 11.9 minutes (714.0 s).

In that period we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 13 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.3 km/h. These near-misses happened because drivers ignored the crossing markings. A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. We recorded 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 3 cases the vehicle arrived first, with 0 cases where both arrived at once.

The engineering assessment notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 11.9 minutes, so rates are not reported. It also notes that 95.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 12 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 gaps of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 85.1 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a car at 56.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front is 14.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved a car at 34.6 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 2.2%, falling to 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 18.5 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 29.1 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 1.4%, with 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit and an impact speed of 20.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved a car at 13.2 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 0.3%, remaining 0.3% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 13.2 km/h. One close pass involved a car at 50.5 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.8 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 4.3%, falling to 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

Given the high speeds and repeated close interactions, we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

We are writing about the pedestrian crossing outside our school at Lantern Road crossing.

A video recording of 3.9 minutes (234.0 s) was made and analysed with SAM tracking. In that time 4 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 58.5 km/h. We would be glad to walk the crossing with your engineers whenever it suits them.

Another involved an auto-rickshaw at 19.6 km/h with 0.9 s between pedestrian and moving vehicle at the same spot. If hit, the adult death risk given for that speed is 0.6% (same source, for adults hit by a car front).

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children crossing.

We can share the video and measurement data on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning safety at the Canal Road crossing. A Crossing Watch analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) of 2.1 minutes (126.0 s) recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 11 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 52.5 km/h.

In that period there were 2 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s.

The most severe serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s with a car travelling at 46.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.2% at an impact speed of 5.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 23.9 km/h.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.6 s with a car travelling at 35.6 km/h. In 3 encounters the pedestrian arrived at the shared spot ahead of the vehicle.

On engineering use, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this video is 2.1 minutes. About 82.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.
We would be pleased to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Our school arranged video measurement at Ring Road crossing for 44.1 minutes (2646.0 s). In that time 36 people crossed and 25 moving vehicles passed. The 85th percentile speed was 42.1 km/h. Many unaccompanied schoolchildren use this crossing on their way to class each morning.

Another close pass involved a car at 13.9 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.9 s.
A further close pass involved a car at 24.2 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s.

For context, PV2 in the recording was 0.0 x 10^8, from 49 pedestrians and 34 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 44.1 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice, 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 56.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with high-visibility markings and curb build-outs at this crossing.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share it. Please let us know the next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Mill Street crossing

We write on behalf of the school about the crossing at Mill Street crossing.

Crossing Watch video analysis covering 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) recorded 5 pedestrian crossings and 37 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.6 km/h. The recording showed 2 serious near-misses in all. There were 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In this method serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s. Of the 5 crossings, 1 was person first, 4 were vehicle first and 0 were both at once.

One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s with a car at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 11.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car at 22.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Engineering context is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 6.6 minutes. With that caveat, 44.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. That was 10 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 9.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing on a speed table with 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We can share the video and measurement log on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing at Bridge Street crossing

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Bridge Street crossing. A Crossing Watch review of 26.7 minutes of video (1602.0 s) recorded 30 crossings and 31 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 49.4 km/h.

The review found 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. One serious near-miss involved a car at 48.5 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. Another serious near-miss involved a bus at 46.2 km/h with a gap of 1.1 s. A third serious near-miss involved a car at 30.4 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s. A close pass involved a bus at 35.5 km/h with a gap of 2.3 s.

For adults hit by a car front, the estimated death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts) if hit at the measured speeds would be 7.3% for the first incident, 6.0% for the second and 1.5% for the third, compared with 0.4%, 0.0% and 0.6% at impact speeds of 14.2 km/h, 0.0 km/h and 20.0 km/h respectively under a 20 km/h limit.

In that period, 2 people crossed first, 1 vehicle passed first, and 1 arrived at once.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 67 pedestrians and 70 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 26.7 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice. 86.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 such gaps including 2 of 12 s or more and longest 33.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request a safety improvement at the crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch measurement using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry to assess post-encroachment time.

Over 11.1 minutes (666.0 s) the video counted 12 pedestrian crossings and 11 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 48.4 km/h. By these figures the crossing already qualifies for a signal-controlled crossing. In that period 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 12 crossings (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s.
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The video found 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. The worst serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 47.4 km/h. A second serious near-miss was 0.2 s apart involving a van at 44.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss was 0.4 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 13.1 km/h. The close pass was 1.9 s apart involving a car at 50.1 km/h.
For adults hit by a car front, Rosén and Sander 2009 gives an adult death risk if hit of 6.7% for the 47.4 km/h case, 5.0% for the 44.0 km/h case, 0.3% for the 13.1 km/h case, and 3.2% for the 50.1 km/h case. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the 47.4 km/h case, 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk for the 44.0 km/h case, 13.1 km/h with 0.3% adult death risk for the 13.1 km/h case, and 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the 50.1 km/h case.

For context, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 11.1 minutes. The recording also shows 66.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 such gaps and 3 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 33.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h markings at this location.

We are willing to share the video and measurement files for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about safety at Orchard Lane crossing. A video recording of 10.1 minutes (606.0 s) measured 5 pedestrian crossings and 10 vehicles, with 85th percentile speed 58.8 km/h. A young pupil hit by the fastest vehicle would probably not have survived.

Headline result: 3 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 3 of 5 (1 in 1.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 14.7-94.7% and 14.7-94.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Within that time there were 3 serious near-misses and 0 close passes, where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a van at 52.0 km/h with 0.8 s between road users.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 48.5 km/h with 1.1 s between road users.

A third serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 22.9 km/h with 1.4 s between road users.

For adults hit by a car front the estimated death risks for those speeds are 9.8%, 7.3% and 0.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact speeds would be 0.0 km/h, 0.0 km/h and 17.3 km/h with death risks 0.0%, 0.0% and 0.5%.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 10.1 minutes with 5 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles. 50.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more, 0 gaps of 12 s or more and longest gap 11.3 s, with the main caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and measurement log for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning safety at the Canal Road crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch video assessment using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

In 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) of video, 12 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles were counted, with an 85th percentile speed of 53.7 km/h. The closest of these near-misses was the fault of Mr. Tarun Mehra, who runs the tea stall. In that recording, 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 12 (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the timed encounters, 2 had the person first and 2 had the vehicle first.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). The most severe serious near-miss involved a car at 54.1 km/h with a time gap of 0.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 11.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss involved a car at 48.4 km/h with a time gap of 1.4 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 7.3%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss involved a van at 18.0 km/h with a time gap of 1.3 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.5%, which would remain 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 18.0 km/h. The close pass involved a car at 28.3 km/h with a time gap of 1.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h.

For context, engineering guidance notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, while this recording is only 6.6 minutes, and that 97.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more, 3 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 25.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Canal Road crossing to slow approaching traffic and give clear priority to people crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

The worst events were both classified as serious. Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Mill Street crossing following a video recording of 4.0 minutes (240.0 s) at the site. In that time we counted 8 pedestrian crossings and 11 moving vehicles.

4 of 8 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person; 3 of 8 (1 in 2.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 15.7-84.3% and 8.5-75.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 4 cases, 3 were serious (less than 1.5 s) and 1 was a close pass (1.5-3.0 s).

The worst near-misses were as follows. 1 serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s with a motorcycle travelling at 38.8 mph and an adult death risk if hit of 3.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s with a car travelling at 29.8 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 1.4%.
A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s with a bus travelling at 23.2 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 0.8%.
1 close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.5 s with a van travelling at 31.3 km/h and an adult death risk if hit of 1.7%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 4.0. Counted: 8 pedestrian crossings, 11 moving vehicles. 76.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 5 gaps, 5 of them 12 s or more, longest 37.1 s (the first and last are cut short by the video). UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2): 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds; other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We would be pleased to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Road Authority,

I write on behalf of the school regarding the Garden Road crossing.

We commissioned a 9.5 minute (570.0 s) video survey at the crossing. In that time 3 pedestrian crossings and 24 moving vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 62.6 km/h. 3 of 3 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 3 (1 in 1.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 29.2-100.0% and 9.4-99.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 2 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s apart); the vehicle arrived first in 3 of 3 cases.

The worst serious near-miss involved a car at 56.4 km/h passing 0.8 s from the person, with an adult death risk of 13.9% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 22.3 km/h passing 0.2 s from the person, with an adult death risk of 0.7% if hit, and 20.0 km/h impact with 0.6% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

A close pass involved a bus at 37.2 km/h passing 2.8 s from the person.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 9.5 minutes, so those rates cannot be reliably used. 93.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 6 gaps of 12 s or more, the longest 32.9 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Garden Road crossing to reduce speeds and provide priority where the 3 crossings were observed.

We can share the video and the full measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) on request and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The worst incidents were as follows. A bus at 55.2 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 12.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.
A car at 37.3 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 2.8%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

The UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4 to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10 to 12 s or longer.

We ask you to install the raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and to consider a 20 km/h zone with signs. We are ready to share the video and the measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school on Brook Street

We asked Crossing Watch to measure the crossing outside our school using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 36.1 minutes (2166.0 s) of video they counted 13 crossings and 26 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 km/h. The first and last gaps of 6 s or more are cut short by the video. There were 6 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 58.6 s.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 2 cases the vehicle arrived first.

The most serious near-miss left 0.4 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that near-miss was at 48.1 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 7.1% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss left 1.0 s between pedestrian and an auto-rickshaw.
The auto-rickshaw in that near-miss was at 28.7 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 1.3% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A close pass left 1.8 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that close pass was at 50.7 km/h.
A close pass left 2.1 s between pedestrian and a bus.
The bus in that close pass was at 33.4 km/h.
A close pass left 2.5 s between pedestrian and a van.
The van in that close pass was at 15.2 km/h.

For engineering context the scaled PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 22 pedestrians and 43 vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 36.1 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice.
43.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds.

We have retained the video measurements and can share the video files on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Park Avenue

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitored the crossing outside it for 38.4 minutes (2304.0 s). In that time we recorded 32 crossings and 17 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 26.3 km/h. There have already been injuries at this spot this school year. We observed 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

By definition, a serious near-miss is when a pedestrian and a moving vehicle are on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s apart.

The serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s and involved a car at 14.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 14.2 km/h the death risk from Rosén & Sander 2009 is 0.4%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.1 s and involved a van at 13.8 km/h.

A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s and involved a car at 24.6 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 50 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.4 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice, by 1.3x in our drone test. 

Also, 67.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and 7 of them 12 s or more and longest gap 33.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and to give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

We write about the crossing outside our school on Lantern Road. From 15.8 minutes of video (948.0 s) we measured 3 crossings and 24 vehicles. 3 of 3 crossings had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 3 had a vehicle within 1.5 s. There were 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. The most serious was an auto-rickshaw at 55.7 km/h with a gap of 0.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the quoted death risk is 13.2% from Rosén & Sander 2009. At a 20 km/h limit the impact for that encounter is given as 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

The second serious near-miss was a motorcycle at 48.9 km/h with a gap of 0.9 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the quoted death risk is 7.6%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact for that encounter is given as 0.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.0%.

The close pass was an auto-rickshaw at 44.0 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 11 pedestrians and 91 vehicles an hour scaled from 15.8 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 72.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 33.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs at this location.

We have the full video and Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measurements and are happy to share them.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

From the Head of the School, Ring Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We request that you make the crossing outside our school safer by installing a raised zebra crossing with speed table.

Crossing Watch made measurements from video of the crossing using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. The video covered 6.7 minutes (402.0 s). In that time there were 6 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 57.1 km/h. These figures come from a single recording and may differ on other days.

There were 3 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s. Of the interactions, 3 were person first, 1 was vehicle first and 0 were both at once.

The worst incidents were as follows. A bus at 55.2 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 12.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.
A car at 37.3 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 2.8%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.
A van at 18.0 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 0.5%. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 18.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.5%.
A car at 47.4 km/h had a post-encroachment time of 2.7 s in the close pass category. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with a death risk of 0.0%.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video. This video is 6.7 minutes with 6 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles, so PV² cannot be assessed. 44.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. There were 5 such gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 47.1 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4 to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, while other groups, such as children, may need 10 to 12 s or longer.

We ask you to install the raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and to consider a 20 km/h zone with signs. We are ready to share the video and the measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing point.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Market Street crossing

We write on behalf of the school adjoining Market Street crossing. Crossing Watch measurements from 34.0 minutes of video (2040.0 s) recorded 6 crossings and 1 vehicle. No serious near-misses were recorded. There was 1 close pass, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot 1.5-3.0 s apart. The worst was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 2.6 s. The vehicle involved was a motorcycle travelling at 40.3 km/h. The estimated adult death risk if hit at that speed by a car front is 0.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

Engineering notes indicate PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 or 11 pedestrians and 2 moving vehicles an hour when scaled from 34 minutes of video. A formal check counts the full peak hour. A recent parent survey found that 90% of families avoid Market Street crossing because they consider it dangerous. Also, 61.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We are willing to share the video and underlying measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

We are writing about the pedestrian crossing outside our school at Lantern Road crossing.

A video recording of 3.9 minutes (234.0 s) was made and analysed with SAM tracking. In that time 4 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 58.5 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 1.4 s the vehicle was going at 19.6 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 0.9 s it was going at 55.0 km/h.

Of the 4 crossings, 2 of 4 (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 4 (1 in 2) within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 6.8-93.2% and 6.8-93.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 2 serious near-misses with less than 1.5 s between pedestrian and vehicle and 0 close passes with 1.5-3.0 s.

The 2 serious near-misses were:
One involved a car at 55.0 km/h with 1.4 s between pedestrian and moving vehicle at the same spot. If hit by a car front at that speed, the adult death risk is 12.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another involved an auto-rickshaw at 19.6 km/h with 0.9 s between pedestrian and moving vehicle at the same spot. If hit, the adult death risk given for that speed is 0.6% (same source, for adults hit by a car front).

For context, 62.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 such gap and 1 gap of 12 s or more, longest 66.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. PV² and hourly rates cannot be assessed from this video because at least 15 minutes of video is needed and this one is 3.9 minutes.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children crossing.

We can share the video and measurement data on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Cedar Lane outside our school. Crossing Watch video for 23.1 minutes (1386.0 s) recorded 16 crossings and 20 vehicles, with 85th percentile speed 59.9 km/h. In one of these events the vehicle struck the pedestrian.

In that recording, 4 of 16 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 16 (1 in 16) was within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 7.3-52.4% and 0.2-30.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.1-10.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. There was 1 serious near-miss and 3 close passes.

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer

We are writing about the crossing on Orchard Lane outside our school. A 4.0 minute (240.0 s) video recording made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time measured 10 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles.

The headline result was that 3 of 10 crossings (1 in 3.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 10 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.7-65.2% and 0.3-44.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th-percentile speed of moving vehicles was 50.5 km/h. Using the standard definitions where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart, there was 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 32.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates a death risk of 1.8%. 
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s with a car travelling at 44.3 km/h. 
Another close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 37.3 km/h.

Also 81.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps, 11 of them 12 s or more, longest 22.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for school children and other pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We write as the school using the crossing outside our gate. Crossing Watch video covering 25.6 minutes (1536.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 35 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.9 km/h. We would be glad to walk the crossing with your engineers whenever it suits them.

The analysis found 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Of the 8 potential conflicts, 4 had the person first, 2 had the vehicle first, and 0 had both at once.

The worst near-misses were:
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with an auto-rickshaw at 59.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 18.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s with a van at 51.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 9.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 19.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.9 s with a bus at 40.7 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 3.8%, compared with 0.2% at an impact of 8.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with a car at 30.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.5%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with a car at 51.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.4%, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
All death-risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15+ hit by car fronts.

For context, the video gives PV² of 0.0 x 10^8 from 19 pedestrians and 82 vehicles per hour, with the caveat that this is scaled from 25.6 minutes not a full peak hour and our test shows broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also, 62.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 11 such gaps including 3 of 12 s or more and longest 74.2 s, with the caveat that first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We have the video and Crossing Watch data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school on Lake View Road

We write regarding the crossing outside our school on Lake View Road. A Crossing Watch review of 21.4 minutes of video (1284.0 s) recorded 11 crossings and 22 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 50.9 km/h. The video showed 1 gap of 12 s or more with no moving vehicle.

The review found 4 of 11 crossings (1 in 2.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 11 (1 in 3.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 10.9-69.2% and 6.0-61.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 3 serious near-misses and 1 close pass as defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1.5-3.0 s respectively.

The worst near-misses were:
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s with a car at 51.3 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 9.2% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s with an auto-rickshaw at 42.7 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.5%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s with an auto-rickshaw at 37.7 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 2.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s with a car at 51.5 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 6.1%.

In engineering terms, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 31 pedestrians and 62 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 21.4 minutes of video, and a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice as 1.3x the true count in our drone test. Also 43.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more and longest 17.6 s, with the caveat that the first and last are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning safety at the Canal Road crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch video assessment using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

In 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) of video, 12 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles were counted, with an 85th percentile speed of 53.7 km/h. In that recording, 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 3 of 12 (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the timed encounters, 2 had the person first and 2 had the vehicle first.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). Most drivers on Canal Road were regularly breaking the speed limit during the school run. The most severe serious near-miss involved a car at 54.1 km/h with a time gap of 0.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 11.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss involved a car at 48.4 km/h with a time gap of 1.4 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 7.3%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss involved a van at 18.0 km/h with a time gap of 1.3 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.5%, which would remain 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 18.0 km/h. The close pass involved a car at 28.3 km/h with a time gap of 1.8 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with impact at 0.0 km/h.

For context, engineering guidance notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, while this recording is only 6.6 minutes, and that 97.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more, 3 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 25.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Canal Road crossing to slow approaching traffic and give clear priority to people crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the crossing outside our school on Ring Road, where Crossing Watch analysis using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles in 6.1 minutes (366.0 s).

The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 km/h.

Overall, 3 of 8 crossings (1 in 2.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 8 (1 in 8) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.5-75.5% and 0.3-52.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most serious near-miss was an auto-rickshaw at 19.5 km/h with a gap of 1.3 s, with an adult death risk of 0.6% if hit by a car front at that speed (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), which would remain 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 19.5 km/h.

A second near-miss was a motorcycle at 48.1 km/h with a gap of 1.7 s, with an adult death risk of 4.5% if hit by a car front at that speed, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

A third near-miss was a van at 35.6 km/h with a gap of 2.8 s, with an adult death risk of 0.0% if hit by a car front at that speed, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 6.1 minutes, so they were not calculated. 64.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps and a longest gap of 10.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Cedar Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 35.9 minutes (2154.0 s) recorded 21 crossings and 23 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 63.8 km/h. The closest of these near-misses was the fault of Mr. Tarun Mehra, who runs the tea stall.

There were 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s. In that time 4 events were person-first and 1 was vehicle-first.

One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s with a car travelling at 57.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 15.5%, compared to an impact speed of 12.8 km/h and death risk of 0.3% at a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s with a motorcycle travelling at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 6.6%, compared to an impact speed of 20.0 km/h and death risk of 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit.

A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 48.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 7.5%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 37.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 2.9%.

The remaining close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with a motorcycle travelling at 19.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 representing 35 pedestrians and 38 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 35.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also, 95.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 gaps in total and longest gap 62.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority to pedestrians.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
