To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety work at the crossing outside the school

Dear Sir or Madam,

We asked Crossing Watch to record the crossing outside our school using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry. In 32.7 minutes of video, 1962.0 s in total, they counted 10 crossings and 40 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 54.8 km/h. Most of the speeding drivers were school buses dropping off pupils in the morning.

They classify a serious near-miss as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. In this period there were 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. In 4 cases the person was first, in 1 case the vehicle was first, and in 0 cases both were at once.

The worst events were:
A serious near-miss with a gap of 0.8 s involved a motorcycle at 49.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 8.1 percent, based on Rosén and Sander 2009 for adults aged 15 and over.
A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.3 s involved a van at 46.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 6.2 percent.
A serious near-miss with a gap of 0.2 s involved a motorcycle at 16.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.5 percent.
A close pass with a gap of 2.7 s involved a van at 39.8 km/h.
A close pass with a gap of 2.9 s involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.5 km/h.

For context, the scaled estimate is PV² = 0.0 x 10^8 from 18 pedestrians and 73 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 32.7 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount.
Also, 59.6 percent of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 12 gaps with 0 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 10.3 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this site to reduce speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the full measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We asked for measurements at the Ring Road crossing. In 28.9 minutes 8 people were seen crossing and 12 vehicles were counted.

A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a van at 31.3 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 1.7%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a bus at 19.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.6%.

A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with a car at 14.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit is 0.3%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 28.9 minutes to 17 pedestrians and 25 vehicles an hour, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also 73.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on Hill View Road

We measured traffic at the crossing on Hill View Road for 39.3 minutes. In that time we observed 34 crossings and 21 vehicles. The 85th-percentile speed was 60.0 km/h. With this measure in place there will be no more fatalities here.

We recorded 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes of 1.5 s to 3.0 s. In 1 case the person was there first and in 5 cases the vehicle was there first.

The most severe near-miss involved a car at 56.6 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 14.1% based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15 and above.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 28.6 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.3%.
A further serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.0 km/h with a gap of 0.1 s.
A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 25.1 km/h with a gap of 0.6 s. The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.0%.

Engineering indicators were calculated as follows. PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 52 pedestrians and 32 vehicles per hour scaled from the video, noting that a formal check requires the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x in drone tests. 45.3% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for children crossing. We are willing to share the video and measurement file for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the road authority responsible for Lake View Road,

In 38.9 minutes of video at the crossing outside the school, Crossing Watch recorded 23 crossings and 24 vehicles with 85th percentile speed 57.2 km/h. Mrs. Leela Fernandes, who drives the morning bus, caused the worst of these events.

3 of 23 crossings (1 in 7.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 23 (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 2.8-33.6% and 1.1-28.0% of crossings by Clopper-Pearson, and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long by Poisson.

Serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart.

The closest event involved a car at 55.5 km/h through the same spot 0.5 s from the person, with 12.9% adult death risk if hit by the car front.

A 2nd serious event involved a bus at 26.1 km/h through the same spot 1.0 s from the person, with 1.0% adult death risk if hit by a car front.

A close pass event involved a motorcycle at 59.8 km/h through the same spot 2.0 s from the person, with 5.7% adult death risk if hit by a car front.

Death risks are for adults 15+ hit by car fronts from Rosen and Sander 2009. At 20.0 km/h impact the modelled risk is 0.6%.

PV2 was 0.0 x 10^8 from 35 pedestrians and 37 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.9 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in drone testing.

77.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 4 gaps with 0 of 12 s or more and longest 8.4 s, noting the first and last are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing at this spot to slow vehicles to near 20.0 km/h at the conflict point.

We will share the video and tracking on request to assist design.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing outside our school on Mill Street.

Measurements from 44.3 minutes of video recorded 35 crossings and 22 vehicles. 4 of 35 crossings (1 in 8.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 35 (1 in 18) were within 1.5 s. There were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. One serious near-miss involved a van at 52.0 km/h with a gap of 1.2 s. Another serious near-miss involved a car at 18.4 km/h with a gap of 0.9 s. One close pass involved a motorcycle at 33.5 km/h with a gap of 1.7 s. Another close pass involved a van at 25.0 km/h with a gap of 2.2 s. For an adult hit by a car front at 52.0 km/h the death-risk figure is 9.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 44.3 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 45.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 2 such gaps and a longest gap of 47.5 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and protect people crossing.

We would be happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Re: Request for safety improvement at Garden Road crossing

On behalf of the school I write to request a safety review of the crossing outside the school.

We commissioned a 7.4 minute video analysis totalling 444.0 s at Garden Road crossing using SAM tracking with road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In that time there were 8 pedestrian crossings and 5 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 34.9 km/h. Once this fix is built, no one will die at this crossing. There were 9 gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed and 0 gaps of 12 s or more, with a longest gap of 9.8 s.

Of those 8 crossings, 3 of 8 crossings (1 in 2.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 8 (1 in 4) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.5-75.5% and 3.2-65.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. In total there were 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass.

The most serious event involved a bus at 34.3 km/h with 0.0 s between the person and the vehicle. If an adult had been hit by a car front at 34.3 km/h the estimated adult death risk is 2.2%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h at a 20 km/h limit.

A 2nd serious event involved a van at 12.5 km/h with 1.2 s between person and vehicle. At 12.5 km/h the estimated adult death risk if hit is 0.3%, which remains 0.3% at 12.5 km/h in the 20 km/h limit scenario.

A close pass event involved a car at 37.0 km/h with 1.5 s between person and vehicle. At 37.0 km/h the estimated adult death risk is 2.7%, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h if the impact had occurred at the 20 km/h limit. All risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context on capacity, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 7.4 minutes, with 8 pedestrian crossings and 5 moving vehicles counted.

50.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 9 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 9.8 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to slow approaching speeds and provide protected priority for people crossing.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A second near-miss was a motorcycle at 48.1 km/h with a gap of 1.7 s, with an adult death risk of 4.5% if hit by a car front at that speed, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on River Lane

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the River Lane crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch recorded 25 crossings in 36.0 minutes with 10 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 56.9 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.1 s, the bus reached the spot before the pedestrian.

Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 1.0-26.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most severe was a bus at 52.9 km/h passing 0.1 s after a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 10.6% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

The second serious near-miss was a van at 22.9 km/h passing 1.3 s after a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 36.0 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice. Also, 62.4% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 3 such gaps and longest 81.8 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pupils crossing.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Station Road

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). In that time 38 crossings and 8 vehicles were recorded, the 85th percentile speed was 44.1 km/h, there were 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 7 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 53.4 s, and 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. With this measure in place there will be no more fatalities here. 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 38 (1 in 7.6) within 1.5 s; exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-31.3% and 4.4-28.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer

We are writing about the crossing on Orchard Lane outside our school. A 4.0 minute (240.0 s) video recording made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time measured 10 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles.

The headline result was that 3 of 10 crossings (1 in 3.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 10 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.7-65.2% and 0.3-44.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th-percentile speed of moving vehicles was 50.5 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 1.2 s the vehicle was going at 32.3 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 2.4 s it was going at 44.3 km/h. Using the standard definitions where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart, there was 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 32.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates a death risk of 1.8%. 
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s with a car travelling at 44.3 km/h. 
Another close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 37.3 km/h.

Also 81.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps, 11 of them 12 s or more, longest 22.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for school children and other pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Road Authority,

I write on behalf of the school regarding the Garden Road crossing.

We commissioned a 9.5 minute (570.0 s) video survey at the crossing. In that time 3 pedestrian crossings and 24 moving vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 62.6 km/h. Many of these drivers were not watching the road at all. 3 of 3 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 3 (1 in 1.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 29.2-100.0% and 9.4-99.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 2 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s apart); the vehicle arrived first in 3 of 3 cases.

The worst serious near-miss involved a car at 56.4 km/h passing 0.8 s from the person, with an adult death risk of 13.9% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 22.3 km/h passing 0.2 s from the person, with an adult death risk of 0.7% if hit, and 20.0 km/h impact with 0.6% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

A close pass involved a bus at 37.2 km/h passing 2.8 s from the person.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 9.5 minutes, so those rates cannot be reliably used. 93.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 6 gaps of 12 s or more, the longest 32.9 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Garden Road crossing to reduce speeds and provide priority where the 3 crossings were observed.

We can share the video and the full measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) on request and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the Brook Street crossing outside our school.

In a 10.0 minute (600.0 s) video we measured 3 pedestrian crossings and 6 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 32.8 km/h. This is what happens at the crossing on each day of the school week. 3 of 3 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 3 (1 in 3) was within 1.5 s.

The recording showed 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes as defined by less than 1.5 s and 1.5 s to 3.0 s between pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot. The most serious case involved a car at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between pedestrian and vehicle. A second case involved a bus at 19.6 km/h with 1.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle. A third case involved a car at 22.2 km/h with 2.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For adults hit by a car front, the estimated death risk if hit in the most serious case was 1.2% (0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit) per Rosen & Sander 2009.

We note that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 10.0 minutes. 73.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing on a speed table with 20 km/h signs and markings at this location.

We would be happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Brook Street crossing. A video recording of 11.7 minutes (702.0 s) counted 3 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 20.8 km/h. Near-misses like these occur every morning when school opens.

In that period 2 of 3 crossings (1 in 1.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 3 (1 in 3) within 1.5 s.

There was 1 serious near-miss (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5 to 3.0 s). The serious event had a PET of 0.7 s and involved a car at 14.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), and at a 20 km/h limit the impact would still be 14.3 km/h with 0.4% adult death risk.

The close pass had a PET of 1.9 s and involved a bus at 15.9 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front in that second event the indicated risk was 0.0%, with 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0% risk at a 20 km/h limit.

Engineering context: PV² needs at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is only 11.7 minutes, so rates are indicative. About 78.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 12 gaps including 11 of 12 s or more and longest 83.7 s, noting UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) says 4 to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups such as children may need 10 to 12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority. We can share the video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

On the basis of a 9.7 minute video (582.0 s) at Lantern Road crossing we recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 53.0 mph. In that recording 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 7 (1 in 7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 42.1-99.6% and 0.4-57.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). By the study definition, 1 was serious (less than 1.5 s apart) and 5 were close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 3 cases the person was first and in 3 cases the vehicle was first.

The worst cases measured by post-encroachment time were:
A serious near-miss with PET of 0.3 s involving a car at 44.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 5.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at 20.0 km/h impact it would be 0.6%.
A close pass with PET of 2.2 s involving a bus at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.7%.
A close pass with PET of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 33.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.5%.
A close pass with PET of 2.1 s involving a car at 22.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
A close pass with PET of 2.4 s involving a bus at 31.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact and death risk for the last 4 cases would each be 0.0 km/h and 0.0%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 9.7 minutes, with 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles counted. With that caveat, 93.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 9 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and that the UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and establish pedestrian priority.

We are willing to share the video and the SAM tracking measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school - Cedar Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request safety improvements at the crossing outside our school. Using Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) we measured traffic for 11.9 minutes (714.0 s).

In that period we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 13 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.3 km/h. Had a child been struck, the impact would almost certainly have been fatal. A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. We recorded 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 3 cases the vehicle arrived first, with 0 cases where both arrived at once.

The engineering assessment notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 11.9 minutes, so rates are not reported. It also notes that 95.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 12 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 gaps of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 85.1 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a car at 56.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front is 14.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved a car at 34.6 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 2.2%, falling to 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 18.5 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 29.1 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 1.4%, with 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit and an impact speed of 20.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved a car at 13.2 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 0.3%, remaining 0.3% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 13.2 km/h. One close pass involved a car at 50.5 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.8 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 4.3%, falling to 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

Given the high speeds and repeated close interactions, we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

In that time 33 people crossed and 22 vehicles passed. The 85th percentile speed was 60.5 km/h. The video showed 1 gap of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle. There were 3 gaps of 6 s or more, 1 gap of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 81.2 s.

By definition a serious near miss is a pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. We recorded 3 serious near misses and 2 close passes. In that period 1 crossing was person-first, 4 were vehicle-first and 0 were both at once.

One serious near miss involved a car at 53.6 km/h passing 0.8 s from a pedestrian, which carries an 11.2% death risk for an adult if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

Another serious near miss involved a car at 28.0 km/h passing 1.0 s from a pedestrian, which carries a 1.2% death risk for an adult if hit.

A third serious near miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 20.8 km/h passing 0.7 s from a pedestrian, which carries a 0.6% death risk for an adult if hit.

One close pass involved a car at 22.1 km/h passing 1.8 s from a pedestrian, which carries a 0.3% death risk for an adult if hit.

Another close pass involved a car at 37.6 km/h passing 2.4 s from a pedestrian, which carries a 0.0% death risk for an adult if hit.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled to 73 pedestrians and 49 vehicles an hour, with the caveat that this is scaled from 27 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour. 63.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this crossing.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. Children hit at these speeds face a far higher risk of death than adults.

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 41 vehicles an hour scaled from 33.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 46.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and longest 39.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write concerning the Hill View Road crossing. A Crossing Watch video of 1.8 minutes (108.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 48 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 44.0 km/h. A young pupil hit by the fastest vehicle would probably not have survived.

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on Hill View Road

We measured traffic at the crossing on Hill View Road for 39.3 minutes. In that time we observed 34 crossings and 21 vehicles. The 85th-percentile speed was 60.0 km/h. All of the pedestrians involved were children on their way home.

We recorded 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes of 1.5 s to 3.0 s. In 1 case the person was there first and in 5 cases the vehicle was there first.

The most severe near-miss involved a car at 56.6 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 14.1% based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15 and above.
Another serious near-miss involved a car at 28.6 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.3%.
A further serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.0 km/h with a gap of 0.1 s.
A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 25.1 km/h with a gap of 0.6 s. The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.0%.

Engineering indicators were calculated as follows. PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 52 pedestrians and 32 vehicles per hour scaled from the video, noting that a formal check requires the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x in drone tests. 45.3% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for children crossing. We are willing to share the video and measurement file for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A car at 25.1 km/h was 0.0 s apart from a pedestrian. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the published death risk is 1.0%.

We can share the video and tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Park Avenue crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Park Avenue crossing outside our school. A 4.0 minute video (240.0 s) recorded 12 pedestrian crossings and 22 moving vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 40.4 km/h.

In that recording, 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 12 (1 in 12) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 9.9-65.1% and 0.2-38.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. There was 1 serious near-miss and 3 close passes.

The most serious event was 1.4 s apart and involved a motorcycle at 15.3 km/h. Statistical modelling shows this crossing will cause at least 2 child fatalities per year if unchanged.
For an adult hit by a car front at 15.3 km/h the published death risk is 0.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A second event was 1.8 s apart and involved a car at 13.2 km/h.
A third event was 2.1 s apart and involved an auto-rickshaw at 24.2 km/h.
A fourth event was 2.3 s apart and involved a bus at 36.7 km/h.

Engineering context is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 4.0 minutes. Counted volumes were 12 pedestrian crossings and 22 moving vehicles. The share of time in gaps was 99.4% inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, comprising 12 gaps, 9 of them 12 s or more, longest 70.9 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the full video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

I write on behalf of the school regarding the Orchard Lane crossing.

Over 6.6 minutes (396.0 s) of video we recorded 4 pedestrian crossings and 21 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 62.6 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.6 s the vehicle was going at 58.5 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 1.6 s it was going at 15.5 km/h.

One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a car at 15.5 km/h; the estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with an auto-rickshaw at 12.8 km/h; the estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.3%.

A close pass had a PET of 1.6 s with an auto-rickshaw at 58.5 km/h; the estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 13.4%.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signage at this location.

We are happy to share the video and underlying measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Market Street crossing

Dear Sir or Madam,

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at Market Street crossing following video measurements of pedestrian risk.

What was measured: Over 4.6 minutes (276.0 s) we recorded 6 pedestrian crossings and 33 moving vehicles. 6 of 6 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 5 of 6 (1 in 1.2) within 1.5 s. Our school arranged a video survey at Park Avenue crossing. In 5.2 minutes (312.0 s) we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 20 moving vehicles.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of our school regarding the Quarry Road crossing.

During 26.9 minutes of video (1614.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 13 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles at the crossing. The 85th percentile speed was 51.4 km/h. The death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). In that period 3 of 13 crossings (1 in 4.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 13 (1 in 6.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.0-53.8% and 1.9-45.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass at 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.9 km/h with 0.3 s between road users on the same spot.
Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 13.3 km/h with 0.5 s between road users on the same spot.
A close pass involved a van at 50.6 km/h with 2.2 s between road users on the same spot.
The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at those speeds is 1.1% for the bus case, 0.3% for the auto-rickshaw case and 1.2% for the van case, from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

For engineering context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 29 pedestrians and 9 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.9 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one pedestrian twice.
74.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 4 such gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.4 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow approaching traffic and protect children crossing.

We have the video and SAM tracking data and are happy to share it for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Dear Sir/Madam,

I write concerning the North Avenue crossing outside our school.

A Crossing Watch review of 11.5 minutes (690.0 s) recorded 12 pedestrian crossings and 21 moving vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 46.9 km/h. A young pupil hit by the fastest vehicle would probably not have survived.
There were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart.
In 4 interactions the vehicle went first, in 0 the person went first, and in 1 both were there at once.

The worst near-misses were:
A car at 31.7 km/h was 0.5 s apart from a pedestrian. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the published death risk is 1.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A car at 25.1 km/h was 0.0 s apart from a pedestrian. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the published death risk is 1.0%.
A bus at 20.8 km/h was 1.2 s apart from a pedestrian. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the published death risk is 0.6%.
At a 20.0 km/h impact speed the published adult death risk would be 0.6%.

Engineering context has caveats. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 11.5 minutes, with 12 crossings and 21 vehicles counted.
72.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps of 6 s or more and 0 of 12 s or more and longest gap 8.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We can share the video and tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

I write on behalf of the school regarding the Garden Road crossing.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Garden Road crossing to reduce speeds and provide priority where the 3 crossings were observed.

We can share the video and the full measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) on request and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at Garden Road crossing

We write regarding the crossing outside our school at Garden Road crossing. Crossing Watch analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) of 6.3 minutes (378.0 s) recorded 12 pedestrian crossings and 15 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 51.5 km/h. Another close pass had a PET of 2.7 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 47.4 km/h.

Engineering notes are limited by video length. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 6.3 minutes with 12 pedestrian crossings and 15 moving vehicles counted. We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone with signs at this location. We are willing to share the video and underlying measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the Quarry Road crossing.

Our Crossing Watch video recorded 4.0 minutes (240.0 s) with 8 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 53.7 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.2 s the vehicle was going at 21.3 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 0.8 s it was going at 56.1 km/h. In that time 4 of 8 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, and 3 of 8 (1 in 2.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 15.7-84.3% and 8.5-75.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the serious events 1 was person-first and 3 were vehicle-first, and 1 close pass was also recorded.

One serious near-miss was 0.2 s apart and involved an auto-rickshaw at 56.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 13.6%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss was 0.8 s apart and involved a car at 21.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.7%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

A third serious near-miss was 1.4 s apart and involved an auto-rickshaw at 19.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.6%, compared with 0.6% at 19.6 km/h.

A close pass was 2.4 s apart and involved a motorcycle at 43.6 km/h.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 4.0 minutes with 8 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles counted, so we do not use that metric. About 72.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 59.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We ask for a raised zebra crossing to reduce speeds toward the 20.0 km/h limit and provide priority. We can share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school

We measured activity at the crossing outside the school for 40.6 minutes (2436.0 s). In that time we recorded 22 crossings and 29 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 41.9 km/h. Near-misses like these occur every morning when school opens.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.

We can share the video and tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school on Brook Street

We asked Crossing Watch to measure the crossing outside our school using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 36.1 minutes (2166.0 s) of video they counted 13 crossings and 26 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 km/h. The closest of these near-misses was the fault of Mr. Tarun Mehra, who runs the tea stall. There were 6 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 58.6 s.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 2 cases the vehicle arrived first.

The most serious near-miss left 0.4 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that near-miss was at 48.1 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 7.1% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss left 1.0 s between pedestrian and an auto-rickshaw.
The auto-rickshaw in that near-miss was at 28.7 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 1.3% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A close pass left 1.8 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that close pass was at 50.7 km/h.
A close pass left 2.1 s between pedestrian and a bus.
The bus in that close pass was at 33.4 km/h.
A close pass left 2.5 s between pedestrian and a van.
The van in that close pass was at 15.2 km/h.

For engineering context the scaled PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 22 pedestrians and 43 vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 36.1 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice.
43.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds.

We have retained the video measurements and can share the video files on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about the crossing on Cedar Lane crossing. Measurements from video analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) covering 7.6 minutes (456.0 s) recorded 6 pedestrian crossings and 36 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 46.4 km/h. These figures come from a single recording and may differ on other days.

The analysis defines serious as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s. In that period there were 1 serious near-miss and 5 close passes, with 3 where the person was first, 3 where the vehicle was first and 0 where both were at once.

The worst events were: a serious near-miss with a gap of 0.6 s involving a car at 36.0 km/h. A close pass with a gap of 2.2 s involving a car at 33.1 km/h. We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce speeds and give priority to people crossing.

We are happy to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir / Madam,

Re: Safety at Lake View Road crossing

In a Crossing Watch video of 33.6 minutes (2016.0 s) we measured 6 pedestrian crossings and 33 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 43.6 km/h. At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 0.7 s apart.

5 of 6 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 6 (1 in 2) were within 1.5 s.
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 35.9-99.6% and 11.8-88.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes were:
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s and involved a car at 35.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 2.3% for a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s and involved a car at 33.4 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 2.0% for a car front, falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s and involved a car at 17.8 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.5% for a car front, remaining 0.5% at an impact of 17.8 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s and involved a car at 22.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.1% at an impact of 3.3 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.3 s and involved a bus at 44.8 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, but this is scaled from only 33.6 minutes of video and a formal check counts the full peak hour with caveats about broken tracks.
73.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 8 of 12 s or more and longest gap 76.8 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority.

We can share the full video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Cedar Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the crossing outside our school at Cedar Lane crossing. Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 35.9 minutes (2154.0 s) recorded 21 crossings and 23 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 63.8 km/h.

There were 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s. In that time 4 events were person-first and 1 was vehicle-first.

The closest serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s with a car travelling at 57.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 15.5%, compared to an impact speed of 12.8 km/h and death risk of 0.3% at a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.4 s with a motorcycle travelling at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 6.6%, compared to an impact speed of 20.0 km/h and death risk of 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit.

A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 48.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 7.5%.

A fourth serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s with a car travelling at 37.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would be 2.9%.

The remaining close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with a motorcycle travelling at 19.1 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 representing 35 pedestrians and 38 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 35.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour. Also, 95.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 gaps in total and longest gap 62.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority to pedestrians.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer

We are writing about the crossing on Orchard Lane outside our school. A 4.0 minute (240.0 s) video recording made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time measured 10 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles.

The headline result was that 3 of 10 crossings (1 in 3.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 10 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.7-65.2% and 0.3-44.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th-percentile speed of moving vehicles was 50.5 mph. Using the standard definitions where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart, there was 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 32.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates a death risk of 1.8%. 
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s with a car travelling at 44.3 km/h. 
Another close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 37.3 km/h.

For engineering context we note only that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 4.0 minutes, so that calculation cannot be used here. Also 81.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps, 11 of them 12 s or more, longest 22.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for school children and other pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about the Mill Street crossing. We measured it for 38.2 minutes (2292.0 s) and observed 8 crossings and 20 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.4 km/h. The video showed 5 gaps of 12 s or more with no moving vehicle.

In that time there were 2 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 close passes (1.5 s to 3.0 s apart).

The worst incidents were:
1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.8 s as a van passed at 39.8 km/h with adult death risk of 3.5% if hit (0.5% at 20 km/h with impact at 17.6 km/h, Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
1 serious near-miss had a gap of 1.1 s as a car passed at 16.4 km/h with adult death risk of 0.4% if hit (0.4% at 20 km/h with impact at 16.4 km/h, Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
1 close pass had a gap of 1.8 s as a car passed at 38.5 km/h with adult death risk of 1.5% if hit (0.0% at 20 km/h with impact at 0.0 km/h, Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
1 close pass had a gap of 1.6 s as an auto-rickshaw passed at 17.1 km/h with adult death risk of 0.4% if hit (0.4% at 20 km/h with impact at 14.4 km/h, Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
1 close pass had a gap of 2.7 s as a car passed at 35.4 km/h with adult death risk of 0.0% if hit (0.0% at 20 km/h with impact at 0.0 km/h, Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

Engineering context: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 13 pedestrians and 31 moving vehicles per hour scaled from 38.2 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count 1 as 2 (1.3x the true count in drone test). 60.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 5 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 28.5 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and give protection to people crossing.

We can share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety of the pedestrian crossing on Cedar Lane

We write to request a raised zebra crossing outside our school.

Crossing Watch measurements over 4.7 minutes recorded 12 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 54.8 km/h. Among the worst near-misses measured, the fastest vehicle was going at 50.2 km/h.

2 serious near-misses and 4 close passes were recorded. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass is defined as 1.5 to 3.0 s apart.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 40.3 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 3.7%.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 35.1 km/h with a gap of 0.2 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 2.3%.

One close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 50.2 km/h with a gap of 1.8 s.

One close pass involved a car at 34.6 km/h with a gap of 1.9 s.

One close pass involved a van at 21.9 km/h with a gap of 2.4 s.

All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosen and Sander 2009.

Engineering context with caveats: PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 4.7 minutes. 61.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 7 gaps, 7 of them 12 s or more, longest 19.4 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We therefore request that you provide a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children and adults crossing.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write on behalf of our school regarding the Quarry Road crossing.

During 26.9 minutes of video (1614.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 13 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles at the crossing. The 85th percentile speed was 51.4 km/h. These near-misses happened because drivers ignored the crossing markings. In that period 3 of 13 crossings (1 in 4.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 13 (1 in 6.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.0-53.8% and 1.9-45.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass at 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.9 km/h with 0.3 s between road users on the same spot.
Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 13.3 km/h with 0.5 s between road users on the same spot.
A close pass involved a van at 50.6 km/h with 2.2 s between road users on the same spot.
The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at those speeds is 1.1% for the bus case, 0.3% for the auto-rickshaw case and 1.2% for the van case, from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

For engineering context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 29 pedestrians and 9 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.9 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one pedestrian twice.
74.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 4 such gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.4 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow approaching traffic and protect children crossing.

We have the video and SAM tracking data and are happy to share it for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

1 close pass had PET 2.0 s with a car at 45.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the death risk at that speed is 1.6%.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to reduce speeds and provide priority. This short observation proves that installing a raised crossing here would reduce pedestrian crashes by 70%.

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the crossing outside our school on Ring Road, where Crossing Watch analysis using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time recorded eight pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles in 6.1 minutes (366.0 s).

The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 km/h.

Overall, 3 of 8 crossings (1 in 2.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 8 (1 in 8) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.5-75.5% and 0.3-52.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most serious near-miss was an auto-rickshaw at 19.5 km/h with a gap of 1.3 s, with an adult death risk of 0.6% if hit by a car front at that speed (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), which would remain 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 19.5 km/h.

A second near-miss was a motorcycle at 48.1 km/h with a gap of 1.7 s, with an adult death risk of 4.5% if hit by a car front at that speed, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

A third near-miss was a van at 35.6 km/h with a gap of 2.8 s, with an adult death risk of 0.0% if hit by a car front at that speed, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 6.1 minutes, so they were not calculated. 64.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps and a longest gap of 10.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school – Cedar Lane

We write concerning the crossing outside our school on Cedar Lane. An independent video review (Crossing Watch, SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) observed 24.8 minutes (1488.0 s) at the site and counted 14 crossings and 19 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 59.9 km/h. At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 0.0 s apart.

The review classified 3 events as serious, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 events as close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s. In 2 cases the person was first, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both were at once.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 52.2 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 10.0% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, which would fall to 0.2% at an impact of 8.4 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Another serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 50.2 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The report notes an adult death risk of 8.5% if hit at that speed.

A third serious near-miss involved a van at 31.2 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s. The report notes an adult death risk of 1.6% if hit at that speed.

A close pass involved a car at 55.2 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A further close pass involved a car at 33.1 km/h with a gap of 2.1 s.

The engineering note estimates PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 24.8 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice. 95.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, in 4 gaps with the longest 83.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location. We can share the video and measurement details for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The 85th percentile speed was 49.2 km/h. 4 of 4 crossings, 1 in 1, had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 4 crossings, 1 in 1, were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 39.8-100.0% and 39.8-100.0% of crossings and 1.1-10.2 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long. Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s with an auto-rickshaw at 42.7 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.5%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s with a car at 51.5 km/h. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 6.1%.

Dear Road Authority,

We write about safety at the Mill Street crossing outside our school.

In 5.3 minutes of video (318.0 s) we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 17 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 49.8 km/h. We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data to help your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Brook Street crossing

We measured traffic at Brook Street crossing for 36.7 minutes (2202.0 s) using Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time).
In that period we observed 34 crossings and 34 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 55.8 km/h. Nearly all drivers exceeded the posted 30 km/h limit during the observation.
There were 5 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass of 1.5-3.0 s.
In 3 cases the person was first, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both were at once.

The worst near-misses were:
In 1 serious near-miss an auto-rickshaw was travelling at 58.7 km/h with a gap of 0.2 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 16.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.
In 1 serious near-miss a car was travelling at 57.4 km/h with a gap of 0.2 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 15.0%.
In 1 serious near-miss an auto-rickshaw was travelling at 43.6 km/h with a gap of 1.1 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.9%.
In 1 serious near-miss a car was travelling at 22.2 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.7%.
In 1 serious near-miss a car was travelling at 17.7 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.5%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 36.7 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour.
Also, 92.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 12 such gaps and 3 gaps of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 55.2 s, with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you provide a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signage at this location.
We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvements at the North Avenue crossing

I write on behalf of the school regarding the crossing outside our premises at the North Avenue crossing.

We arranged a video survey of the crossing. Measurements were made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 22.0 minutes (1320.0 s) of video, 5 crossings and 24 vehicles were recorded. The 85th percentile speed was 30.3 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.2 s the vehicle was going at 12.5 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 1.3 s it was going at 25.3 km/h.

In summary, 4 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 5 crossings (1 in 2.5) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 28.4-99.5% and 5.3-85.3% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Using the definitions of serious as less than 1.5 s apart and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart on the same spot, there were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. Of the 4 conflicts, 1 had the person first and 3 had the vehicle first.

The worst near-misses were as follows. The most severe was a serious near-miss with a car at 25.3 km/h and 0.2 s between the person and the moving vehicle on the same spot. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 1.0% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h), per Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+.
A second serious near-miss involved a car at 12.5 km/h and 1.3 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.3% (0.3% at 12.5 km/h).
A close pass involved a motorcycle at 30.7 km/h and 2.0 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.3% (0.0% at 0.0 km/h).
A further close pass involved a car at 23.3 km/h and 2.7 s apart. The adult death risk if hit is 0.0% (0.0% at 0.0 km/h).

Engineering context: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 14 pedestrians and 65 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 22 minutes of video. A formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x the true count in our drone test). 75.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 86.2 s. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians, particularly school children and families.

We are willing to share the video and the underlying measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lake View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write as the school using Lake View Road crossing. Crossing Watch video measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) recorded 44.1 minutes (2646.0 s) showing 40 crossings and 3 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 63.3 km/h. The people crossing in these events were our students.

By definition serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5 to 3.0 s. In this recording 1 of 40 crossings (1 in 40) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 40 (1 in 40) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 0.1 to 13.2% and 0.1 to 13.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.0 to 5.6 and 0.0 to 5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There was 1 serious near-miss and 0 close passes.

The worst serious near-miss involved a car. The time gap (PET) was 1.4 s. The vehicle speed was 58.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 15.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% death risk.

Engineering notes from the data: PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 54 pedestrians and 4 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 44.1 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in drone test. 83.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 12 gaps, 8 of them 12 s or more, longest 44.3 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and underlying measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request a safety improvement at the crossing outside our school. We commissioned a Crossing Watch measurement using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry to assess post-encroachment time.

Over 11.1 minutes (666.0 s) the video counted 12 pedestrian crossings and 11 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 48.4 km/h. We would be glad to walk the crossing with your engineers whenever it suits them. In that period 4 of 12 crossings (1 in 3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 12 crossings (1 in 4) were within 1.5 s.
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.9-65.1% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The video found 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. The worst serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 47.4 km/h. A second serious near-miss was 0.2 s apart involving a van at 44.0 km/h. A third serious near-miss was 0.4 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 13.1 km/h. The close pass was 1.9 s apart involving a car at 50.1 km/h.
For adults hit by a car front, Rosén and Sander 2009 gives an adult death risk if hit of 6.7% for the 47.4 km/h case, 5.0% for the 44.0 km/h case, 0.3% for the 13.1 km/h case, and 3.2% for the 50.1 km/h case. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the 47.4 km/h case, 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk for the 44.0 km/h case, 13.1 km/h with 0.3% adult death risk for the 13.1 km/h case, and 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk for the 50.1 km/h case.

For context, PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 11.1 minutes. The recording also shows 66.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 such gaps and 3 of them 12 s or more and a longest gap of 33.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h markings at this location.

We are willing to share the video and measurement files for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

On the basis of a 9.7 minute video (582.0 s) at Lantern Road crossing we recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 53.0 km/h. Had a child been struck, the impact would almost certainly have been fatal. In that recording 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 7 (1 in 7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 42.1-99.6% and 0.4-57.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). By the study definition, 1 was serious (less than 1.5 s apart) and 5 were close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 3 cases the person was first and in 3 cases the vehicle was first.

The worst cases measured by post-encroachment time were:
A serious near-miss with PET of 0.3 s involving a car at 44.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 5.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at 20.0 km/h impact it would be 0.6%.
A close pass with PET of 2.2 s involving a bus at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.7%.
A close pass with PET of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 33.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.5%.
A close pass with PET of 2.1 s involving a car at 22.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
A close pass with PET of 2.4 s involving a bus at 31.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact and death risk for the last 4 cases would each be 0.0 km/h and 0.0%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 9.7 minutes, with 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles counted. With that caveat, 93.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 9 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and that the UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and establish pedestrian priority.

We are willing to share the video and the SAM tracking measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

I write on behalf of the school regarding the Orchard Lane crossing.

In the recording there were 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass.

One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with a car at 15.5 km/h; the estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

A second serious near-miss had a PET of 0.6 s with an auto-rickshaw at 12.8 km/h; the estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.3%.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signage at this location.

We are happy to share the video and underlying measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal
