LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. In total, 3 close passes were measured.

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 41 vehicles an hour scaled from 33.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 46.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and longest 39.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write regarding the River Lane crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch recorded 25 crossings in 36.0 minutes with 10 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 56.9 km/h. At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 0.1 s apart.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pupils crossing.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the Market Street crossing following a video survey of 10.9 minutes (654.0 s) that recorded 10 pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 52.4 km/h. There have already been injuries at this spot this school year.

The analysis found 5 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. A serious near-miss is defined as a pedestrian and a moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. In 1 case the pedestrian was first, in 5 cases the vehicle was first, and in 0 cases both were at once.

The most severe event involved a car at 53.7 km/h with 0.5 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 11.3%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

A second event involved an auto-rickshaw at 41.9 km/h with 0.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 4.2%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A third event involved a van at 35.0 km/h with 0.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 2.3%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A fourth event involved an auto-rickshaw at 18.9 km/h with 0.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5%, which remains 0.5% at an impact of 18.9 km/h.

A fifth event involved a van at 18.6 km/h with 0.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5%, which remains 0.5% at an impact of 18.6 km/h.

Risk estimates are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

Engineering context is limited. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, while this video is 10.9 minutes with 10 pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles. In this video 66.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps of 6 s or more including 1 gap of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 68.3 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location and we are willing to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.0-39.7% and 2.2-27.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 close passes (1.5-3.0 s).

The worst serious incidents were: a motorcycle with a gap of 1.1 s at 34.0 km/h with adult death risk if hit by a car front of 2.1% (5.2 km/h and 0.2% at 20 km/h limit); an auto-rickshaw with a gap of 0.3 s at 13.5 km/h with adult death risk of 0.3% (13.5 km/h and 0.3% at 20 km/h limit); and a bus with a gap of 1.1 s at 13.6 km/h with adult death risk of 0.3% (13.6 km/h and 0.3% at 20 km/h limit). Close passes included a bus with a gap of 2.0 s at 39.1 km/h with adult death risk of 0.8% and a car with a gap of 2.3 s at 14.2 km/h with adult death risk of 0.0%. Risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 67 pedestrians and 87 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.1 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 29 crossings were recorded across 1566.0 s containing 10 gaps lasting 6 s or longer. 62.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 10 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more, longest 49.0 s, with the first and last cut short by the video; UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs at this location. We will share the full video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the crossing on School Lane outside our school.

We measured traffic for 11.9 minutes and counted 7 pedestrian crossings and 40 moving vehicles.

The 85th percentile speed was 42.3 km/h. Had a child been struck, the impact would almost certainly have been fatal.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses and 3 close passes.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 34.8 km/h with 0.7 s between road users, with a 2.3% adult death risk if hit by a car front, which would fall to 0.6% adult death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Another serious near-miss involved a van at 27.0 km/h with 0.4 s between road users, with a 1.1% adult death risk if hit by a car front, which would fall to 0.6% adult death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

A third serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 24.4 km/h with 1.3 s between road users, with a 0.9% adult death risk if hit by a car front, which would fall to 0.5% adult death risk at an impact of 17.7 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 11.9 minutes.

Only 40.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to reduce speeds and provide a safe crossing point.

We are willing to share the video of the crossing for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer

We are writing about the crossing on Orchard Lane outside our school. A 4.0 minute (240.0 s) video recording made by Crossing Watch using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time measured 10 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles.

The headline result was that 3 of 10 crossings (1 in 3.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 10 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.7-65.2% and 0.3-44.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 85th-percentile speed of moving vehicles was 50.5 km/h. The people crossing in these events were our students. Using the standard definitions where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s apart, there was 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car travelling at 32.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates a death risk of 1.8%. 
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s with a car travelling at 44.3 km/h. 
Another close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.5 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 37.3 km/h.

For engineering context we note only that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 4.0 minutes, so that calculation cannot be used here. Also 81.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps, 11 of them 12 s or more, longest 22.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for school children and other pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The 85th percentile speed was 66.6 km/h.

The 4th event was 2.3 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 18.7 km/h; adult death risk if hit is 0.0%, compared to 0.0% at 0.0 km/h.
The 5th event was 2.9 s apart involving a car at 52.9 km/h; adult death risk if hit is 0.0%, compared to 0.0% at 0.0 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, based on 24 pedestrians and 51 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.7 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x. 51.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 4 gaps and 0 gaps of 12 s or more and longest 10.7 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at River Lane crossing to lower speeds and give adequate gaps.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Dear Sir/Madam,

I write on behalf of our school about the crossing on Station Road outside the school. We arranged a video survey of 15.2 minutes (912.0 s) which recorded 12 crossings and 32 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.0 km/h. 12 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video.

Of the 12 crossings, 5 of 12 crossings (1 in 2.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 12 crossings (1 in 4) had a vehicle within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 15.2-72.3% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 3 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5-3.0 s). One serious near-miss involved a van with a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s at 45.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 5.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). Another serious near-miss involved a car with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s at 41.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 4.0%. A third serious near-miss involved a bus with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.7%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (47 pedestrians and 126 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 15.2 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour). Also 78.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed (the first and last gaps are cut short by the video).

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children and other pedestrians.

We would be happy to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your engineers to review. Please let us know how you will assess this site for safety improvements.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Re: Request for safety improvement at Canal Road crossing

We write as the school that uses Canal Road crossing. Crossing Watch video measurements were made by SAM tracking with road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

In 5.3 minutes of video (318.0 s) there were 12 pedestrian crossings and 6 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 19.5 km/h.

There was 1 serious near-miss and 0 close passes. Serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. Close pass means 1.5 to 3.0 s. In this case 1 vehicle arrived first, 0 person first and 0 both at once.

The worst case was a serious near-miss with a car. The vehicle speed was 16.2 km/h. The gap between the pedestrian and vehicle on the same spot was 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at 16.2 km/h the death risk is 0.4% based on Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts. At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 16.2 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.4%.

On engineering use of the data, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 5.3. 54.3% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed. There were 10 gaps of 6 s or more and 6 gaps of 12 s or more. The longest gap was 49.2 s. Many children were forced to run across the road to avoid being hit during the survey. The first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4 to 6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10 to 12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to slow vehicles and provide protected priority for pedestrians.

We can share the video and tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.8 s with a car at 25.8 km/h, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.4%.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

I write concerning the North Avenue crossing outside our school.

A Crossing Watch review of 11.5 minutes (690.0 s) recorded 12 pedestrian crossings and 21 moving vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 46.9 km/h. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began.
There were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart.
In 4 interactions the vehicle went first, in 0 the person went first, and in 1 both were there at once.

The worst near-misses were:
A car at 31.7 km/h was 0.5 s apart from a pedestrian. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the published death risk is 1.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A car at 25.1 km/h was 0.0 s apart from a pedestrian. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the published death risk is 1.0%.
A bus at 20.8 km/h was 1.2 s apart from a pedestrian. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the published death risk is 0.6%.
At a 20.0 km/h impact speed the published adult death risk would be 0.6%.

Engineering context has caveats. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 11.5 minutes, with 12 crossings and 21 vehicles counted.
72.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 gaps of 6 s or more and 0 of 12 s or more and longest gap 8.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We can share the video and tracking data on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about pedestrian safety outside our school. A video review using SAM tracking and road-plane geometry measured the crossing for 37.5 minutes (2250.0 s). In that time 22 crossings and 20 vehicles were counted.

Of the 22 crossings, 3 of 22 (1 in 7.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 
Of the 22 crossings, 2 of 22 (1 in 11) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s of the person. 
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 2.9-34.9% and 1.1-29.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile vehicle speed was 61.3 km/h. In total, 2 close passes were measured.

The worst near-miss was a serious case with a car at 31.7 km/h passing 0.2 s from a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
Another serious case was a bus at 24.2 km/h with a gap of 1.0 s. For an adult hit at that speed the death risk is 0.9%, compared to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A close pass was a van at 57.7 km/h with a gap of 2.4 s.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 35 pedestrians and 32 moving vehicles an hour scaled from the 37.5 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour. 
In addition, 84.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, from 12 gaps with longest 9.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Cedar Lane crossing. Measurements from video analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) covering 7.6 minutes (456.0 s) recorded 6 pedestrian crossings and 36 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 46.4 km/h. Children hit at these speeds face a far higher risk of death than adults.

The analysis defines serious as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass as 1.5-3.0 s. In that period there were 1 serious near-miss and 5 close passes, with 3 where the person was first, 3 where the vehicle was first and 0 where both were at once.

The worst events were: a serious near-miss with a gap of 0.6 s involving a car at 36.0 km/h. A close pass with a gap of 2.2 s involving a car at 33.1 km/h. A close pass with a gap of 2.2 s involving a car at 20.7 km/h. A close pass with a gap of 2.6 s involving a car at 16.1 km/h. A close pass with a gap of 2.7 s involving a car at 45.4 km/h. For the serious near-miss the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 2.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 7.6 minutes. 53.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more, 0 gaps of 12 s or more, and a longest gap of 7.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce speeds and give priority to people crossing.

We are happy to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Brook Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked Crossing Watch to record the Brook Street crossing for 40.5 minutes (2430.0 s). In that time there were 24 crossings and 31 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.0 km/h. At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 1.5 s apart. 4 of 24 crossings (1 in 6) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 3 of 24 (1 in 8) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 4.7-37.4% and 2.7-32.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5 s to 3.0 s). The worst cases were:
A serious near-miss with post-encroachment time 0.6 s involved a car at 50.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 8.5%, compared with 0.6% at 19.9 km/h if limited to 20 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A serious near-miss with post-encroachment time 0.6 s involved a motorcycle at 23.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%.
A serious near-miss with post-encroachment time 0.4 s involved a car at 12.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
A close pass with post-encroachment time 1.5 s involved a motorcycle at 34.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 2.1%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (36 pedestrians and 46 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 40.5 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour). 83.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 85.8 s (the first and last are cut short by the video).

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We have the video and tracking data and can share them on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside Brook Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write from the school beside Brook Street crossing. Crossing Watch video for 44.4 minutes recorded 22 crossings and 36 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 46.5 km/h. There were 10 gaps of 6 s or more and 5 gaps of 12 s or more, longest 66.7 s.

The video showed 5 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes of 1.5 to 3.0 s. One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.2 s with an auto-rickshaw at 46.4 km/h. If an adult had been hit at that speed the death risk from a car front is 6.1% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+. LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We are writing about the crossing outside our school at the Hill View Road site monitored by Crossing Watch.

In a 3.0 minute recording of 180.0 s we counted 8 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 32.2 km/h. These near-misses happened because drivers ignored the crossing markings. 3 of 8 crossings (1 in 2.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 2 of 8 (1 in 4) within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.5-75.5% and 3.2-65.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

For an adult hit by a car front at 33.9 km/h the estimated death risk is 2.1% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
A 2nd serious near-miss had a PET of 0.0 s with a motorcycle at 16.6 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at 16.6 km/h the estimated death risk is 0.4% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
A close pass had a PET of 1.5 s with a car at 24.7 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at 24.7 km/h the estimated death risk is 0.9% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.
At a 20 km/h limit the impact speeds would have been 5.9 km/h, 16.6 km/h and 6.5 km/h with adult death risks of 0.2%, 0.4% and 0.2% respectively.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 3.0 minutes. 73.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.5 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to lower speeds and provide protected gaps.

We have the tracking data and can share the video file on request to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school - Cedar Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request safety improvements at the crossing outside our school. Using Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) we measured traffic for 11.9 minutes (714.0 s).

In that period we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 13 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.3 km/h. The recording these figures come from lasted 11.9 minutes. A serious near-miss is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s. We recorded 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 3 cases the vehicle arrived first, with 0 cases where both arrived at once.

The engineering assessment notes that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 11.9 minutes, so rates are not reported. It also notes that 95.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 12 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 gaps of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 85.1 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a car at 56.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front is 14.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), falling to 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved a car at 34.6 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 2.2%, falling to 0.5% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 18.5 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 29.1 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 1.4%, with 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit and an impact speed of 20.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved a car at 13.2 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.6 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 0.3%, remaining 0.3% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 13.2 km/h. One close pass involved a car at 50.5 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.8 s. At that speed the estimated adult death risk is 4.3%, falling to 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

Given the high speeds and repeated close interactions, we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at North Avenue crossing

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at North Avenue crossing. Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry) for 18.2 minutes recorded 40 crossings and 28 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 45.1 km/h. Had a child been struck, the impact would almost certainly have been fatal.

In that period 6 of 40 crossings (1 in 6.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 4 of 40 crossings (1 in 10) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 5.7-29.8% and 2.8-23.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 with 132 pedestrians and 92 moving vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 18.2 minutes while a formal check counts the full peak hour. 62.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

The worst near-misses illustrate the risk. One serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 38.7 km/h with 1.3 s between road users. For an adult hit by a car front at 38.7 km/h the estimated death risk is 3.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk.

One serious near-miss involved a van at 32.9 km/h with 0.1 s between road users. For an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.9%.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 31.6 km/h with 0.7 s between road users. For an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.7%.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 26.9 km/h with 1.4 s between road users. For an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.1%.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 3.3 km/h with 0.1% adult death risk.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds to the 20 km/h limit. We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We write on behalf of the school beside Station Road crossing to request a raised zebra crossing with a speed table.

A Crossing Watch video of the crossing recorded 11.4 minutes (684.0 s) with 3 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles and an 85th percentile speed of 42.6 km/h. At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 1.0 s apart.

In that recording, 3 of 3 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 3 of 3 (1 in 1) within 1.5 s.

If this recording is typical, the exact 95% ranges are 29.2-100.0% of crossings within 3 s and 29.2-100.0% within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long for each measure (Poisson).

There were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart.

1 serious near-miss involved a car at 38.2 km/h with a gap of 1.0 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.0% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

1 serious near-miss involved a car at 14.7 km/h with a gap of 1.0 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.4%.

1 serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 13.5 km/h with a gap of 0.5 s.

For context, 85.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 2 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 19.7 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 11.4 minutes with 3 crossings and 4 vehicles, so rates cannot be reliably calculated.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to lower speeds and provide a protected crossing point.

We are willing to share the video and underlying measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Garden Road outside our school.

In a 10.8 minute recording we counted 11 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles.
5 of 11 crossings (1 in 2.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person.
2 of 11 crossings (1 in 5.5) were within 1.5 s.
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 16.7-76.6% and 2.3-51.8% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.6-11.7 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).
By definition, serious is less than 1.5 s apart and close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

The worst incidents recorded were:
A car at 48.2 km/h was 0.6 s from a person, with adult death risk if hit of 7.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). Children hit at these speeds face a far higher risk of death than adults.
A van at 26.9 km/h was 0.7 s from a person, with adult death risk if hit of 1.1%.
A car at 51.0 km/h was 1.5 s from a person, with adult death risk if hit of 9.0%.
A car at 42.6 km/h was 1.6 s from a person, with adult death risk if hit of 3.6%.
A van at 23.8 km/h was 2.1 s from a person.
The 85th percentile speed was 56.8 km/h.
At a 20 km/h limit the adult death risk would be 0.6% for the 2 serious cases.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 10.8 minutes.
46.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed; 11 gaps, 9 of them 12 s or more, longest 20.2 s, with the first and last cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.
We offer to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We measured traffic at Brook Street crossing for 36.7 minutes (2202.0 s) using Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time).
In that period we observed 34 crossings and 34 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 55.8 km/h. The van that came closest is driven by Mr. Ashok Varghese of the corner shop.
There were 5 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass of 1.5-3.0 s.
In 3 cases the person was first, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both were at once.

The worst near-misses were:

In 1 serious near-miss a car was travelling at 57.4 km/h with a gap of 0.2 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 15.0%.
In 1 serious near-miss an auto-rickshaw was travelling at 43.6 km/h with a gap of 1.1 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.9%.
In 1 serious near-miss a car was travelling at 22.2 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.7%.
In 1 serious near-miss a car was travelling at 17.7 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s; the adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.5%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 36.7 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We write about the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We write as the school using the crossing outside our gate. Crossing Watch video covering 25.6 minutes (1536.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 35 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.9 km/h. At its tightest, a vehicle and a person were on the same spot 0.6 s apart.

The analysis found 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Of the 8 potential conflicts, 4 had the person first, 2 had the vehicle first, and 0 had both at once.

The worst near-misses were:
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with an auto-rickshaw at 59.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 18.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s with a van at 51.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 9.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 19.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.9 s with a bus at 40.7 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 3.8%, compared with 0.2% at an impact of 8.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with a car at 30.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.5%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with a car at 51.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.4%, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
All death-risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15+ hit by car fronts.

For context, the video gives PV² of 0.0 x 10^8 from 19 pedestrians and 82 vehicles per hour, with the caveat that this is scaled from 25.6 minutes not a full peak hour and our test shows broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also, 62.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 11 such gaps including 3 of 12 s or more and longest 74.2 s, with the caveat that first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We have the video and Crossing Watch data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We write as the school by Station Road crossing. A Crossing Watch video survey of 28.5 minutes, duration 1710.0 s, recorded 7 crossings and 26 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 47.0 mph.

The review found 2 serious near-misses defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 2 close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. Of 4 events, 1 was person first, 2 were vehicle first and 1 was both at once.

The most severe event was a serious near-miss with a car at 39.7 km/h and a gap of 0.0 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 3.5% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 36.5 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 2.6%, falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

One close pass involved a bus at 47.1 km/h with a gap of 1.7 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 4.1%.

One close pass involved a motorcycle at 34.8 km/h with a gap of 1.7 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 1.4%.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 15 pedestrians and 55 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 28.5 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x high in our drone test. Also 57.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 10 gaps, 10 of them 12 s or more, longest 68.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected crossing time.

We can share the full video and measurements for your review and welcome a joint site inspection.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s and involved a car at 22.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.1% at an impact of 3.3 km/h.

73.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 8 of 12 s or more and longest gap 76.8 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority. The recording lasting 2016.0 s captured 6 crossings alongside 33 vehicles.

We can share the full video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. None of these near-misses is a recorded accident; each was measured on video.

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 41 vehicles an hour scaled from 33.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 46.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and longest 39.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We are writing to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our school.

We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir / Madam,

Re: Safety at Lake View Road crossing

In a Crossing Watch video of 33.6 minutes (2016.0 s) we measured 6 pedestrian crossings and 33 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 43.6 km/h. Among the worst near-misses measured, the fastest vehicle was going at 44.8 km/h.

5 of 6 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 6 (1 in 2) were within 1.5 s.
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 35.9-99.6% and 11.8-88.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes were:
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s and involved a car at 35.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 2.3% for a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s and involved a car at 33.4 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 2.0% for a car front, falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s and involved a car at 17.8 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.5% for a car front, remaining 0.5% at an impact of 17.8 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s and involved a car at 22.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.1% at an impact of 3.3 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.3 s and involved a bus at 44.8 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, but this is scaled from only 33.6 minutes of video and a formal check counts the full peak hour with caveats about broken tracks.
73.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 8 of 12 s or more and longest gap 76.8 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority.

We can share the full video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside the school

We write to request a raised zebra crossing with 20 km/h zone, signs and markings outside our school. The closest of these near-misses was the fault of Mr. Tarun Mehra, who runs the tea stall. A supervised video measurement of 6.8 minutes recorded 5 pedestrian crossings and 38 moving vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 53.1 km/h.

Of 5 crossings, 5 had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s and 3 were within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, the exact 95 percent ranges are 47.8-100.0 percent and 14.7-94.7 percent of crossings and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long.

The worst near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 48.3 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s. The adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is given as 7.2 percent, compared with 0.6 percent at 20.0 km/h. 
A second serious near-miss involved a car at 17.5 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s. 
A third serious near-miss involved a van at 12.9 km/h with a gap of 0.4 s.

Engineering values are limited: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 6.8 minutes, and 43.2 percent of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request the fix above to reduce speeds and protect children crossing. We are willing to share the video and measurement file for verification.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Station Road

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). In that time 38 crossings and eight vehicles were recorded, the 85th percentile speed was 44.1 km/h, there were 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 7 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 53.4 s, and 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 38 (1 in 7.6) within 1.5 s; exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-31.3% and 4.4-28.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. One involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The worst near-misses illustrate the risk. One serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 38.7 km/h with 1.3 s between road users. For an adult hit by a car front at 38.7 km/h the estimated death risk is 3.2% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 0.0 km/h with 0.0% adult death risk.

One serious near-miss involved a van at 32.9 km/h with 0.1 s between road users. For an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.9%.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 31.6 km/h with 0.7 s between road users. For an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.7%.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 26.9 km/h with 1.4 s between road users. For an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 1.1%.

At 20 km/h the impact speed for that event would have been 3.3 km/h with 0.1% adult death risk.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds to the 20 km/h limit. We are willing to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the crossing outside our school at Canal Road crossing.

In a recording lasting 126.0 s (2.1 minutes) we counted 3 pedestrian crossings and 14 moving vehicles. 3 of 3 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 3 of 3 (1 in 1) within 1.5 s. The 85th percentile speed was 42.2 km/h. Several children have been hurt at this crossing since the term began.

We recorded 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. One near-miss involved a car at 44.2 km/h with a gap of 0.9 s. Another near-miss involved a van at 33.6 km/h with a gap of 0.1 s. A third near-miss involved a car at 19.1 km/h with a gap of 0.9 s. For adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), the death risk if hit was 5.1% at 44.2 km/h, 2.0% at 33.6 km/h and 0.6% at 19.1 km/h.

Engineering context is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 2.1 minutes. Counted: 3 pedestrian crossings, 14 moving vehicles. 79.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 3 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 7.7 s (the first and last are cut short by the video).

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.

We would be happy to share the video and data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the safety of the crossing outside our school at the North Avenue crossing.

In 43.7 minutes of video we recorded 23 crossings and 8 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 54.6 km/h. 23 gaps were cut short by the start or end of the video. 2 of 23 crossings (1 in 12) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 1 of 23 crossings (1 in 23) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, the exact 95% ranges are 1.1-28.0% and 0.1-21.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 0.2-7.2 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 48.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s. An adult hit by a car front at that speed would face a 7.5% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact speed of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

A second close pass involved a car at 53.3 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s. An adult hit by a car front at that speed would face a 1.6% death risk, compared with 0.0% at 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 32 pedestrians and 11 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 43.7 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. 95.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 9 such gaps and longest 7.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and speed table at this location.

We have the video measurements and are ready to share them to help your assessment. Please let us know how to proceed.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Orchard Lane crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about safety at Orchard Lane crossing. A video recording of 10.1 minutes (606.0 s) measured 5 pedestrian crossings and 10 vehicles, with 85th percentile speed 58.8 km/h. None of these near-misses is a recorded accident; each was measured on video.

Headline result: 3 of 5 crossings (1 in 1.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 3 of 5 (1 in 1.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 14.7-94.7% and 14.7-94.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Within that time there were 3 serious near-misses and 0 close passes, where serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a van at 52.0 km/h with 0.8 s between road users.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 48.5 km/h with 1.1 s between road users.

A third serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 22.9 km/h with 1.4 s between road users.

For adults hit by a car front the estimated death risks for those speeds are 9.8%, 7.3% and 0.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact speeds would be 0.0 km/h, 0.0 km/h and 17.3 km/h with death risks 0.0%, 0.0% and 0.5%.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 10.1 minutes with 5 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles. 50.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 1 gap of 6 s or more, 0 gaps of 12 s or more and longest gap 11.3 s, with the main caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and measurement log for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam, We write about the crossing outside our school on Orchard Lane. A Crossing Watch review of 29.7 minutes of video (1782.0 s) recorded 23 crossings and 3 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 27.5 km/h. The death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). During that period 5 gaps of 6 s or more were available, including 2 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 60.4 s. In that same period we observed 2 serious near-misses (defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 1 close pass (1.5-3.0 s). One serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 23.9 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s; for an adult hit at that speed the Rosén & Sander 2009 car-front risk is 0.9%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. A second serious near-miss involved a car at 23.1 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s; for an adult hit at that speed the risk is 0.8%. A close pass involved a motorcycle at 19.6 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.8 s. Engineering notes indicate PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 when scaled from 29.7 minutes to 46 pedestrians and 6 vehicles an hour, noting a formal check requires the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount. 87.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children crossing. We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review. Yours faithfully, The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school – Cedar Lane

We write concerning the crossing outside our school on Cedar Lane. An independent video review (Crossing Watch, SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) observed 24.8 minutes (1488.0 s) at the site and counted 14 crossings and 19 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 59.9 km/h.

The review classified three events as serious, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 events as close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s. In 2 cases the person was first, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both were at once.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 52.2 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 10.0% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, which would fall to 0.2% at an impact of 8.4 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Another serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 50.2 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The report notes an adult death risk of 8.5% if hit at that speed.

A third serious near-miss involved a van at 31.2 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s. The report notes an adult death risk of 1.6% if hit at that speed.

A close pass involved a car at 55.2 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A further close pass involved a car at 33.1 km/h with a gap of 2.1 s.

The engineering note estimates PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 24.8 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice. 95.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, in 4 gaps with the longest 83.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location. We can share the video and measurement details for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Hill View Road crossing. A Crossing Watch video of 1.8 minutes (108.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 48 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 44.0 km/h. To sum up, the recording showed 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes.

Engineering assessment is limited because PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 1.8. Within the recording, 43.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 9 gaps, 8 of them 12 s or more, longest 52.6 s (the first and last are cut short by the video).

In that same 1.8 minutes there were 4 serious near-misses and 2 close passes. Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 36.8 km/h with 1.2 s between pedestrian and vehicle.

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 35.9 km/h with 0.2 s between users.

A third serious near-miss involved a car at 22.5 km/h with 0.1 s between users.

A fourth serious near-miss involved a car at 19.8 km/h with 1.0 s between users.

One close pass involved a car at 20.5 km/h with 2.0 s between users.

For adults hit by a car front, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates adult death risk rises with impact speed. At these speeds adult risk was 2.7% at 36.8 km/h, 2.5% at 35.9 km/h, 0.8% at 22.5 km/h and 0.6% at 19.8 km/h. At a 20 km/h limit the impact speed and adult death risk would be lower, for example 20.0 km/h with 0.6% adult death risk.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing to slow vehicles and provide protected priority for pedestrians at this school crossing.

We are happy to share the video and SAM tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing on Park Avenue outside the school

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school arranged a Crossing Watch on the crossing on Park Avenue. In 6.9 minutes (414.0 s) we counted 7 pedestrian crossings and 23 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 47.9 km/h. The van that came closest is driven by Mr. Ashok Varghese of the corner shop.

We record a serious near-miss as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass as 1.5-3.0 s apart. We observed 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass, with 1 case where the person was first and 2 cases where the vehicle was first.

One serious near-miss involved a van at 45.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 5.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 44.2 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 5.1% (same source).

A close pass involved a car at 22.1 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s.

We note that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 6.9 minutes. In this short sample 50.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 7 gaps of 6 s or more and 6 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 79.0 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We can share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on River Lane

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the River Lane crossing outside our school. Crossing Watch recorded 25 crossings in 36.0 minutes with 10 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 56.9 km/h.

In that period 2 of 25 crossings (1 in 12) were serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 of 25 (1 in 12) were within 3 s. Exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 1.0-26.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most severe was a bus at 52.9 km/h passing 0.1 s after a person. A child hit by the bus at 52.9 km/h would have faced a 10.6% risk of death. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 10.6% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

The second serious near-miss was a van at 22.9 km/h passing 1.3 s after a person. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, scaled from 36.0 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice. Also, 62.4% of time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 3 such gaps and longest 81.8 s, though the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide priority for pupils crossing.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We write as the school using the crossing outside our gate. Crossing Watch video covering 25.6 minutes (1536.0 s) recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 35 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.9 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 0.5 s the vehicle was going at 51.1 km/h, and in the one with a time gap of 0.6 s it was going at 59.9 km/h.

The analysis found 4 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Of the 8 potential conflicts, 4 had the person first, 2 had the vehicle first, and 0 had both at once.

The worst near-misses were:
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with an auto-rickshaw at 59.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 18.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.6 s with a van at 51.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 9.1%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 19.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.9 s with a bus at 40.7 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 3.8%, compared with 0.2% at an impact of 8.1 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 serious near-miss had a gap of 0.5 s with a car at 30.1 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.5%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
- 1 close pass had a gap of 2.2 s with a car at 51.9 km/h. If an adult had been hit by a car front at that speed the death risk would have been 1.4%, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.
All death-risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults aged 15+ hit by car fronts.

For context, the video gives PV² of 0.0 x 10^8 from 19 pedestrians and 82 vehicles per hour, with the caveat that this is scaled from 25.6 minutes not a full peak hour and our test shows broken tracks can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x. Also, 62.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 11 such gaps including 3 of 12 s or more and longest 74.2 s, with the caveat that first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We have the video and Crossing Watch data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Road Authority,

We write about safety at the Mill Street crossing outside our school.

In 5.3 minutes of video (318.0 s) we counted 6 pedestrian crossings and 17 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 49.8 km/h. The video showed 5 gaps of 12 s or more with no moving vehicle. There were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes by the definition of less than 1.5 s for serious and 1.5-3.0 s for close pass, with 3 events where the person was first and 1 where the vehicle was first and 0 where both arrived at once.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this video is 5.3 minutes with 6 crossings and 17 vehicles counted. 71.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more, longest 70.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

The worst events recorded were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a bus at 43.0 km/h with a time gap of 0.9 s, where the death risk for an adult hit by a car front would have been 4.6% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts. A second serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 34.5 km/h with a time gap of 1.1 s, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 2.2%. A close pass involved a car at 43.5 km/h with a time gap of 1.5 s, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 4.8%. Another close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 26.9 km/h with a time gap of 2.6 s, where the adult death risk if hit by a car front would have been 0.0%.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data to help your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Re: Safety improvement for Mill Street crossing

We are writing on behalf of the school beside Mill Street crossing. A video of the crossing was analysed with SAM tracking and road-plane geometry.

Yours faithfully,

To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school arranged a video measurement at Quarry Road crossing for 10.3 minutes (618.0 s). In that time 4 pedestrian crossings and 21 moving vehicles were counted. The 85th percentile speed was 59.8 km/h. Most crossings involved young pupils walking home alone after classes.

The recording found 4 of 4 crossings (1 in 1) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 4 of 4 (1 in 1) within 1.5 s.

Serious near-misses were defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart. There were 4 serious near-misses:
- One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.2 s with a car at 59.1 km/h. Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by a car front gives 17.0% adult death risk if hit, compared to 0.0% death risk if impact were at 0.0 km/h with a 20 km/h limit.
- One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.0 s with a car at 57.4 km/h. Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by a car front gives 15.0% adult death risk if hit, compared to 0.6% death risk if impact were at 20.0 km/h with a 20 km/h limit.
- One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.0 s with a car at 39.5 km/h. Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by a car front gives 3.4% adult death risk if hit, compared to 0.6% death risk if impact were at 20.0 km/h with a 20 km/h limit.
- One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s with an auto-rickshaw at 17.8 km/h.

For context on gaps, 68.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 5 gaps of 6 s and 2 gaps of 12 s, longest 25.9 s. PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 10.3 minutes, and first and last gaps are cut short by the video, so these gap figures are only indicative.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and protect people crossing.

We can share the video and Crossing Watch measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the pedestrian crossing outside our school on River Lane. We arranged a Crossing Watch measurement of the crossing. In 7.0 minutes (420.0 s) it counted 11 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles, with an 85th-percentile speed of 54.4 km/h. Mrs. Leela Fernandes, who drives the morning bus, caused the worst of these events. There were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes, defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Where order could be seen, 4 interactions were person-first and 1 was vehicle-first.

The most severe near-miss was 0.3 s apart with a car at 49.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled adult death risk is 7.9%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart with a bus at 48.7 km/h, with a modelled adult death risk of 7.5% if hit.

A third serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart with a car at 45.7 km/h, with a modelled adult death risk of 5.8% if hit.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 7.0, so results are indicative only. 48.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, and the longest 8.8 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and give pedestrians clear priority.

We can share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and would welcome a site visit to discuss the design.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
Approved by The Principal as head of the school

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Request for safety improvements at the Brook Street crossing

We write following a 4.5 minute (270.0 s) video recording at the Brook Street crossing, which captured 6 pedestrian crossings and 24 moving vehicles.

Headline findings were that 4 of 6 crossings (1 in 1.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 2 of 6 (1 in 3) were within 1.5 s. The recording also showed 2 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 2 close passes (1.5 to 3.0 s).

In that recording the 85th percentile speed was 56.6 km/h.

Our most serious near-miss involved a van at 17.4 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.5 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss involved a car at 13.8 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.

Our closest near-miss was a car at 51.0 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s.

Another close pass involved an auto-rickshaw at 29.3 km/h with a post-encroachment time of 2.8 s.

On engineering context, we note that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 4.5. Also, 74.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 9 such gaps and 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 23.5 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given the speeds and the proportion of crossings with close vehicle interactions, we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location.

We would be happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We are writing about the Market Street crossing following a video survey of 10.9 minutes (654.0 s) that recorded 10 pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 52.4 km/h. These near-misses happened because drivers ignored the crossing markings.

The analysis found 5 serious near-misses and 1 close pass. A serious near-miss is defined as a pedestrian and a moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. In 1 case the pedestrian was first, in 5 cases the vehicle was first, and in 0 cases both were at once.

The most severe event involved a car at 53.7 km/h with 0.5 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 11.3%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

A second event involved an auto-rickshaw at 41.9 km/h with 0.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 4.2%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A third event involved a van at 35.0 km/h with 0.3 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 2.3%, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A fourth event involved an auto-rickshaw at 18.9 km/h with 0.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5%, which remains 0.5% at an impact of 18.9 km/h.

A fifth event involved a van at 18.6 km/h with 0.8 s between pedestrian and vehicle. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.5%, which remains 0.5% at an impact of 18.6 km/h.

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing at School Lane crossing

We write about the School Lane crossing outside our school. The footage lasted 36.5 minutes and captured 21 crossings alongside 31 vehicles. A Crossing Watch review of 36.5 minutes of video (2190.0 s) measured 21 crossings and 31 vehicles at this location, with an 85th percentile speed of 58.4 km/h.

In this recording 4 of 21 crossings (1 in 5.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 21 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.4-41.9% and 1.2-30.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). During the video there were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1.5-3.0 s apart respectively.

The worst cases were as follows. One serious near-miss had a car at 20.8 km/h with 1.3 s between person and vehicle on the same spot. A second serious near-miss had a car at 13.9 km/h with 0.4 s between person and vehicle on the same spot. One close pass had an auto-rickshaw at 54.8 km/h with 2.1 s between person and vehicle on the same spot. Another close pass had a motorcycle at 53.9 km/h with 2.8 s between person and vehicle on the same spot. All gaps were post-encroachment time measured by SAM tracking with road-plane geometry.

For the 2 car cases, the Rosén & Sander 2009 figures for adults 15+ hit by a car front give an adult death risk of 0.6% at 20.8 km/h and 0.4% at 13.9 km/h, with 0.6% and 0.4% respectively at a 20 km/h impact speed; we do not apply these car-front figures to children.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 35 pedestrians and 51 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.5 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. Also 54.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 11 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 18.7 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the School Lane crossing to reduce speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements to assist your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
