To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make the crossing outside the school safer - Bridge Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Bridge Street.

Crossing Watch measurements (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) for 33.9 minutes recorded 24 crossings and 23 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.2 km/h. In total, 9 close passes were measured.

In that period 6 of 24 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 24 crossings (1 in 8) were within 1.5 s, classified as serious.

Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 9.8-46.7% for within 3 s and 2.7-32.4% for within 1.5 s (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss had a PET of 1.2 s with a car at 49.3 km/h and an adult death risk of 7.9% if hit. Another serious near-miss had a PET of 1.1 s with a motorcycle at 38.9 km/h and an adult death risk of 3.2% if hit. A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.2 s with a car at 25.0 km/h and an adult death risk of 0.9% if hit. One close pass had a PET of 1.9 s with a car at 13.5 km/h. A further close pass had a PET of 2.8 s with a car at 33.3 km/h. Death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

For context, PV² was estimated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 42 pedestrians and 41 vehicles an hour scaled from 33.9 minutes of video, with the caveat that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in a drone test and a formal check counts the full peak hour. 46.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps and 9 of them 12 s or more and longest 39.1 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school on Brook Street

We asked Crossing Watch to measure the crossing outside our school using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 36.1 minutes (2166.0 s) of video they counted 13 crossings and 26 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 km/h. The video showed 2 gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle. There were 6 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 58.6 s.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 3 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 2 cases the vehicle arrived first.

The most serious near-miss left 0.4 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that near-miss was at 48.1 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 7.1% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss left 1.0 s between pedestrian and an auto-rickshaw.
The auto-rickshaw in that near-miss was at 28.7 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 1.3% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A close pass left 1.8 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that close pass was at 50.7 km/h.
A close pass left 2.1 s between pedestrian and a bus.
The bus in that close pass was at 33.4 km/h.
A close pass left 2.5 s between pedestrian and a van.
The van in that close pass was at 15.2 km/h.

For engineering context the scaled PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 22 pedestrians and 43 vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 36.1 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice.
43.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds.

We have retained the video measurements and can share the video files on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Brook Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning the Brook Street crossing outside our school. In a video recording lasting 43.6 minutes we measured 14 crossings and 14 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 58.2 km/h.

Of the 14 crossings, 4 of 14 crossings (1 in 3.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 3 of 14 (1 in 4.7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.4-58.1% and 4.7-50.8% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.1-10.2 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss was 1.0 s apart involving an auto-rickshaw at 54.5 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 11.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). This means a child hit at the observed speeds would have an 11.9% chance of dying.
A second serious near-miss was 0.3 s apart involving a car at 50.5 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 8.7%.
A third serious near-miss was 0.4 s apart involving a motorcycle at 29.5 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.4%.
A close pass was 2.4 s apart involving a car at 46.1 km/h; for an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.2%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, being 19 pedestrians and 19 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 43.6 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one twice: 1.3x the true count in our drone test.
Also, 48.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 9 gaps, 4 of them 12 s or more, longest 25.4 s, with the caveat that the first and last are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children crossing.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review and would welcome a site inspection.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location.


Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write to request safety improvements at the crossing outside our school. Measurements from a video of the crossing were made by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time).

In 5.5 minutes of recording (330.0 s) we recorded 5 pedestrian crossings and 9 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 57.3 km/h. This change is certain to save lives at this crossing. In this recording 2 of 5 crossings (1 in 2.5) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, including 1 of 5 (1 in 5) within 1.5 s.

The most serious near-miss was an auto-rickshaw at 59.4 km/h with a gap of 1.1 s to the person on the same spot, carrying an adult death risk of 17.4% if hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). A second close pass was a car at 57.5 km/h with a gap of 1.9 s to the person on the same spot, carrying an adult death risk of 6.1% if hit by a car front.

On engineering review, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this recording is 5.5 minutes with 5 crossings and 9 vehicles, so they cannot be assessed. For gaps, 87.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 6 such gaps including 5 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 16.7 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and provide a protected crossing point.

We would be pleased to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data to help your assessment.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request to make Park Avenue crossing safer

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked for a video survey of Park Avenue crossing. In 26.1 minutes (1566.0 s) of video, 29 crossings and 38 vehicles were observed. The 85th percentile speed was 39.3 km/h.

6 of 29 crossings (1 in 4.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person and 3 of 29 (1 in 9.7) within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.0-39.7% and 2.2-27.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). There were 3 serious near-misses (less than 1.5 s apart) and 6 close passes (1.5-3.0 s).

The worst serious incidents were: a motorcycle with a gap of 1.1 s at 34.0 km/h with adult death risk if hit by a car front of 2.1% (5.2 km/h and 0.2% at 20 km/h limit); an auto-rickshaw with a gap of 0.3 s at 13.5 km/h with adult death risk of 0.3% (13.5 km/h and 0.3% at 20 km/h limit); and a bus with a gap of 1.1 s at 13.6 km/h with adult death risk of 0.3% (13.6 km/h and 0.3% at 20 km/h limit). Close passes included a bus with a gap of 2.0 s at 39.1 km/h with adult death risk of 0.8% and a car with a gap of 2.3 s at 14.2 km/h with adult death risk of 0.0%. Risk figures are from Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by car fronts.

PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 67 pedestrians and 87 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.1 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x the true count in our drone test. 62.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 10 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more, longest 49.0 s, with the first and last cut short by the video; UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds while other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone with signs at this location. We will share the full video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The worst serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s with a car travelling at 12.1 km/h. Based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by a car front, the adult death risk if hit at that speed would be 0.3%, and at a 20 km/h limit the impact speed would be 12.1 km/h with the same 0.3% risk. The road user was not reviewed.

For context, 41.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 gaps of 6 s or more, 5 of them 12 s or more, and the longest gap 22.2 s. The engineering note cautions that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video, and that PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video while this recording is 8.5 minutes with 3 pedestrian crossings and 5 moving vehicles counted.

We request a raised zebra crossing to provide a protected priority crossing and to reduce vehicle speeds at the desire point. Young pupils face a severe danger of being killed here every school day.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

To the Road Authority

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Market Street.

We arranged a video-based Crossing Watch for 36.4 minutes (2184.0 s). In that time 35 crossings and 39 vehicles were observed. 6 of 35 crossings (1 in 5.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 35 crossings (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.6-33.6% and 1.8-23.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h. These figures come from a single recording and may differ on other days.

By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart.
One serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s with a car at 57.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 14.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s with a van at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.5 s with a car at 39.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.3%.
A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
A further close pass had a PET of 2.7 s with a van at 59.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the recorded death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled adult death risks for these events would fall to 0.0%, 0.0%, 0.6%, 0.0% and 0.0% respectively.

In engineering terms, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, from 58 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 69.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 56.1 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given these measurements we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the crossing on Station Road outside our school, where we made video measurements using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time.

During 6.1 minutes (366.0 s) we observed 12 pedestrian crossings and 20 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 30.3 km/h. One near-miss ended with the vehicle hitting the person crossing.
3 of 12 crossings (1 in 4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 2 of 12 (1 in 6) within 1.5 s.
If this recording is typical, exact 95% ranges are 5.5-57.2% and 2.1-48.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

For context on gaps, 50.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 12 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more, longest 59.7 s, with the first and last cut short by the video.
PV2 and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 6.1, with 12 crossings and 20 vehicles counted.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.
We recorded 2 serious near-misses and 1 close pass.
One serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.0 s and involved a car at 29.3 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.4%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
Another serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s and involved a car at 17.3 km/h.
For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.5%, compared with 0.5% at 17.3 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.7 s and involved a van at 32.1 km/h.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and provide protected gaps.

We have the video and measurements available and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a raised zebra crossing at the crossing studied on Park Avenue crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write as the school using the crossing outside our premises. A Crossing Watch analysis of 38.6 minutes of video recorded 32 crossings and 30 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 63.7 km/h. Near-misses like these occur every morning when school opens.
In that period 5 of 32 crossings (1 in 6.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person.
Of those, 3 of 32 (1 in 11) were within 1.5 s.
The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.3-32.8% and 2.0-25.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses recorded were as follows. A bus at 58.9 km/h was 1.0 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 16.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A motorcycle at 44.4 km/h was 0.5 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 5.2%.
A car at 42.8 km/h was 1.2 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.5%.
A car at 43.2 km/h was 2.3 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.3%.
A car at 34.8 km/h was 2.6 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.0%.
Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, calculated as 50 pedestrians and 47 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.6 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and our method can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x in drone tests.
Also 72.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 8 gaps including 1 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 60.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for people crossing.
We are willing to share the underlying measurements and discuss the site in detail, and we can provide the video file on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Garden Road crossing

We write about the crossing outside our school at Garden Road crossing. Crossing Watch analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) measured 2.1 minutes (126.0 s) of video with 7 pedestrian crossings and 1 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 51.7 km/h. Many of these drivers were not watching the road at all.

PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 2.1, so rates are only indicative.

In that period there was 1 serious near-miss and 0 close passes. Serious means pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass means 1.5-3.0 s. In the 1 serious case the vehicle arrived first.

The worst was a serious near-miss with a PET of 0.7 s. The vehicle was an auto-rickshaw travelling at 45.5 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 5.7% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact speed would be 17.5 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.5%.

We request a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to reduce speeds and give priority to pedestrians.

We can share the video and measurement file on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lake View Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school asked for a video survey of the Lake View Road crossing. In 41.9 minutes (2514.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 38 crossings and 7 vehicles; the 85th percentile speed was 46.6 km/h.

Of the 38 crossings, 2 of 38 (1 in 19) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 38 (1 in 19) had a vehicle within 1.5 s. There were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes.

The worst serious near-miss was a car at 44.1 km/h passing 1.4 s after a person; based on Rosén & Sander 2009 for adults 15+ hit by a car front, the death risk at that speed is 5.1%, compared with 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit where the impact would be 0.0 km/h.

The other serious near-miss was an auto-rickshaw at 23.5 km/h passing 0.7 s from a person; for an adult hit at that speed the death risk is 0.8%, compared with 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit where the impact would be 20.0 km/h.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 54 pedestrians and 10 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 41.9 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can overcount. 44.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with 3 such gaps and a longest gap of 51.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect those crossing.

We are willing to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Park Avenue crossing outside our school. A video survey measured 8.5 minutes (510.0 s) with 10 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles.

In that recording 5 of 10 crossings (1 in 2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 4 of 10 (1 in 2.5) within 1.5 s. Pet is defined as serious when less than 1.5 s apart and close pass when 1.5-3.0 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 18.7-81.3% and 12.2-73.8% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 1.1-10.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 50.5 km/h.

The worst near-misses were:
One serious near-miss had a car at 48.9 km/h with 1.0 s between the pedestrian and vehicle. Adult death risk if hit by the car front would be 7.6% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A second serious near-miss had a car at 40.7 km/h with 1.1 s between. Adult death risk if hit would be 3.8%.
A third serious near-miss had a van at 17.3 km/h with 0.3 s between. Adult death risk if hit would be 0.5%.
A fourth serious near-miss had a car at 14.5 km/h with 1.1 s between. Adult death risk if hit would be 0.4%.
A close pass had a car at 39.1 km/h with 1.6 s between. Adult death risk if hit would be 2.6%.
At a 20 km/h limit 3 of these would have had 0.0 km/h impact and 0.0% adult death risk.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this one is 8.5 minutes with 10 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles. Also 94.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 7 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 34.0 s (the first and last are cut short by the video). UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds; other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to give pedestrians priority and reduce vehicle speeds. Most children hit at these speeds would have little chance of survival.

We can share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school – Cedar Lane

We write concerning the crossing outside our school on Cedar Lane. An independent video review (Crossing Watch, SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) observed 24.8 minutes (1488.0 s) at the site and counted 14 crossings and 19 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 59.9 km/h.

The review classified 3 events as serious, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 events as close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s. In 2 cases the person was first, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 1 case both were at once.

One serious near-miss involved a car at 52.2 km/h with a gap of 0.7 s, the closest gap recorded. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 10.0% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, which would fall to 0.2% at an impact of 8.4 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

Another serious near-miss involved a motorcycle at 50.2 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. The report notes an adult death risk of 8.5% if hit at that speed.

A third serious near-miss involved a van at 31.2 km/h with a gap of 0.0 s. The report notes an adult death risk of 1.6% if hit at that speed.

A close pass involved a car at 55.2 km/h with a gap of 2.5 s.

A further close pass involved a car at 33.1 km/h with a gap of 2.1 s.

The engineering note estimates PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 scaled from 24.8 minutes of video, noting that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice. 95.6% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, in 4 gaps with the longest 83.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location. We can share the video and measurement details for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside Brook Street crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write from the school beside Brook Street crossing. Crossing Watch video for 44.4 minutes recorded 22 crossings and 36 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 46.5 km/h. There were 10 gaps of 6 s or more and 5 gaps of 12 s or more, longest 66.7 s. During 44.4 minutes, 3 crossings had the person go first and 2 had the vehicle go first.

The video showed 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes of 1.5 to 3.0 s. One serious near-miss had a gap of 0.2 s with an auto-rickshaw at 46.4 km/h. If an adult had been hit at that speed the death risk from a car front is 6.1% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+. Another serious near-miss had a gap of 0.2 s with an auto-rickshaw at 37.9 km/h. Adult death risk at that speed is 3.0%. A third serious near-miss had a gap of 1.0 s with a van at 33.6 km/h. Adult death risk at that speed is 2.0%. One close pass had a gap of 1.5 s with a car at 28.0 km/h. Another close pass had a gap of 2.4 s with a motorcycle at 31.4 km/h.

PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 30 pedestrians and 49 vehicles per hour, scaled from 44.4 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount. 88.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location. We offer to share the full video and measurements.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the pedestrian crossing outside our school on River Lane. We arranged a Crossing Watch measurement of the crossing. In 7.0 minutes (420.0 s) it counted 11 pedestrian crossings and 10 moving vehicles, with an 85th-percentile speed of 54.4 km/h. There were 3 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes, defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s apart. Where order could be seen, 4 interactions were person-first and 1 was vehicle-first.

The severest close encounter involved a 0.3 s separation from an automobile travelling at 49.4 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled adult death risk is 7.9%, compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss was 1.2 s apart with a bus at 48.7 km/h, with a modelled adult death risk of 7.5% if hit.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and give pedestrians clear priority.

We can share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your review and would welcome a site visit to discuss the design.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitored the crossing outside it for 38.4 minutes (2304.0 s). In that time we recorded 32 crossings and 17 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 26.3 km/h. We observed 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

The serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s and involved a car at 14.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 14.2 km/h the death risk from Rosén & Sander 2009 is 0.4%.

The fastest close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.1 s and involved a van at 13.8 km/h.

A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s and involved a car at 24.6 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 50 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.4 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice, by 1.3x in our drone test. 

Also, 67.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and 7 of them 12 s or more and longest gap 33.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and to give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Park Avenue

Dear Sir/Madam,

Our school monitored the crossing outside it for 38.4 minutes (2304.0 s). In that time we recorded 32 crossings and 17 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 26.3 km/h. We observed 1 serious near-miss and 2 close passes.

By definition, a serious near-miss is when a pedestrian and a moving vehicle are on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5 to 3.0 s apart.

The serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.4 s and involved a car at 14.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at 14.2 km/h the death risk from Rosén & Sander 2009 is 0.4%.

A van travelling at 13.8 km/h was involved in a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 2.1 s.

A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s and involved a car at 24.6 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 50 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.4 minutes of video, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice, by 1.3x in our drone test. 

Also, 67.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps and 7 of them 12 s or more and longest gap 33.8 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds and to give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the video and Crossing Watch measurements to assist your assessment.

Yours faithfully,

The Principal

To the Road Authority

Dear Sir/Madam,

I write on behalf of our school about the crossing on Station Road outside the school. We arranged a video survey of 15.2 minutes (912.0 s) which recorded 12 crossings and 32 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 60.0 km/h. These near-misses happened because drivers ignored the crossing markings.

Of the 12 crossings, 5 of 12 crossings (1 in 2.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 12 crossings (1 in 4) had a vehicle within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 15.2-72.3% and 5.5-57.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

One serious near-miss involved a van with a post-encroachment time of 1.1 s at 45.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 5.5% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts). Another serious near-miss involved a car with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s at 41.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 4.0%. A third serious near-miss involved a bus with a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the estimated death risk is 0.7%.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 (47 pedestrians and 126 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 15.2 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour). Also 78.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed (the first and last gaps are cut short by the video).

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and protect children and other pedestrians.

We would be happy to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements for your engineers to review. Please let us know how you will assess this site for safety improvements.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a safer crossing outside the school on Station Road

We write following a Crossing Watch measurement at the Station Road crossing over 24.2 minutes (1452.0 s). In that time 38 crossings and 8 vehicles were recorded, the 85th percentile speed was 44.1 km/h, there were 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 7 gaps of 12 s or more with the longest gap 53.4 s, and 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more. 6 of 38 crossings (1 in 6.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 5 of 38 (1 in 7.6) within 1.5 s; exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.0-31.3% and 4.4-28.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 1.6-11.7 people in a recording this long (Poisson). Of the 6 events within 3 s, 4 were person first and 2 were vehicle first, with 5 serious near-misses less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass 1.5-3.0 s apart as defined.

The 5 serious near-misses were as follows. The closest serious near-miss involved a bus at 44.5 km/h with 1.0 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 5.2% death risk (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 39.5 km/h with 1.2 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 3.4% death risk, compared with 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 37.6 km/h with 0.3 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 2.9% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved an auto-rickshaw at 27.9 km/h with 0.7 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 1.2% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. One involved a car at 21.4 km/h with 0.5 s between the person and the vehicle; an adult hit by a car front at that speed would have faced a 0.7% death risk, compared with 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

The engineering note recorded PV² as 0.0 x 10^8 from 94 pedestrians and 20 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 24.2 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice (1.3x in our drone test). It also recorded that 89.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to slow traffic to 20 km/h and protect those crossing. We will share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements on request and welcome a site visit.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

We write regarding the safety of the crossing outside our school on Market Street.

We arranged a video-based Crossing Watch for 36.4 minutes (2184.0 s). In that time 35 crossings and 39 vehicles were observed. 6 of 35 crossings (1 in 5.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 35 crossings (1 in 12) were within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 6.6-33.6% and 1.8-23.1% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 2.2-13.1 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 57.4 km/h.

By definition a serious near-miss is less than 1.5 s apart and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart.
The closest serious near-miss had a PET of 0.7 s with a car at 57.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 14.9% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+).
A second serious near-miss had a PET of 1.0 s with a van at 47.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.6%.
A third serious near-miss had a PET of 0.5 s with a car at 39.2 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 3.3%.
A close pass had a PET of 1.8 s with a car at 21.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 0.3%.
A further close pass had a PET of 2.7 s with a van at 59.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front the recorded death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled adult death risks for these events would fall to 0.0%, 0.0%, 0.6%, 0.0% and 0.0% respectively.

In engineering terms, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, from 58 pedestrians and 64 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.4 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour. 69.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 10 such gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more and the longest 56.1 s; the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

Given these measurements we request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We are willing to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

Re: Safety at North Avenue crossing

We are writing to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our school.

Measurements from a Crossing Watch survey over 6.9 minutes (414.0 s) recorded 11 pedestrian crossings and 7 moving vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 50.5 km/h.

The most serious event had a post-encroachment time of 0.2 s and involved a car at 16.9 km/h.

The closest near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 2.2 s and involved a motorcycle at 44.4 km/h.

A separate close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.6 s and involved a bus at 17.6 km/h.

For the car event, published figures for adults hit by a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+) give an adult death risk if hit of 0.5% at 16.9 km/h.

Engineering context carries caveats: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this video is 6.9 minutes, and 81.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more (4 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 41.7 s) with the first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that the road authority install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and protect children crossing.

We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We would be pleased to share the Crossing Watch recording and measurements for your review and to discuss the site further.

Yours faithfully,

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the crossing outside our school on Ring Road, where Crossing Watch analysis using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 8 moving vehicles in 6.1 minutes (366.0 s).

The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 km/h.

Overall, 3 of 8 crossings (1 in 2.7) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 1 of 8 (1 in 8) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 8.5-75.5% and 0.3-52.7% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The most serious near-miss was an auto-rickshaw at 19.5 km/h with a gap of 1.3 s, with an adult death risk of 0.6% if hit by a car front at that speed (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), which would remain 0.6% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 19.5 km/h.

The closest near-miss was a motorcycle at 48.1 km/h with a gap of 1.7 s, with an adult death risk of 4.5% if hit by a car front at that speed, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

A third near-miss was a van at 35.6 km/h with a gap of 2.8 s, with an adult death risk of 0.0% if hit by a car front at that speed, which would be 0.0% at a 20 km/h limit with an impact speed of 0.0 km/h.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 6.1 minutes, so they were not calculated. 64.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 3 such gaps and a longest gap of 10.2 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.

We are happy to share the underlying video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on Canal Road

Dear Sir/Madam,

On behalf of our school, I write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our premises.

A recording lasting 19.7 minutes counted 37 crossings and 9 vehicles. Of those crossings, 3 of 37 (1 in 12) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s, and 2 of 37 (1 in 18) within 1.5 s. There were 3 serious near-misses with a gap of less than 1.5 s and 1 close pass between 1.5 s and 3.0 s. One serious near-miss left 0.3 s between the person and a motorcycle at 52.0 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 9.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss left 0.5 s between the person and a van at 21.4 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.7%. The close pass left 2.7 s between the person and an auto-rickshaw at 30.3 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 113 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 19.7 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount. 69.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The site record is described as Canal Road crossing.

We request the raised zebra crossing with speed table to lower vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing. We are willing to share the underlying video-derived measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside school on Canal Road

Dear Sir/Madam,

On behalf of our school, I write to request a raised zebra crossing with speed table outside our premises.

A recording lasting 19.7 minutes counted 37 crossings and 9 vehicles. Of those crossings, 3 of 37 (1 in 12) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s, and 2 of 37 (1 in 18) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 1.7-21.9% and 0.7-18.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). The 85th percentile speed was 52.4 km/h. There were 9 gaps of 6 s or more and 0 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 7.1 s.

We logged 2 serious near-misses with a gap of less than 1.5 s plus 1 close pass between 1.5 s and 3.0 s. One serious near-miss left 0.3 s between the person and a motorcycle at 52.0 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 9.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.6% at 20.0 km/h. Another serious near-miss left 0.5 s between the person and a van at 21.4 km/h. At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.7%. The close pass left 2.7 s between the person and an auto-rickshaw at 30.3 km/h.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 113 pedestrians and 27 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 19.7 minutes of video; a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can overcount. 69.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video. The site record is described as Canal Road crossing.

We request the raised zebra crossing with speed table to lower vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing. We are willing to share the underlying video-derived measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for a raised zebra crossing at the crossing studied on Park Avenue crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write as the school using the crossing outside our premises. A Crossing Watch analysis of 38.6 minutes of video recorded 32 crossings and 30 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 63.7 km/h.
In that period 5 of 32 crossings (1 in 6.4) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person.
Of those, 3 of 32 (1 in 11) were within 1.5 s.
The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.3-32.8% and 2.0-25.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The worst near-misses recorded were as follows. A person and a bus moving at 58.9 km/h occupied the same spot 1.0 s apart; the modelled adult death risk if struck by a car front at that speed is 16.8% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).
A motorcycle at 44.4 km/h was 0.5 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 5.2%.
A car at 42.8 km/h was 1.2 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 4.5%.
A car at 43.2 km/h was 2.3 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.3%.
A car at 34.8 km/h was 2.6 s from a person on the same spot; the modelled adult death risk if hit by a car front at that speed is 0.0%.
Serious is defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart; close pass is 1.5-3.0 s.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, calculated as 50 pedestrians and 47 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 38.6 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and our method can overcount pedestrians by 1.3x in drone tests.
Also 72.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 8 gaps including 1 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 60.4 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority for people crossing.
We are willing to share the underlying measurements and discuss the site in detail, and we can provide the video file on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Re: Safety at Garden Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We are writing about the pedestrian crossing outside our school at Garden Road crossing.

Crossing Watch video (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) recorded 3.2 minutes (192.0 s) at the crossing. In that time there were 9 pedestrian crossings and 5 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 58.0 km/h. These results satisfy the official criteria for a pedestrian signal at this spot.

5 of 9 crossings (1 in 1.8) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3.0 s of the person, and 2 of 9 (1 in 4.5) within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges if this recording is typical are 21.2-86.3% and 2.8-60.0% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Of the near-misses, 2 were serious (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 were close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 3 cases the person was first, in 2 cases the vehicle was first, and in 0 cases both were at once.

The worst events were:

The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.1 s. The vehicle was a bus at 59.4 km/h.
At that speed the risk of death for an adult hit by a car front is 17.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+). At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact speed would be 20.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.6%.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 1.3 s. The vehicle was a motorcycle at 33.3 km/h.
At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 2.0%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.0%.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s. The vehicle was a van at 50.7 km/h.
At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.4%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.0%.

Another close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s. The vehicle was a bus at 33.4 km/h.
At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.0%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.0%.

A further close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.9 s. The vehicle was a car at 35.3 km/h.
At that speed the adult death risk if hit is 0.0%. At a 20.0 km/h limit the impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.0%.

On engineering context: PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video, this recording is only 3.2 minutes with 9 pedestrian crossings and 5 moving vehicles. 80.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 6 gaps, 5 of them 12 s or more, longest 68.5 s (the first and last gaps are cut short by the video). UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds, other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request a raised zebra crossing on a speed table with 20 km/h zone signs and markings at Garden Road crossing to reduce speeds and provide priority for people crossing.

We would be pleased to share the video and the full measurements for your review and to discuss next steps.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We would be pleased to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing outside our school on Brook Street

We asked Crossing Watch to measure the crossing outside our school using SAM tracking, road-plane geometry and post-encroachment time. In 36.1 minutes (2166.0 s) of video they counted 13 crossings and 26 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 47.9 km/h. There were 6 gaps of 6 s or more, 2 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 58.6 s.

By definition a serious near-miss is pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and a close pass is 1.5-3.0 s apart. Our footage captured 2 serious near-misses along with 3 close passes. In 3 cases the person arrived first and in 2 cases the vehicle arrived first.

The most serious near-miss left 0.4 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that near-miss was at 48.1 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 7.1% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts).

A second serious near-miss left 1.0 s between pedestrian and an auto-rickshaw.
The auto-rickshaw in that near-miss was at 28.7 km/h.
At that speed an adult hit by a car front has a 1.3% death risk, compared with 0.6% death risk at an impact of 20.0 km/h.

A close pass left 1.8 s between pedestrian and a car.
The car in that close pass was at 50.7 km/h.
A close pass left 2.1 s between pedestrian and a bus.
The bus in that close pass was at 33.4 km/h.
A close pass left 2.5 s between pedestrian and a van.
The van in that close pass was at 15.2 km/h.

For engineering context the scaled PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 from 22 pedestrians and 43 vehicles an hour, but this is scaled from 36.1 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice.
43.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you provide a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this crossing to reduce vehicle speeds.

We have retained the video measurements and can share the video files on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write regarding the crossing outside our school on Lantern Road. We had 41.9 minutes of video reviewed by Crossing Watch (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time). In that time 22 people crossed and 29 vehicles passed, with an 85th percentile speed of 51.8 km/h.

The review found 6 serious near-misses (pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart) and 3 close passes (1.5-3.0 s), with person first in 2 cases and vehicle first in 4 cases.

The worst events were:
A serious near-miss with a gap of 0.2 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 51.0 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 9.1% (0.6% at 20.0 km/h impact).
A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.4 s involving a car at 44.5 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 5.2%.
A serious near-miss with a gap of 1.1 s involving a car at 44.2 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 5.1%.
A close pass with a gap of 1.9 s involving a van at 22.6 km/h, carrying an adult death risk if hit of 0.2%.
A close pass with a gap of 2.2 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 28.1 km/h.
All death-risk figures are for adults hit by a car front from Rosén & Sander 2009.

For engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 for 32 pedestrians and 42 moving vehicles an hour, scaled from 41.9 minutes of video while a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. 81.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 6 gaps of 6 s or more and 2 of 12 s or more and a longest gap of 75.2 s, with first and last gaps cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this crossing to lower speeds and provide a protected crossing point.

We have the video and tracking data and are happy to share them for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,

LETTER:
To the Road Authority
Subject: Request for safety improvement at Ring Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write about the Ring Road crossing outside our school. A video survey of 33.9 minutes recorded 37 crossings and 1 moving vehicle. The 85th percentile speed was 24.6 km/h. In the near-miss with a time gap of 2.4 s, the car reached the spot before the pedestrian. There were 8 gaps of 6 s or more, including 6 gaps of 12 s or more, with the longest gap 39.3 s, and 66.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more.

Of the 37 crossings, 1 of 37 had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 0 of 37 within 1.5 s. The exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 0.1-14.2% and 0.0-9.5% of crossings and 0.0-5.6 and 0.0-3.7 people in a recording this long. By definition serious means less than 1.5 s and close pass means 1.5-3.0 s.

The worst event was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 2.4 s. The vehicle was a car travelling at 17.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed, Rosén & Sander 2009 estimates a death risk of 0.0%. At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact speed would be 0.0 km/h with an adult death risk of 0.0%.

For context, the observed flow scales to PV² = 0.0 x 10^8 from 65 pedestrians and 2 moving vehicles an hour, with the caveat that this is scaled from 33.9 minutes and a formal check counts the full peak hour and that broken tracks can count one person twice at 1.3x the true count in our drone test. IRC:103-2012 cl. 6.7.4.1.2 notes a controlled crossing may be warranted above 1 x 10^8 on an undivided road and 2 x 10^8 on a divided road. Also, 66.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you provide a raised zebra crossing at this location. We would be pleased to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir or Madam,

We write about safety at the Orchard Lane crossing outside our school. A 10.0 minute video recording was analysed with SAM tracking and road-plane geometry.

In that 10.0 minutes there were 12 pedestrian crossings and 3 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 25.4 km/h. Most vehicles through the crossing were exceeding the posted speed limit. Overall, 1 of 12 crossings (1 in 12) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 12 (1 in 12) had a vehicle within 1.5 s. If this recording is typical, the exact 95% ranges are 0.2-38.5% and 0.2-38.5% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.0-5.6 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

Of these, 1 was a serious near-miss as defined by less than 1.5 s apart and 0 were close passes of 1.5-3.0 s. The worst case was a serious interaction with a gap of 1.3 s between the person and a motorcycle. The motorcycle speed was 25.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 1.0% based on Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+.

At a 20 km/h limit the estimated impact speed in that case would be 15.1 km/h. The corresponding adult death risk if hit by a car front would be 0.4%.

For engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is 10.0 minutes, so that assessment cannot be made reliably from this sample. 67.1% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 11 gaps of 6 s or more and 4 gaps of 12 s or more, the longest 70.6 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow vehicles and give pedestrian priority.

We are happy to share the video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the road authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Mill Street crossing

We write about pedestrian safety outside our school at the Mill Street crossing. Crossing Watch measured the site for 29.6 minutes (1776.0 s) and recorded 33 crossings and 21 vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 57.9 km/h. Over half of the drivers observed were exceeding the posted speed limit.

In that period there was 1 serious near-miss, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 2 close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. The most serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.9 s involving a bus at 57.2 km/h. A second event was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s involving a van at 15.7 km/h. A third event was a close pass with a post-encroachment time of 2.9 s involving a bus at 55.8 km/h. The adult death-risk figures if hit by a car front are from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, with the highest risk in these events given as 14.8%.

The engineering estimates for context were PV² = 0.0 x 10^8 based on 67 pedestrians and 43 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 29.6 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour. 63.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 12 gaps observed, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide a protected crossing point.

We are happy to share the video and underlying measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Station Road crossing

We write as the school by Station Road crossing. Speeds have been rising every month and a child will be killed here within weeks without action. A Crossing Watch video survey of 28.5 minutes, duration 1710.0 s, recorded 7 crossings and 26 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 47.0 km/h.

The review found 2 serious near-misses defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 2 close passes defined as 1.5-3.0 s apart. Of 4 events, 1 was person first, 2 were vehicle first and 1 was both at once.

The most severe event was a serious near-miss with a car at 39.7 km/h and a gap of 0.0 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 3.5% per Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

Another serious near-miss involved an auto-rickshaw at 36.5 km/h with a gap of 0.3 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 2.6%, falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h in a 20 km/h zone.

One close pass involved a bus at 47.1 km/h with a gap of 1.7 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 4.1%.

One close pass involved a motorcycle at 34.8 km/h with a gap of 1.7 s. At that speed the adult death risk if hit by a car front is 1.4%.

For context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 15 pedestrians and 55 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 28.5 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count 1.3x high in our drone test. Also 57.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 10 gaps, 10 of them 12 s or more, longest 68.9 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with a 20 km/h zone and signs at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected crossing time.

We can share the full video and measurements for your review and welcome a joint site inspection.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Park Avenue crossing

We write from the school regarding the crossing outside our premises at Park Avenue crossing. A Crossing Watch analysis of 186.0 s of video recorded 8 pedestrian crossings and 19 moving vehicles. In that period, 6 of 8 crossings had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 5 of 8 were within 1.5 s and are classified as serious near-misses, with 1 additional close pass between 1.5 s and 3.0 s.

The 85th percentile speed was 59.6 km/h. The drivers involved were speeding because they were late for work. Of the 8 crossings, in 2 cases the person crossed first and in 4 cases the vehicle passed first.

The worst near-misses were as follows. One serious near-miss involved a car at 58.0 km/h with 0.6 s between road users; for an adult hit at that speed the estimated death risk is 15.7% from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts, compared to 0.3% at an impact speed of 12.6 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. Another serious near-miss involved a bus at 46.7 km/h with 0.6 s between road users; the adult death risk estimate is 6.3%, compared to 0.6% at 20.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. A third serious near-miss involved a car at 36.0 km/h with 1.3 s between road users; the adult death risk estimate is 2.5%, compared to 0.0% at 0.0 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. A fourth serious near-miss involved a bus at 19.2 km/h with 0.8 s between road users; the adult death risk estimate is 0.6%, unchanged at 19.2 km/h if limited to 20 km/h. A fifth serious near-miss involved a car at 14.1 km/h with 0.3 s between road users; the adult death risk estimate is 0.4%, unchanged at 14.1 km/h if limited to 20 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this recording is only 3.1 minutes, so no hourly rate is relied upon. In the recording, 98.9% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, comprising 2 gaps, 1 of them 12 s or more, with the longest gap 37.0 s.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table and 20 km/h zone signs at this location to reduce speeds and protect people crossing.

We are willing to share the full video and measurement data for your review and to meet on site.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir / Madam,

Crossing Watch tracked 13 crossings and 34 vehicles in 36.4 minutes on River Lane, with 85th speed of 57.9 km/h.

5 of 13 crossings (1 in 2.6) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person; 3 of 13 (1 in 4.3) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical: 13.9-68.4% and 5.0-53.8% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson); 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

A motorcycle passed within 0.1 s of a person at 51.4 km/h, with 9.4% adult death risk if hit by a car front per Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

A bus passed within 0.9 s of a person at 22.6 km/h, with 0.8% adult death risk if hit by a car front per Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

A car passed within 1.7 s of a person at 27.4 km/h, with 0.7% adult death risk if hit by a car front per Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

An auto-rickshaw passed within 1.9 s of a person at 33.8 km/h, with 0.7% adult death risk if hit by a car front per Rosen and Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

PV2 was 0.0 x 10^8 from 21 pedestrians and 56 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.4 minutes, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour.

46.7% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed: 10 gaps, 6 of them 12 s or more, longest 20.6 s, noting video edge truncation.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table on River Lane.

We offer to share the video for review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The closest pass was a close pass with a pet of 1.7 s and a car at 21.4 km/h; the adult death risk if hit at that speed is 0.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact would be 8.9 km/h with death risk 0.2%. We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table to reduce speeds at the crossing.

We are happy to share the video and measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safer crossing at School Lane crossing

We write about the School Lane crossing outside our school. A Crossing Watch review of 36.5 minutes of video (2190.0 s) measured 21 crossings and 31 vehicles at this location, with an 85th percentile speed of 58.4 km/h.

In this recording 4 of 21 crossings (1 in 5.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person, and 2 of 21 (1 in 10) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.4-41.9% and 1.2-30.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson), and 1.1-10.2 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson). During the video there were 2 serious near-misses and 2 close passes, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1.5-3.0 s apart respectively.

The worst cases were as follows. The closest serious near-miss had a car at 20.8 km/h with 1.3 s between person and vehicle on the same spot. A second serious near-miss had a car at 13.9 km/h with 0.4 s between person and vehicle on the same spot. One close pass had an auto-rickshaw at 54.8 km/h with 2.1 s between person and vehicle on the same spot. Another close pass had a motorcycle at 53.9 km/h with 2.8 s between person and vehicle on the same spot. All gaps were post-encroachment time measured by SAM tracking with road-plane geometry.

For the 2 car cases, the Rosén & Sander 2009 figures for adults 15+ hit by a car front give an adult death risk of 0.6% at 20.8 km/h and 0.4% at 13.9 km/h, with 0.6% and 0.4% respectively at a 20 km/h impact speed; we do not apply these car-front figures to children.

For context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8 based on 35 pedestrians and 51 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 36.5 minutes of video, noting a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one person twice. Also 54.4% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with 11 gaps, 3 of them 12 s or more, longest 18.7 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at the School Lane crossing to reduce speeds and provide priority for pedestrians.

We are willing to share the video and the Crossing Watch measurements to assist your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

The Principal

We can share the video and measurements on request.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Quarry Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of our school regarding the Quarry Road crossing.

During 26.9 minutes of video (1614.0 s) Crossing Watch recorded 13 pedestrian crossings and 4 moving vehicles at the crossing. The 85th percentile speed was 51.4 km/h. In that period 3 of 13 crossings (1 in 4.3) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 2 of 13 (1 in 6.5) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 5.0-53.8% and 1.9-45.4% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 0.6-8.8 and 0.2-7.2 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

There were 2 serious near-misses where pedestrian and moving vehicle were on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart and 1 close pass at 1.5-3.0 s.

One serious near-miss involved a bus at 26.9 km/h with 0.3 s between road users on the same spot.
An auto-rickshaw travelling at 13.3 km/h featured in another serious near-miss with 0.5 s between road users on the same spot.
A close pass involved a van at 50.6 km/h with 2.2 s between road users on the same spot.
The estimated adult death risk if hit by a car front at those speeds is 1.1% for the bus case, 0.3% for the auto-rickshaw case and 1.2% for the van case, from Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts.

For engineering context, PV² was calculated as 0.0 x 10^8 from 29 pedestrians and 9 moving vehicles an hour scaled from 26.9 minutes, with the caveat that a formal check counts the full peak hour and broken tracks can count one pedestrian twice.
74.8% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 4 such gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more and longest 24.4 s, with the caveat that the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to slow approaching traffic and protect children crossing.

We have the video and SAM tracking data and are happy to share it for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir / Madam,

Re: Safety at Lake View Road crossing

In a Crossing Watch video of 33.6 minutes (2016.0 s) we measured 6 pedestrian crossings and 33 vehicles with an 85th percentile speed of 43.6 km/h.

5 of 6 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person. 3 of 6 (1 in 2) were within 1.5 s.
Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 35.9-99.6% and 11.8-88.2% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 1.6-11.7 and 0.6-8.8 people in a recording this long (Poisson).

The 3 serious near-misses and 2 close passes were:
The closest serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s and involved a car at 35.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 2.3% for a car front (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+), falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.8 s and involved a car at 33.4 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 2.0% for a car front, falling to 0.6% at an impact of 20.0 km/h.
A third serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.7 s and involved a car at 17.8 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.5% for a car front, remaining 0.5% at an impact of 17.8 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.7 s and involved a car at 22.2 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.1% at an impact of 3.3 km/h.
One close pass had a post-encroachment time of 2.3 s and involved a bus at 44.8 km/h, with an adult death risk if hit of 0.4% for a car front, falling to 0.0% at an impact of 0.0 km/h.

On engineering context, PV² was 0.0 x 10^8, but this is scaled from only 33.6 minutes of video and a formal check counts the full peak hour with caveats about broken tracks.
73.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, with 8 gaps of 6 s or more and 8 of 12 s or more and longest gap 76.8 s, but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce vehicle speeds and provide protected priority.

We can share the full video and tracking data for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Dear Sir/Madam,

We write concerning safety at the Canal Road crossing. A Crossing Watch analysis (SAM tracking, road-plane geometry, post-encroachment time) of 2.1 minutes (126.0 s) recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 11 vehicles.
The 85th percentile speed was 52.5 km/h.

In that period there were 2 serious near-misses, defined as pedestrian and moving vehicle on the same spot less than 1.5 s apart, and 1 close pass defined as 1.5 s to 3.0 s.

The serious near-miss of highest severity showed 0.8 s of post-encroachment time involving a car moving at 46.8 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the death risk is 6.4% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), compared with 0.2% at an impact speed of 5.0 km/h under a 20 km/h limit.

A second serious near-miss had a post-encroachment time of 0.3 s with an auto-rickshaw travelling at 23.9 km/h.

A close pass had a post-encroachment time of 1.6 s with a car travelling at 35.6 km/h.

On engineering use, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video; this video is 2.1 minutes. About 82.5% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more.

We request installation of a raised zebra crossing at this location to reduce speeds and give pedestrians priority.
We would be pleased to share the video for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

To the Road Authority

We are writing about the crossing outside our school at Park Avenue crossing.

In a video of 16.8 minutes (1008.0 s) there were 35 crossings and 10 vehicles, with an 85th percentile speed of 57.3 km/h. A second serious near miss involved a motorcycle at 20.7 km/h with 0.0 s between road users. At that speed the published adult death risk if hit by a car front is 0.6%, also 0.6% at 20.0 km/h.

Preliminary engineering notes, with caveats, are that PV² was scaled to 0.0 x 10^8 from 125 pedestrians and 36 moving vehicles an hour based on 16.8 minutes of video, while a formal check counts the full peak hour and our test showed tracking can count 1.3x the true pedestrian count, and that 94.2% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more (3 gaps, 0 of them 12 s or more, longest 7.7 s), but the first and last gaps are cut short by the video.

We request that you install a raised zebra crossing with a speed table at this location.

We can share the video and measurements on request and would welcome a site meeting.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

Yours faithfully,
The Principal

LETTER:
To the Road Authority

Subject: Request for safety improvement at Lantern Road crossing

Dear Sir/Madam,

On the basis of a 9.7 minute video (582.0 s) at Lantern Road crossing we recorded 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles. The 85th percentile speed was 53.0 km/h. In that recording 6 of 7 crossings (1 in 1.2) had a moving vehicle through the same spot within 3 s of the person and 1 of 7 (1 in 7) within 1.5 s. Exact 95% ranges, if this recording is typical, are 42.1-99.6% and 0.4-57.9% of crossings (Clopper-Pearson) and 2.2-13.1 and 0.0-5.6 people in a recording this long (Poisson). By the study definition, 6 were serious (less than 1.5 s apart) and 5 were close passes (1.5-3.0 s). In 3 cases the person was first and in 3 cases the vehicle was first.

The worst cases measured by post-encroachment time were:
A serious near-miss with PET of 0.3 s involving a car at 44.1 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 5.1% (Rosén & Sander 2009, adults 15+, car fronts), and at 20.0 km/h impact it would be 0.6%.
A close pass with PET of 2.2 s involving a bus at 53.6 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.7%.
A close pass with PET of 1.6 s involving an auto-rickshaw at 33.0 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 1.5%.
A close pass with PET of 2.1 s involving a car at 22.7 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
A close pass with PET of 2.4 s involving a bus at 31.3 km/h. For an adult hit by a car front at that speed the modelled death risk is 0.0%.
At a 20 km/h limit the modelled impact and death risk for the last 4 cases would each be 0.0 km/h and 0.0%.

For context, PV² and hourly rates need at least 15 minutes of video and this one is 9.7 minutes, with 7 pedestrian crossings and 28 moving vehicles counted. With that caveat, 93.0% of the time was inside gaps of 6 s or more with no moving vehicle where people crossed, based on 9 gaps, 2 of them 12 s or more, longest 51.0 s, noting the first and last gaps are cut short by the video and that the UK Traffic Signs Manual ch. 6 (13.5.2) notes 4-6 s is an acceptable gap at urban speeds and other groups, such as children, may need 10-12 s or longer.

We request you install a raised zebra crossing with speed table at this location to reduce approach speeds and establish pedestrian priority.

We are willing to share the video and the SAM tracking measurements for your review.

Yours faithfully,
The Principal
